self.pctl.OpenPlotfile( layer_info[0], pcbnew.PLOT_FORMAT_GERBER, layer_info[2]) self.pctl.PlotLayer() self.pctl.ClosePlot() def get_netlist_file(self, temp_dir): drlwriter = pcbnew.EXCELLON_WRITER(self.board) drlwriter.SetOptions( False, True, self.board.GetDesignSettings().GetAuxOrigin(), False) drlwriter.SetFormat(False) drlwriter.CreateDrillandMapFilesSet(self.pctl.GetPlotDirName(), True, False) netlist_writer = pcbnew.IPC356D_WRITER(self.board) netlist_writer.Write(os.path.join(temp_dir, netlistFilename)) def get_components_file(self, temp_dir): if hasattr(self.board, 'GetModules'): footprints = list(self.board.GetModules()) else: footprints = list(self.board.GetFootprints()) footprints.sort(key=lambda x: x.GetReference()) for i, f in enumerate(footprints): try: footprint_name = str(f.GetFPID().GetFootprintName()) except AttributeError: footprint_name = str(f.GetFPID().GetLibItemName()) layer = { pcbnew.F_Cu: 'top', pcbnew.B_Cu: 'bottom', }.get(f.GetLayer()) f_attrs = f.GetAttributes() parsed_attrs = self.parse_attrs(f_attrs) mount_type = 'smt' if parsed_attrs['smd'] else 'tht' placed = not parsed_attrs['not_in_bom'] rotation = f.GetOrientation().AsDegrees() if hasattr(f.GetOrientation(), 'AsDegrees') else f.GetOrientation() / 10.0 designator = f.GetReference() pos_x = (f.GetPosition()[0] - self.board.GetDesignSettings().GetAuxOrigin()[0]) / 1000000.0 pos_y = (f.GetPosition()[1] - self.board.GetDesignSettings().GetAuxOrigin()[1]) * -1.0 / 1000000.0 mpn = self.get_mpn_from_footprint(f) pack = self.get_pack_from_footprint(f) if pack: footprint_name = pack value = f.GetValue() self.components.append({ 'pos_x': pos_x, 'pos_y': pos_y, 'rotation': rotation, 'side': layer, 'designator': designator, 'mpn': mpn, 'pack': footprint_name, 'value': value, 'mount_type': mount_type, 'place': placed }) is_exist_bom = False for exist_bom in self.bom: if exist_bom['mpn'] == mpn and exist_bom['pack'] == footprint_name and exist_bom['value'] == value: exist_bom['designator'] += ', ' + designator exist_bom['quantity'] += 1 is_exist_bom = True if is_exist_bom == False and placed == True: self.bom.append({ 'designator': designator, 'quantity': 1, 'value': value, 'pack': footprint_name, 'mpn': mpn, 'mount_type': mount_type }) if len(self.components) > 0: with open((os.path.join(temp_dir, positionsFilename)), 'w', newline='', encoding='utf-8-sig') as outfile: csvobj = csv.writer(outfile) csvobj.writerow(self.components[0].keys()) for component in self.components: if ('**' not in component['designator']): csvobj.writerow(component.values()) if len(self.bom) > 0: with open((os.path.join(temp_dir, bomFilename)), 'w', newline='', encoding='utf-8-sig') as outfile: csvobj = csv.writer(outfile) csvobj.writerow(self.bom[0].keys()) for component in self.bom: if ('**' not in component['designator']): csvobj.writerow(component.values()) def get_gerber_parameter(self): boardWidth = pcbnew.ToMM(self.board.GetBoardEdgesBoundingBox().GetWidth()) boardHeight = pcbnew.ToMM(self.board.GetBoardEdgesBoundingBox().GetHeight()) if hasattr(self.board, 'GetCopperLayerCount'): boardLayer = self.board.GetCopperLayerCount() gerberData = {'boardWidth':boardWidth,'boardHeight':boardHeight,'boardLayer':boardLayer} return gerberData def get_name(self): p_name = self.board.GetFileName() return p_name def parse_attrs(self, attrs): return {} if not isinstance(attrs, int) else { 'tht': self.parse_attr_flag(attrs, pcbnew.FP_THROUGH_HOLE), 'smd': self.parse_attr_flag(attrs, pcbnew.FP_SMD), 'not_in_pos': self.parse_attr_flag(attrs, pcbnew.FP_EXCLUDE_FROM_POS_FILES), 'not_in_bom': self.parse_attr_flag(attrs, pcbnew.FP_EXCLUDE_FROM_BOM), 'not_in_plan': self.parse_attr_flag(attrs, pcbnew.FP_BOARD_ONLY) } def get_mpn_from_footprint(self, f): keys = ['mpn', 'MPN', 'Mpn', 'PCBWay_MPN' ,'part number', 'Part Number', 'Part No.', 'Mfr. Part No.', 'Mfg Part'] for key in keys: try: if f.HasField(key): return f.GetFieldByName(key).GetText() except Exception as e: if f.HasProperty(key): return f.GetProperty(key) def get_pack_from_footprint(self, f): keys = ['pack', 'PACK', 'Pack', 'package' ,'PACKAGE', 'Package', 'case', 'CASE', 'Case'] for key in keys: try: if f.HasField(key): return f.GetFieldByName(key).GetText() except Exception as e: if f.HasProperty(key): return f.GetProperty(key) def parse_attr_flag(self, attr, mask): return mask == (attr & mask) Upload photo 0 /10000 You can upload up to 5 images! Verify Now Blog > PCBWay Plug-In for KiCad PCBWay Plug-In for KiCad by: Anson Apr 01,2022 Posted in News Kicad PCB design Send your layout to PCBWay for instant production with just one click. Have you ever thought that when you complete the design on KiCad, you can place an order on pcbway with just one click? Now this idea is finally achieved (it's not an April Fool's joke). When you click PCBWay Plug-in button on Kicad, we will export these files in your project ( Please make sure you have installed the latest version of the plugin released at 2026 )： 1.Gerber files in correct format for production 2.IPC-Netlist file 3.Bom-file that includes all information of components 4.Pick and Place-file used in assembly You can click "Save to Cart" to place an order immediately after uploading the files( usually only takes a few seconds), our engineers will double check the files before the production. Note:We have updated plugin for Kicad 10,you could also place assembly order directly now. But we need to get the component "Manufacture Part Number". Please confirm you run the "Update Board from Schematic" and install the latest version of the plugin. ﻿ Installation from the official KiCad repositories Just open the "Plugin and Content Manager" from the KiCad main menu an install the "PCBWay Plug-in for KiCad" plugin from the selection list. Manual installation You can also download the latest ZIP file from https://github.com/pcbway/PCBWay-Plug-in-for-Kicad , then open the "Plugin and Content Manager" from the main window of KiCad and install the ZIP file via "Install from File". About Bom We can get all information of components used in your design ( please make sure you have installed the latest version of the plugin) . In order to speed up the quotation of components, we need this information: 1. Designator (necessary) 2. Quantity (necessary) 3. MPN/Part Number (necessary) 4. Package/Footprint (necessary) 5. Manufacturer (optional) 6. Description/value (optional) You just need to add the properties in your schematic like the picture shows: As a sponsor of KiCad, we will always support its development. Note: Thanks to the open source community. Since we are not skilled enough to edit on github at the moment, any feedback or questions please contact with anson@pcbway.com Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > PCBWay to Exhibit at SIDO Lyon 2026: Meet Us at Booth E122 PCBWay to Exhibit at SIDO Lyon 2026: Meet Us at Booth E122 by: Mila Sep 07,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in News As smart technologies continue to transform industrial products and connected devices, reliable hardware manufacturing has become an essential part of turning innovative concepts into real-world products. From September 16 to 17, 2026, SIDO Lyon 2026 will bring together technology providers, industrial companies, startups, and innovation professionals at the Lyon Convention Centre in France. The event focuses on the convergence of IoT, Artificial Intelligence, Robotics, and Extended Reality (XR), with a strong emphasis on practical industrial applications and digital transformation. PCBWay will be exhibiting at Booth E122. We warmly invite you to visit us and explore how our manufacturing services can support your next hardware project. PCBWay at SIDO Lyon 2026 Event: SIDO Lyon 2026 Date: September 16–17, 2026 Venue: Lyon Convention Centre, Cité Internationale, Lyon, France Booth: E122 SIDO Lyon is designed to connect technology solutions with companies working on real-world digitalization and Industry 4.0 projects. The 2026 edition is expected to bring together more than 300 exhibitors, with technologies covering IoT, AI, robotics, digital twins, XR, cybersecurity, and prototyping. For hardware developers, these technologies ultimately depend on one critical foundation: reliable physical products that can move efficiently from concept to production. From Prototype to Production Developing an IoT device, robotic system, industrial controller, or smart product often involves more than designing a PCB. Hardware teams may need to coordinate electronics, mechanical components, enclosures, prototypes, and final assembly throughout the development process. PCBWay provides a range of manufacturing services to support these requirements, including: PCB Manufacturing PCB Assembly (PCBA) HDI and Flex PCB Rigid-Flex PCB CNC Machining 3D Printing Injection Molding Sheet Metal Fabrication Box Build Assembly This integrated approach helps hardware teams reduce the complexity of working with multiple manufacturing suppliers and makes it easier to move from an initial prototype toward small-batch and production manufacturing. Meet PCBWay at Booth E122 If you are attending SIDO Lyon 2026, come and visit PCBWay at Booth E122. Verify Now Blog > Turning Student Ideas into Real Projects with the PCBWay Future Innovators Program Turning Student Ideas into Real Projects with the PCBWay Future Innovators Program by: Mila Sep 15,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in News For students, turning an engineering idea into a working prototype is an important part of learning. But moving from a schematic or CAD model to a manufactured product can be challenging when budget and access to manufacturing resources are limited. The PCBWay Future Innovators Program is designed to help students and educational institutions bridge that gap. By providing manufacturing support for eligible educational and non-commercial projects, PCBWay helps students gain hands-on experience and turn their ideas into real, testable hardware. Why Hands-On Manufacturing Matters for Students Engineering education goes beyond textbooks and simulations. Designing a circuit, creating a PCB, building a mechanical enclosure, and testing a working prototype allow students to understand how engineering concepts translate into real-world products. For many student projects, however, manufacturing can become a practical challenge. Prototype costs, limited access to equipment, and the difficulty of producing small quantities may prevent students from taking a project beyond the design stage. This is where manufacturing support can make a difference. With the Future Innovators Program, eligible students can receive support for projects related to education, research, competitions, graduation projects, open-source development, and social-impact innovation. Supporting Student Projects from PCB to Prototype The program is intended to support more than just PCB fabrication. Eligible manufacturing charges can include: PCB manufacturing PCBA assembly services 3D printing CNC machining Sheet metal fabrication Other approved in-house manufacturing services This gives students more flexibility when developing complete prototypes that combine electronics, mechanical parts, and enclosures. For example, a robotics team may need a custom PCB, CNC-machined structural parts, and 3D-printed components. A student developing an IoT device may need both PCB assembly and a custom enclosure. By bringing these manufacturing capabilities together, PCBWay can help students move more efficiently from concept to physical prototype. Support for Individual Students and Schools The Future Innovators Program provides two support options based on who is purchasing and how the products will be used. Individual Student Projects Verified students working on educational, research, competition, graduation, or non-commercial maker projects can receive 50% off eligible manufacturing charges, up to USD 200 per approved project. The support is project-specific and intended for genuine student participation. Commercial production, resale, and customer-delivery orders are not eligible. School Educational Purchases Schools, departments, laboratories, and educational programs can apply for expanded support when purchasing products for classroom teaching, laboratory training, workshops, or student projects. Eligible school purchases can receive 50% off eligible manufacturing charges, up to USD 2,000 per approved purchase. This option can be particularly useful for educators who need multiple PCBs or prototype parts for laboratory exercises, teaching kits, workshops, or student training. What Types of Projects Can Apply? The program is designed around practical learning and innovation. Eligible projects can include: Course & Lab Projects — curriculum-based assignments, experiments, and engineering exercises Research Prototypes — academic research, thesis projects, and proof-of-concept development Student Competitions — robotics, electronics, automation, and engineering competitions Graduation Projects — capstone and final-year engineering projects Open-Source & Maker Projects — student-led, non-commercial projects that encourage learning and sharing Social-Impact Innovation — projects focused on environmental, accessibility, education, or community needs Classroom & Lab Batches — manufacturing support for institutional teaching and training The goal is not simply to reduce manufacturing costs, but to make it easier for students to learn by building. From Design Files to a Working Prototype A student project often develops through several stages: defining a problem, designing the solution, creating hardware, manufacturing prototypes, testing the result, and improving the design. Manufacturing is an important part of this process. A fabricated PCB can reveal layout or assembly issues that are difficult to identify from a schematic alone. A 3D-printed enclosure can expose mechanical interference. A CNC-machined part can help students evaluate fit, strength, and usability. These iterations turn manufacturing into part of the learning experience rather than simply the final step of a project. How the Future Innovators Program Works Applying for the program is designed to be straightforward: 01 — Create a Quote Prepare the relevant PCBWay quotation or order for your project. 02 — Submit Your Application Provide your student or institutional information, project details, and quote or order number. 03 — Eligibility Review PCBWay reviews student status or institutional eligibility, project purpose, feasibility, branding requirements, and other program conditions. 04 — Receive the Result Approved support is linked to the verified account and designated project. 05 — Pay & Produce After approval, pay the adjusted amount and continue with the normal manufacturing process. Approved support should normally be used within 30 days, and changes to the materials or order may require another review. Helping the Next Generation Build, Test, and Learn Innovation often starts with a simple idea: a circuit a student wants to build, a robot they want to improve, or a problem they believe they can solve. At PCBWay, we believe students should have the opportunity to take those ideas beyond the screen and into the real world. Through the PCBWay Future Innovators Program, we aim to lower some of the manufacturing barriers faced by students and educational institutions while encouraging hands-on engineering, experimentation, and innovation. Whether it is a graduation project, research prototype, competition entry, classroom project, or social-impact idea, the next great project can start with a student willing to build it. Have a student project ready to build? Explore the PCBWay Future Innovators Program and see if your project qualifies for support. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Unlock Color PCB Printing with PCBWay! by: PCBWay Mar 08,2024 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in News Color PCB Printing PCBWay Service Nowadays, traditional PCB printing technology can no longer meet the aesthetic requirements of modern circuit board production. To better fulfill customers' design needs, we are pleased to announce that PCBWay has introduced UV printing equipment. This equipment utilizes UV-curable inks to achieve high-quality image printing on various materials, including fiberglass boards, metal substrates, ceramic substrates, flexible boards, and rigid-flex boards. Entrance https://www.pcbway.com/orderonline.aspx Prerequisites for Ordering Maximum size for a single piece: 270*470MM; Selection of background soldermask color required. Design Specifications Drill holes, traces, soldermasks, and outline designs must comply with specifications. Avoid placing colored characters in areas with solder mask openings, such as surface-mount pads or through-hole pads. What kind of files should be provided for color printing? Method One : Draw colored characters on the silkscreen layer of the Gerber and provide reference pictures. For example: Method Two : If you include information about colored silkscreen in the Gerber layer, each individual color must have its own layer. If there is only one layer, we can only print one color. [This method is not recommended] . If you need to print in multiple colors, we recommend using method One and providing us with a reference picture. 4.Please send the images you want to print on the PCB in the following formats: AI, PDF, JPEG, PNG, TIFF, etc., and indicate your desired printing location on the board. 5.If the image contains a QR code, please ensure that the QR code can be accurately scanned and recognized. Note : If you choose UV printing Multi-color, we will use matte UV color printing by default. When designing the colored characters on the bottom layer, be careful not to design the colored characters as mirrored inverses. (The process of color printing is different from that of standard PCB silkscreen printing. When printing colorful characters on the bottom layer, they are printed with the bottom layer of the PCB facing up.) For situations where the entire top or bottom side requires full-color printing, regardless of the solder mask color you choose, we will use a white solder mask on the full-color printed side and then proceed with the color printing. This is for a better printing effect. Please upload the print image, positioning image, and Gerber in one compressed file. By providing a clear positioning image and necessary instructions, you can assist PCBWay in accurately determining and achieving the desired printing position. Matte UV Color Printing vs. Glossy UV Color Printing Matte ink does not increase the overall thickness, and the PCB's appearance looks smooth. Glossy ink increases the overall thickness and may affect the soldering of component pads. The appearance is beautiful but uneven. Features Adopting UV-LED lamp curing, which enables instant drying, can significantly enhances production efficiency. UV printing technology employs UV-curable inks, ensuring firm and clear printing information resistant to fading, thus enhancing product identification and aesthetics. The normal print survives SMT reflow. UV printing technology can present images in various colors and styles, meeting customers' personalized requirements. Professional industrial-grade UV printers support high-precision printing, delivering exquisite results whether on flat panels or rolled materials. Unlike traditional printing methods, UV printing does not produce volatile organic compounds during the production process, ensuring air quality in the production workshop and providing employees with a safer and healthier working environment. FAQ on UV Printing: Can the UV printed surface be cleaned with water? Yes, it can be cleaned with water. Can the UV printed surface be cleaned with alcohol? It is more difficult to clean after being exposed to alcohol and baked (currently, the board undergoes a short baking process after UV printing). However, with increased contact time with alcohol and vigorous scrubbing, it can be removed. This also depends on whether the UV is on the copper surface or the solder mask surface. How hard is the UV printed surface (sensitivity to scratches)? The UV surface is not sensitive to scratches. However, compared to the solder mask, it is less scratch-resistant because UV printing is ink that is sprayed on and is relatively thin. Welcome to give it a try if you're interested! Besides, PCBWay will continue to enhance its manufacturing capabilities to bring more choices and personalized services to customers in the future. Unlock Color PCB Printing with PCBWay! by: PCBWay Mar 08,2024 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in News Color PCB Printing PCBWay Service Nowadays, traditional PCB printing technology can no longer meet the aesthetic requirements of modern circuit board production. To better fulfill customers' design needs, we are pleased to announce that PCBWay has introduced UV printing equipment. This equipment utilizes UV-curable inks to achieve high-quality image printing on various materials, including fiberglass boards, metal substrates, ceramic substrates, flexible boards, and rigid-flex boards. Entrance https://www.pcbway.com/orderonline.aspx Prerequisites for Ordering Maximum size for a single piece: 270*470MM; Selection of background soldermask color required. Design Specifications Drill holes, traces, soldermasks, and outline designs must comply with specifications. Avoid placing colored characters in areas with solder mask openings, such as surface-mount pads or through-hole pads. What kind of files should be provided for color printing? Method One : Draw colored characters on the silkscreen layer of the Gerber and provide reference pictures. For example: Method Two : If you include information about colored silkscreen in the Gerber layer, each individual color must have its own layer. If there is only one layer, we can only print one color. [This method is not recommended] . If you need to print in multiple colors, we recommend using method One and providing us with a reference picture. 4.Please send the images you want to print on the PCB in the following formats: AI, PDF, JPEG, PNG, TIFF, etc., and indicate your desired printing location on the board. 5.If the image contains a QR code, please ensure that the QR code can be accurately scanned and recognized. Note : If you choose UV printing Multi-color, we will use matte UV color printing by default. When designing the colored characters on the bottom layer, be careful not to design the colored characters as mirrored inverses. (The process of color printing is different from that of standard PCB silkscreen printing. When printing colorful characters on the bottom layer, they are printed with the bottom layer of the PCB facing up.) For situations where the entire top or bottom side requires full-color printing, regardless of the solder mask color you choose, we will use a white solder mask on the full-color printed side and then proceed with the color printing. This is for a better printing effect. Please upload the print image, positioning image, and Gerber in one compressed file. By providing a clear positioning image and necessary instructions, you can assist PCBWay in accurately determining and achieving the desired printing position. Matte UV Color Printing vs. Glossy UV Color Printing Matte ink does not increase the overall thickness, and the PCB's appearance looks smooth. Glossy ink increases the overall thickness and may affect the soldering of component pads. The appearance is beautiful but uneven. Features Adopting UV-LED lamp curing, which enables instant drying, can significantly enhances production efficiency. UV printing technology employs UV-curable inks, ensuring firm and clear printing information resistant to fading, thus enhancing product identification and aesthetics. The normal print survives SMT reflow. UV printing technology can present images in various colors and styles, meeting customers' personalized requirements. Professional industrial-grade UV printers support high-precision printing, delivering exquisite results whether on flat panels or rolled materials. Unlike traditional printing methods, UV printing does not produce volatile organic compounds during the production process, ensuring air quality in the production workshop and providing employees with a safer and healthier working environment. FAQ on UV Printing: Can the UV printed surface be cleaned with water? Yes, it can be cleaned with water. Can the UV printed surface be cleaned with alcohol? It is more difficult to clean after being exposed to alcohol and baked (currently, the board undergoes a short baking process after UV printing). However, with increased contact time with alcohol and vigorous scrubbing, it can be removed. This also depends on whether the UV is on the copper surface or the solder mask surface. How hard is the UV printed surface (sensitivity to scratches)? The UV surface is not sensitive to scratches. However, compared to the solder mask, it is less scratch-resistant because UV printing is ink that is sprayed on and is relatively thin. Welcome to give it a try if you're interested! Besides, PCBWay will continue to enhance its manufacturing capabilities to bring more choices and personalized services to customers in the future. Verify Now Blog > PCBWay Store NewArrival Product - AtomS3R AI Chatbot Kit PCBWay Store NewArrival Product - AtomS3R AI Chatbot Kit by: PCBWay Sep 17,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCBWay Store Link： AtomS3R AI Chatbot Kit AtomS3R-AI Chatbot is an AI voice development kit consisting of two core parts: a controller and a voice base. The controller adopts AtomS3R, which is powered by the ESP32-S3 chip and provides a generous 8MB Flash + 8MB PSRAM memory combo. It also integrates a 9-axis IMU (BMI270 + BMM150), an IR transmitter, and other rich peripherals. The voice base is the Atomic Voice Base, built on the ES8311 audio codec, delivering high-fidelity audio decoding together with microphone and speaker driving capability. The kit supports multiple voice assistants such as XiaoZhi Voice Assistant, OpenAI Voice Assistant, and Volcano Engine Voice Assistant, enabling real-time voice interaction, custom wake-words, and low-latency recognition. Verify Now Blog > KiCad PCB editor shows a ratline (thin connection line) that does not exist or shouldn't be there KiCad PCB editor shows a ratline (thin connection line) that does not exist or shouldn't be there by: William Harter Sep 11,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Basic Information I discovered an unexpected KiCad issue after receiving new PCBs yesterday for an Arduino Shield project. After assembly, the board didn't work correctly. Arduino Shield PCBs are easier to troubleshoot by modifying the code and commenting out features to disable them. I traced the problem to a short between digital pin 12 and analog pin 1. It was not a solder bridge but a board-design error, which I confirmed by testing another unassembled board. The short appeared only on the PCB, not in the schematic: the PCB contained a connection that the schematic did not. Updating the PCB from the schematic did not resolve it. The schematic's electrical rules check reported no errors, and the PCB's design rules check found no schematic parity errors. An online search produced this explanation: “When the KiCad PCB editor shows a ratline (thin connection line) that does not exist or shouldn't be there, it usually means the schematic still defines a net connection that you removed or changed.” The PCB contained an incorrect connection beginning at pin A1. To clear it, I removed the correctly displayed connection from the schematic, added a no-connect flag to A1, saved the schematic, and updated the PCB. After the bad PCB connection disappeared, I saved the PCB, restored the connection in the schematic, saved it, and updated the PCB again. The A1 connection is now correct. Once I finish reviewing the board, I will reorder the PCBs. This Arduino Shield design was developed in Tinkercad: https://www.tinkercad.com/things/57Vc8MxJXxy-tic-tac-toe-with-tri-color-leds Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > 0402 vs 0603 Capacitor for High-Speed PCB Decoupling 0402 vs 0603 Capacitor for High-Speed PCB Decoupling by: Mila Sep 16,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout decoupling capacitor 0402 capacitor 0603 capacitor 0402 vs 0603 capacitor A common misconception is that a larger capacitor package stores more energy and therefore provides better filtering performance. However, in high-speed PCB designs such as FPGA, SoC, and DDR applications, 0402 capacitors with a typical value of 0.1 μF are commonly placed near BGA core power pins instead of larger 0603 capacitors. For the same nominal capacitance, the key difference in 0402 vs 0603 capacitor performance is not how much charge the capacitor stores, but its equivalent series inductance (ESL). At lower frequencies, the performance difference between package sizes is usually less significant. As the operating frequency enters the MHz range and above, ESL increasingly affects the impedance and effective frequency range of a decoupling capacitor. The Underlying Principle: Equivalent Series Inductance (ESL) A surface-mount capacitor is not an ideal capacitor. Its equivalent circuit typically consists of an ideal capacitance (C), equivalent series resistance (ESR), and equivalent series inductance (ESL). ESL comes from the entire current path, including the internal electrodes, terminations, PCB pads, traces, and power/ground vias. Inductance opposes rapidly changing current, and its effect becomes more significant as frequency increases. Every capacitor has a self-resonant frequency (SRF): Operating frequency < SRF: The device behaves mainly as a capacitor and can perform its decoupling function normally. Operating frequency > SRF: The device gradually becomes inductive, and its high-frequency decoupling capability decreases. A higher self-resonant frequency generally means that a decoupling capacitor can maintain low impedance over a wider high-frequency range. For example, consider 0402 and 0603 capacitors with the same nominal capacitance of 0.1 μF: 0603 capacitor: Its larger body size generally results in a longer internal current path and higher intrinsic parasitic inductance. 0402 capacitor: Its smaller body size generally provides a shorter current path and lower intrinsic parasitic inductance. Therefore, under similar capacitance and component structures, a 0402 capacitor typically has lower parasitic inductance and a higher self-resonant frequency than a 0603 capacitor, making it more suitable for high-frequency decoupling. The actual ESL and SRF values should be verified from the component datasheet or the manufacturer's high-frequency model. PCB Pads and Vias Also Add Parasitic Inductance Engineers often focus only on the capacitor's intrinsic ESL specified in the datasheet. However, in a complete power delivery network, PCB pads, traces, and vias also introduce parasitic inductance and can sometimes have an even greater impact than the capacitor itself. In an 0402 vs 0603 capacitor comparison, the larger pads and spacing of a 0603 package can make the connection between the capacitor and power/ground vias longer. This additional trace length increases the total loop inductance. The smaller pads of a 0402 capacitor make it easier to place power and ground vias close to the component. When the PCB manufacturing and assembly processes allow it, microvias or Via-in-Pad can also be used to further shorten the current path and reduce the power-to-ground loop area. When an IC core suddenly draws high-frequency transient current, the total inductance of the current loop affects the power response. Even a capacitor with excellent electrical characteristics may provide limited high-frequency decoupling if the current path is too long. This is why the key advantage of a 0402 capacitor is not simply its smaller package size, but its ability to help create a smaller and lower-inductance current loop. （Optimized Layout） 0402 vs 0603 Capacitor: Advantages and Limitations Advantages of 0402 Capacitors Lower intrinsic parasitic inductance and typically higher SRF, providing better performance for high-frequency decoupling; Smaller pads allow the capacitor to be placed closer to BGA power pins and return paths, reducing the power-to-ground loop area; Higher placement density allows more decoupling capacitors to be placed around BGA devices, helping optimize PDN impedance; The smaller package makes it easier to implement compact power and ground via arrangements and, when supported by the PCB process, microvia or Via-in-Pad structures. Limitations of 0402 Capacitors In the same component series, the available capacitance and voltage-rating options may be more limited, while the actual effective capacitance can also decrease under DC bias; For the same capacitance and voltage rating, the component cost may be higher than that of a 0603 capacitor; Manual soldering is more difficult, with a higher risk of insufficient soldering or component loss, and mass production requires tighter stencil and placement process control; At relatively low frequencies, the performance difference between 0402 and 0603 is usually small, so a 0402 capacitor does not need to be selected simply because it is smaller. When to Use 0603 Capacitors They can generally provide sufficient performance in lower-frequency filtering applications; The larger package can make it easier to obtain suitable capacitance, voltage ratings, and mechanical reliability; They are easier to solder manually and can be suitable for general power filtering and decoupling applications where high-frequency performance is not the primary concern. Therefore, the choice between an 0402 vs 0603 capacitor should not be based on a fixed frequency boundary. As frequency increases, the ESL differences introduced by the component package and PCB mounting structure become increasingly important. The actual selection should consider effective capacitance, ESR, ESL, SRF, and the PCB layout together. Key Considerations for Decoupling Capacitor Selection and Layout Place decoupling capacitors as close as possible to BGA core power pins and other power pins that require high-frequency transient current. A 0402 capacitor is often preferred for these applications. The goal is to reduce the total parasitic inductance of the current loop and improve high-frequency PDN impedance. For DC-DC outputs and other applications where mounting inductance is less critical, 0603 or even 0805 packages can be selected according to effective capacitance, voltage rating, cost, and manufacturing requirements. Loop area is more important than package size alone. This is a common misconception in PCB decoupling. A 0402 capacitor placed far away from the IC power and return path may provide poorer high-frequency performance than a 0603 capacitor placed directly along the current path. Package size is only one factor affecting parasitic inductance. The total power-to-ground loop inductance is more important. Component placement, pad design, and via location all play an important role in PCB decoupling. Do not blindly move to a 0201 package. As the package becomes smaller, the reduction in ESL can provide diminishing returns because the PCB mounting structure can become a larger part of the total inductance. At the same time, soldering difficulty, placement requirements, and component costs may increase. A 0402 capacitor is therefore a common balance between performance, board space, and manufacturing cost in many high-speed PDN designs, although the final package should always be selected according to the specific device and manufacturing process. Common Misconceptions About Decoupling Capacitors ❌ Misconception 1: A larger capacitor package stores more energy and therefore provides better decoupling. ✅ Reality: Under the same effective capacitance and operating conditions, package size itself does not determine how much energy a capacitor stores. The high-frequency performance difference between an 0402 capacitor and a 0603 capacitor mainly comes from parasitic parameters associated with the capacitor and its PCB mounting structure, with ESL being an important factor. ❌ Misconception 2: If the capacitance is the same, the package does not matter. ✅ Reality: Even with the same nominal capacitance, different packages can have different ESL, ESR, and SRF characteristics. During decoupling capacitor selection and PDN impedance simulation, models that match the actual component and PCB mounting structure should be used whenever possible. Otherwise, the simulated impedance curve and resonance characteristics may differ significantly from the actual result. For high-speed PCB decoupling, component selection should therefore go beyond nominal capacitance. The package, effective capacitance, ESL, SRF, and—most importantly—the complete current-loop PCB layout should all be considered. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > High-Speed ADC PCB Layout Guide: EPAD, PDS, and Grounding Best Practices High-Speed ADC PCB Layout Guide: EPAD, PDS, and Grounding Best Practices by: Mila Sep 10,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout high speed analog to digital converter high speed adc adc layout adc pcb design High-speed analog-to-digital converter (ADC) PCB layout involves multiple design parameters, and their importance varies depending on the application. For high-speed ADC systems, the focus should not be on optimizing every routing detail, but on avoiding common design deviations and maintaining the overall performance of the signal chain. For a broader overview of PCB Layout principles, designers should also consider signal integrity, power integrity, grounding, and return paths as part of the overall design. 1. EPAD Design Guidelines for ADC PCB Design The exposed pad (EPAD), defined as Pin 0 by ADI, is the core pad located on the bottom of many integrated circuit packages. It typically provides the main grounding and thermal connection and serves as an important path for the internal ground structure. Some converters and amplifiers do not have dedicated ground pins, with their grounding function primarily relying on the EPAD. Therefore, EPAD design directly affects electrical connection stability and thermal performance and should not be overlooked in ADC PCB design. The EPAD must form a reliable solder connection with the PCB to ensure both electrical and thermal connectivity. Poor soldering or insufficient contact can lead to abnormal grounding, inadequate heat dissipation, and even malfunction of the signal chain. For reliable EPAD performance, three key aspects should be considered in ADC PCB design. Multilayer Grounding and Thermal Copper According to the device datasheet and overall thermal requirements, grounding and thermal copper structures can be added on the appropriate PCB layers. These structures should provide reliable electrical and thermal connections to the PCB ground planes, helping improve heat dissipation, particularly in high-power and multichannel signal-chain applications. The bottom layer can also incorporate a corresponding grounding or thermal area when required by the device and system design. Depending on the application, this area can support grounding, thermal management, high-frequency decoupling, or mechanical positioning for a bottom-side thermal structure. （exposed pad pcb design） EPAD Pad Segmentation A large EPAD can be divided into multiple smaller areas using a cross-hatched stencil pattern or solder mask segmentation. During reflow soldering, solder paste distribution can vary across a large continuous pad, potentially resulting in uneven soldering, voids, or insufficient effective contact. Proper EPAD segmentation helps improve solder paste distribution and create a more uniform and stable connection between the device and PCB, improving both electrical and thermal reliability. EPAD Ground Vias and Via Filling Ground vias can be added to individual EPAD sections according to the device recommendations and PCB manufacturing requirements. Whether these vias require solder paste filling, epoxy filling, or other treatment depends on the via dimensions, pad structure, and manufacturing process. For via structures that may allow solder paste to flow into the holes during reflow, appropriate via filling or solder mask treatment should be considered. This helps reduce soldering defects and improves the reliability of the EPAD electrical and thermal connection. (EPAD design: large vs segmented) 2. Power Decoupling and PDS Design for High-Speed ADC The primary goal of PCB power decoupling is to reduce the impedance of the power delivery system (PDS) to ground. A common mistake is to place large numbers of capacitors with different capacitance values without considering their actual frequency response. In practice, a large number of redundant capacitors is not always necessary. Carefully selecting capacitors based on capacitance, component type, package, and process characteristics can optimize PDS impedance while saving PCB space and reducing component cost. Redundant capacitors can introduce layout congestion, additional cost, and potential resonance risks. They do not inherently violate PCB manufacturing requirements, but excessive or poorly planned decoupling can reduce overall design efficiency. Capacitor Selection and PCB Decoupling Layout The performance of a capacitor varies with its package and construction. Even capacitors from the same supplier can have different frequency responses depending on package size, process, and component type. Therefore, there is no universal frequency limit for capacitor decoupling performance. The effective frequency range depends on package size, equivalent series inductance (ESL), component characteristics, and the actual PCB layout. If capacitor selection or placement is inappropriate, multiple capacitors can introduce additional inductive loops. Capacitors with different parameters may also resonate at specific frequencies, potentially increasing rather than reducing PDS impedance. Capacitor frequency-response characteristics should therefore be considered before placement and selection. （ADC decoupling capacitor layout） 3. High-Frequency PDS and PCB Stackup Design The effective decoupling range of discrete capacitors depends on their electrical characteristics and PCB layout, and there is no universal high-frequency cutoff. As frequency increases, package parasitics and ESL increasingly limit the high-frequency performance of discrete capacitors. At higher frequencies, the intrinsic capacitance formed between PCB power and ground planes becomes an important part of PDS design. Proper stackup design can therefore complement conventional discrete decoupling. Six-Layer PCB Stackup A typical six-layer PCB stackup can be arranged as: Top Signal → Ground 1 → Power 1 → Power 2 → Ground 2 → Bottom Signal In high-speed PCB design, keeping the dielectric thickness between adjacent power and ground planes relatively small, such as a typical range of 2–4 mil, helps increase plane capacitance and reduce the impedance of high-frequency current paths. This optimization is achieved primarily through the PCB stackup and does not require additional components. The required stackup and dielectric thickness simply need to be specified in the PCB fabrication documentation. Eight-Layer PCB Stackup Optimization For an eight-layer PCB, additional ground reference layers can be introduced while maintaining a small core-layer spacing, such as 2–3 mil. This can significantly increase the intrinsic plane capacitance, although the actual increase is not necessarily double. It depends on dielectric thickness, copper area, and the overall configuration of the power and ground layers. Compared with simply adding more high-frequency discrete capacitors, stackup optimization can reduce component count and provide a cleaner high-frequency PDS structure. PDS Impedance and Dynamic Current The primary function of the PDS is to suppress voltage fluctuations caused by the dynamic current demand of the circuit. Low-impedance power and ground planes, combined with an appropriate PCB stackup, can reduce voltage fluctuations caused by rapidly changing currents. According to V = IR, if the dynamic current is 1 A and the PDS impedance is 10 mΩ, the corresponding voltage variation is approximately 10 mV. Optimizing the PCB stackup can extend the effective high-frequency low-impedance range, but overall PDS performance is also affected by power-plane integrity, ground-via placement, package parasitics, and local current-loop design. Therefore, conventional low-frequency decoupling capacitors can be placed at key locations such as power-entry points, high-power devices, and surge-current devices. Combining different decoupling mechanisms can help optimize PDS impedance over a broad frequency range. Dense capacitor placement around every IC is not always necessary and may introduce unnecessary cost, space consumption, and resonance risks. （discrete vs plane capacitance） 4. PCB Layer-to-Layer Coupling and Noise Suppression In multilayer PCB layouts, sensitive analog layers, including analog power, ground, and signal layers, can experience crosstalk when placed close to high-frequency digital layers. Because some noise sources are located directly above or below sensitive analog layers, this type of coupling can easily be overlooked. Layer Coupling in ADC Layout Adjacent PCB conductor layers form parasitic capacitive structures, which can produce electric-field coupling under certain frequency and layout conditions. The actual coupling level has no fixed value and depends on factors such as layer spacing, dielectric thickness, copper area, routing length, signal edge rate, return path, and interlayer parasitic capacitance. For example, if simulation or measurement confirms that a high-speed digital signal produces approximately 1 mV of interference at a sensitive analog node through layer coupling, this interference corresponds to about 2 LSB for a 12-bit ADC with a 2 Vpp full-scale range and about 8 LSB for a 14-bit ADC. In high-resolution ADC systems, such coupling can significantly reduce signal margin and system SNR. Therefore, during ADC layout, the signal characteristics of adjacent layers should be carefully evaluated. High-noise digital layers should be kept away from sensitive analog layers where practical, while appropriate stackup, routing, and return-path design should be used to reduce interlayer coupling. 5. Analog and Digital Grounding in ADC PCB Design In ADC PCB design, there is no universal requirement to divide the ground plane into analog ground (AGND) and digital ground (DGND). The appropriate approach depends on the device manufacturer's recommendations, system partitioning, and current return paths. In many conventional applications, a continuous ground plane is preferable to unnecessary segmentation. （Backflow Path） Why Avoid Unnecessary Ground Plane Splitting? Unnecessary ground-plane splitting can increase the inductance of current return paths. According to V = L(di/dt), higher return-path inductance increases transient voltage noise caused by rapidly changing currents and may also worsen the high-frequency impedance characteristics of the local power and ground network. As ADC sampling rates increase, switching currents can change more rapidly, making parasitic inductance in the return path increasingly important. Therefore, a continuous ground plane should generally be maintained unless system requirements indicate otherwise. Optimize ADC Return Paths Through Functional Partitioning The core of grounding design is functional partitioning and return-path optimization. By separating analog and digital circuits through appropriate component placement and controlling the return paths of high-speed digital signals, unwanted interaction between analog and digital sections can be reduced. In many applications, proper PCB layout, a continuous ground reference plane, and controlled return paths can provide good grounding performance without physically splitting the ground plane. Should AGND and DGND Be Connected at a Single Point? Ground-plane segmentation may be considered when layout constraints prevent effective functional partitioning or when high-noise digital circuits and power buses cannot be sufficiently separated from sensitive analog circuitry. However, a single-point AGND-DGND connection is not universally appropriate for every ADC system. The grounding method should be selected based on device characteristics, PCB return-path distribution, and overall system noise performance, with the device datasheet and system requirements serving as the primary references. 6. High-Speed ADC Layout Design Summary High-speed ADC layout should focus on the key factors that directly affect signal-chain performance rather than adding unnecessary design complexity. For system-level, module-level, and evaluation-board designs, a continuous ground plane can generally be preferred, with functional partitioning used to optimize return paths and reduce layer-to-layer coupling. PCB assembly processes can also directly affect system performance. Manufacturing documentation should specify EPAD segmentation, via treatment, and other relevant assembly requirements according to the device and manufacturing process to ensure reliable solder connections. Power decoupling should be based on accurate component selection and targeted placement. Combined with a PCB stackup that places power and ground planes closely together, this approach can improve high-frequency decoupling performance. Conventional low-frequency decoupling capacitors can then be used at appropriate locations to optimize PDS impedance over a broad frequency range. For high-speed analog-to-digital converter applications, ADC PCB design should be adapted to the specific system requirements. A well-planned ADC layout should focus on device connectivity, power integrity, high-frequency impedance, layer-to-layer coupling, and grounding and return paths. By addressing these factors together, designers can improve the stability and overall performance of high-speed ADC systems. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > High-Speed ADC PCB Layout Guide: EPAD, PDS, and Grounding Best Practices High-Speed ADC PCB Layout Guide: EPAD, PDS, and Grounding Best Practices by: Mila Sep 10,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout high speed analog to digital converter high speed adc adc layout adc pcb design High-speed analog-to-digital converter (ADC) PCB layout involves multiple design parameters, and their importance varies depending on the application. For high-speed ADC systems, the focus should not be on optimizing every routing detail, but on avoiding common design deviations and maintaining the overall performance of the signal chain. For a broader overview of PCB Layout principles, designers should also consider signal integrity, power integrity, grounding, and return paths as part of the overall design. 1. EPAD Design Guidelines for ADC PCB Design The exposed pad (EPAD), defined as Pin 0 by ADI, is the core pad located on the bottom of many integrated circuit packages. It typically provides the main grounding and thermal connection and serves as an important path for the internal ground structure. Some converters and amplifiers do not have dedicated ground pins, with their grounding function primarily relying on the EPAD. Therefore, EPAD design directly affects electrical connection stability and thermal performance and should not be overlooked in ADC PCB design. The EPAD must form a reliable solder connection with the PCB to ensure both electrical and thermal connectivity. Poor soldering or insufficient contact can lead to abnormal grounding, inadequate heat dissipation, and even malfunction of the signal chain. For reliable EPAD performance, three key aspects should be considered in ADC PCB design. Multilayer Grounding and Thermal Copper According to the device datasheet and overall thermal requirements, grounding and thermal copper structures can be added on the appropriate PCB layers. These structures should provide reliable electrical and thermal connections to the PCB ground planes, helping improve heat dissipation, particularly in high-power and multichannel signal-chain applications. The bottom layer can also incorporate a corresponding grounding or thermal area when required by the device and system design. Depending on the application, this area can support grounding, thermal management, high-frequency decoupling, or mechanical positioning for a bottom-side thermal structure. （exposed pad pcb design） EPAD Pad Segmentation A large EPAD can be divided into multiple smaller areas using a cross-hatched stencil pattern or solder mask segmentation. During reflow soldering, solder paste distribution can vary across a large continuous pad, potentially resulting in uneven soldering, voids, or insufficient effective contact. Proper EPAD segmentation helps improve solder paste distribution and create a more uniform and stable connection between the device and PCB, improving both electrical and thermal reliability. EPAD Ground Vias and Via Filling Ground vias can be added to individual EPAD sections according to the device recommendations and PCB manufacturing requirements. Whether these vias require solder paste filling, epoxy filling, or other treatment depends on the via dimensions, pad structure, and manufacturing process. For via structures that may allow solder paste to flow into the holes during reflow, appropriate via filling or solder mask treatment should be considered. This helps reduce soldering defects and improves the reliability of the EPAD electrical and thermal connection. (EPAD design: large vs segmented) 2. Power Decoupling and PDS Design for High-Speed ADC The primary goal of PCB power decoupling is to reduce the impedance of the power delivery system (PDS) to ground. A common mistake is to place large numbers of capacitors with different capacitance values without considering their actual frequency response. In practice, a large number of redundant capacitors is not always necessary. Carefully selecting capacitors based on capacitance, component type, package, and process characteristics can optimize PDS impedance while saving PCB space and reducing component cost. Redundant capacitors can introduce layout congestion, additional cost, and potential resonance risks. They do not inherently violate PCB manufacturing requirements, but excessive or poorly planned decoupling can reduce overall design efficiency. Capacitor Selection and PCB Decoupling Layout The performance of a capacitor varies with its package and construction. Even capacitors from the same supplier can have different frequency responses depending on package size, process, and component type. Therefore, there is no universal frequency limit for capacitor decoupling performance. The effective frequency range depends on package size, equivalent series inductance (ESL), component characteristics, and the actual PCB layout. If capacitor selection or placement is inappropriate, multiple capacitors can introduce additional inductive loops. Capacitors with different parameters may also resonate at specific frequencies, potentially increasing rather than reducing PDS impedance. Capacitor frequency-response characteristics should therefore be considered before placement and selection. （ADC decoupling capacitor layout） 3. High-Frequency PDS and PCB Stackup Design The effective decoupling range of discrete capacitors depends on their electrical characteristics and PCB layout, and there is no universal high-frequency cutoff. As frequency increases, package parasitics and ESL increasingly limit the high-frequency performance of discrete capacitors. At higher frequencies, the intrinsic capacitance formed between PCB power and ground planes becomes an important part of PDS design. Proper stackup design can therefore complement conventional discrete decoupling. Six-Layer PCB Stackup A typical six-layer PCB stackup can be arranged as: Top Signal → Ground 1 → Power 1 → Power 2 → Ground 2 → Bottom Signal In high-speed PCB design, keeping the dielectric thickness between adjacent power and ground planes relatively small, such as a typical range of 2–4 mil, helps increase plane capacitance and reduce the impedance of high-frequency current paths. This optimization is achieved primarily through the PCB stackup and does not require additional components. The required stackup and dielectric thickness simply need to be specified in the PCB fabrication documentation. Eight-Layer PCB Stackup Optimization For an eight-layer PCB, additional ground reference layers can be introduced while maintaining a small core-layer spacing, such as 2–3 mil. This can significantly increase the intrinsic plane capacitance, although the actual increase is not necessarily double. It depends on dielectric thickness, copper area, and the overall configuration of the power and ground layers. Compared with simply adding more high-frequency discrete capacitors, stackup optimization can reduce component count and provide a cleaner high-frequency PDS structure. PDS Impedance and Dynamic Current The primary function of the PDS is to suppress voltage fluctuations caused by the dynamic current demand of the circuit. Low-impedance power and ground planes, combined with an appropriate PCB stackup, can reduce voltage fluctuations caused by rapidly changing currents. According to V = IR, if the dynamic current is 1 A and the PDS impedance is 10 mΩ, the corresponding voltage variation is approximately 10 mV. Optimizing the PCB stackup can extend the effective high-frequency low-impedance range, but overall PDS performance is also affected by power-plane integrity, ground-via placement, package parasitics, and local current-loop design. Therefore, conventional low-frequency decoupling capacitors can be placed at key locations such as power-entry points, high-power devices, and surge-current devices. Combining different decoupling mechanisms can help optimize PDS impedance over a broad frequency range. Dense capacitor placement around every IC is not always necessary and may introduce unnecessary cost, space consumption, and resonance risks. （discrete vs plane capacitance） 4. PCB Layer-to-Layer Coupling and Noise Suppression In multilayer PCB layouts, sensitive analog layers, including analog power, ground, and signal layers, can experience crosstalk when placed close to high-frequency digital layers. Because some noise sources are located directly above or below sensitive analog layers, this type of coupling can easily be overlooked. Layer Coupling in ADC Layout Adjacent PCB conductor layers form parasitic capacitive structures, which can produce electric-field coupling under certain frequency and layout conditions. The actual coupling level has no fixed value and depends on factors such as layer spacing, dielectric thickness, copper area, routing length, signal edge rate, return path, and interlayer parasitic capacitance. For example, if simulation or measurement confirms that a high-speed digital signal produces approximately 1 mV of interference at a sensitive analog node through layer coupling, this interference corresponds to about 2 LSB for a 12-bit ADC with a 2 Vpp full-scale range and about 8 LSB for a 14-bit ADC. In high-resolution ADC systems, such coupling can significantly reduce signal margin and system SNR. Therefore, during ADC layout, the signal characteristics of adjacent layers should be carefully evaluated. High-noise digital layers should be kept away from sensitive analog layers where practical, while appropriate stackup, routing, and return-path design should be used to reduce interlayer coupling. 5. Analog and Digital Grounding in ADC PCB Design In ADC PCB design, there is no universal requirement to divide the ground plane into analog ground (AGND) and digital ground (DGND). The appropriate approach depends on the device manufacturer's recommendations, system partitioning, and current return paths. In many conventional applications, a continuous ground plane is preferable to unnecessary segmentation. （Backflow Path） Why Avoid Unnecessary Ground Plane Splitting? Unnecessary ground-plane splitting can increase the inductance of current return paths. According to V = L(di/dt), higher return-path inductance increases transient voltage noise caused by rapidly changing currents and may also worsen the high-frequency impedance characteristics of the local power and ground network. As ADC sampling rates increase, switching currents can change more rapidly, making parasitic inductance in the return path increasingly important. Therefore, a continuous ground plane should generally be maintained unless system requirements indicate otherwise. Optimize ADC Return Paths Through Functional Partitioning The core of grounding design is functional partitioning and return-path optimization. By separating analog and digital circuits through appropriate component placement and controlling the return paths of high-speed digital signals, unwanted interaction between analog and digital sections can be reduced. In many applications, proper PCB layout, a continuous ground reference plane, and controlled return paths can provide good grounding performance without physically splitting the ground plane. Should AGND and DGND Be Connected at a Single Point? Ground-plane segmentation may be considered when layout constraints prevent effective functional partitioning or when high-noise digital circuits and power buses cannot be sufficiently separated from sensitive analog circuitry. However, a single-point AGND-DGND connection is not universally appropriate for every ADC system. The grounding method should be selected based on device characteristics, PCB return-path distribution, and overall system noise performance, with the device datasheet and system requirements serving as the primary references. 6. High-Speed ADC Layout Design Summary High-speed ADC layout should focus on the key factors that directly affect signal-chain performance rather than adding unnecessary design complexity. For system-level, module-level, and evaluation-board designs, a continuous ground plane can generally be preferred, with functional partitioning used to optimize return paths and reduce layer-to-layer coupling. PCB assembly processes can also directly affect system performance. Manufacturing documentation should specify EPAD segmentation, via treatment, and other relevant assembly requirements according to the device and manufacturing process to ensure reliable solder connections. Power decoupling should be based on accurate component selection and targeted placement. Combined with a PCB stackup that places power and ground planes closely together, this approach can improve high-frequency decoupling performance. Conventional low-frequency decoupling capacitors can then be used at appropriate locations to optimize PDS impedance over a broad frequency range. For high-speed analog-to-digital converter applications, ADC PCB design should be adapted to the specific system requirements. A well-planned ADC layout should focus on device connectivity, power integrity, high-frequency impedance, layer-to-layer coupling, and grounding and return paths. By addressing these factors together, designers can improve the stability and overall performance of high-speed ADC systems. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > High-Speed ADC PCB Layout Guide: EPAD, PDS, and Grounding Best Practices High-Speed ADC PCB Layout Guide: EPAD, PDS, and Grounding Best Practices by: Mila Sep 10,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout high speed analog to digital converter high speed adc adc layout adc pcb design High-speed analog-to-digital converter (ADC) PCB layout involves multiple design parameters, and their importance varies depending on the application. For high-speed ADC systems, the focus should not be on optimizing every routing detail, but on avoiding common design deviations and maintaining the overall performance of the signal chain. For a broader overview of PCB Layout principles, designers should also consider signal integrity, power integrity, grounding, and return paths as part of the overall design. 1. EPAD Design Guidelines for ADC PCB Design The exposed pad (EPAD), defined as Pin 0 by ADI, is the core pad located on the bottom of many integrated circuit packages. It typically provides the main grounding and thermal connection and serves as an important path for the internal ground structure. Some converters and amplifiers do not have dedicated ground pins, with their grounding function primarily relying on the EPAD. Therefore, EPAD design directly affects electrical connection stability and thermal performance and should not be overlooked in ADC PCB design. The EPAD must form a reliable solder connection with the PCB to ensure both electrical and thermal connectivity. Poor soldering or insufficient contact can lead to abnormal grounding, inadequate heat dissipation, and even malfunction of the signal chain. For reliable EPAD performance, three key aspects should be considered in ADC PCB design. Multilayer Grounding and Thermal Copper According to the device datasheet and overall thermal requirements, grounding and thermal copper structures can be added on the appropriate PCB layers. These structures should provide reliable electrical and thermal connections to the PCB ground planes, helping improve heat dissipation, particularly in high-power and multichannel signal-chain applications. The bottom layer can also incorporate a corresponding grounding or thermal area when required by the device and system design. Depending on the application, this area can support grounding, thermal management, high-frequency decoupling, or mechanical positioning for a bottom-side thermal structure. （exposed pad pcb design） EPAD Pad Segmentation A large EPAD can be divided into multiple smaller areas using a cross-hatched stencil pattern or solder mask segmentation. During reflow soldering, solder paste distribution can vary across a large continuous pad, potentially resulting in uneven soldering, voids, or insufficient effective contact. Proper EPAD segmentation helps improve solder paste distribution and create a more uniform and stable connection between the device and PCB, improving both electrical and thermal reliability. EPAD Ground Vias and Via Filling Ground vias can be added to individual EPAD sections according to the device recommendations and PCB manufacturing requirements. Whether these vias require solder paste filling, epoxy filling, or other treatment depends on the via dimensions, pad structure, and manufacturing process. For via structures that may allow solder paste to flow into the holes during reflow, appropriate via filling or solder mask treatment should be considered. This helps reduce soldering defects and improves the reliability of the EPAD electrical and thermal connection. (EPAD design: large vs segmented) 2. Power Decoupling and PDS Design for High-Speed ADC The primary goal of PCB power decoupling is to reduce the impedance of the power delivery system (PDS) to ground. A common mistake is to place large numbers of capacitors with different capacitance values without considering their actual frequency response. In practice, a large number of redundant capacitors is not always necessary. Carefully selecting capacitors based on capacitance, component type, package, and process characteristics can optimize PDS impedance while saving PCB space and reducing component cost. Redundant capacitors can introduce layout congestion, additional cost, and potential resonance risks. They do not inherently violate PCB manufacturing requirements, but excessive or poorly planned decoupling can reduce overall design efficiency. Capacitor Selection and PCB Decoupling Layout The performance of a capacitor varies with its package and construction. Even capacitors from the same supplier can have different frequency responses depending on package size, process, and component type. Therefore, there is no universal frequency limit for capacitor decoupling performance. The effective frequency range depends on package size, equivalent series inductance (ESL), component characteristics, and the actual PCB layout. If capacitor selection or placement is inappropriate, multiple capacitors can introduce additional inductive loops. Capacitors with different parameters may also resonate at specific frequencies, potentially increasing rather than reducing PDS impedance. Capacitor frequency-response characteristics should therefore be considered before placement and selection. （ADC decoupling capacitor layout） 3. High-Frequency PDS and PCB Stackup Design The effective decoupling range of discrete capacitors depends on their electrical characteristics and PCB layout, and there is no universal high-frequency cutoff. As frequency increases, package parasitics and ESL increasingly limit the high-frequency performance of discrete capacitors. At higher frequencies, the intrinsic capacitance formed between PCB power and ground planes becomes an important part of PDS design. Proper stackup design can therefore complement conventional discrete decoupling. Six-Layer PCB Stackup A typical six-layer PCB stackup can be arranged as: Top Signal → Ground 1 → Power 1 → Power 2 → Ground 2 → Bottom Signal In high-speed PCB design, keeping the dielectric thickness between adjacent power and ground planes relatively small, such as a typical range of 2–4 mil, helps increase plane capacitance and reduce the impedance of high-frequency current paths. This optimization is achieved primarily through the PCB stackup and does not require additional components. The required stackup and dielectric thickness simply need to be specified in the PCB fabrication documentation. Eight-Layer PCB Stackup Optimization For an eight-layer PCB, additional ground reference layers can be introduced while maintaining a small core-layer spacing, such as 2–3 mil. This can significantly increase the intrinsic plane capacitance, although the actual increase is not necessarily double. It depends on dielectric thickness, copper area, and the overall configuration of the power and ground layers. Compared with simply adding more high-frequency discrete capacitors, stackup optimization can reduce component count and provide a cleaner high-frequency PDS structure. PDS Impedance and Dynamic Current The primary function of the PDS is to suppress voltage fluctuations caused by the dynamic current demand of the circuit. Low-impedance power and ground planes, combined with an appropriate PCB stackup, can reduce voltage fluctuations caused by rapidly changing currents. According to V = IR, if the dynamic current is 1 A and the PDS impedance is 10 mΩ, the corresponding voltage variation is approximately 10 mV. Optimizing the PCB stackup can extend the effective high-frequency low-impedance range, but overall PDS performance is also affected by power-plane integrity, ground-via placement, package parasitics, and local current-loop design. Therefore, conventional low-frequency decoupling capacitors can be placed at key locations such as power-entry points, high-power devices, and surge-current devices. Combining different decoupling mechanisms can help optimize PDS impedance over a broad frequency range. Dense capacitor placement around every IC is not always necessary and may introduce unnecessary cost, space consumption, and resonance risks. （discrete vs plane capacitance） 4. PCB Layer-to-Layer Coupling and Noise Suppression In multilayer PCB layouts, sensitive analog layers, including analog power, ground, and signal layers, can experience crosstalk when placed close to high-frequency digital layers. Because some noise sources are located directly above or below sensitive analog layers, this type of coupling can easily be overlooked. Layer Coupling in ADC Layout Adjacent PCB conductor layers form parasitic capacitive structures, which can produce electric-field coupling under certain frequency and layout conditions. The actual coupling level has no fixed value and depends on factors such as layer spacing, dielectric thickness, copper area, routing length, signal edge rate, return path, and interlayer parasitic capacitance. For example, if simulation or measurement confirms that a high-speed digital signal produces approximately 1 mV of interference at a sensitive analog node through layer coupling, this interference corresponds to about 2 LSB for a 12-bit ADC with a 2 Vpp full-scale range and about 8 LSB for a 14-bit ADC. In high-resolution ADC systems, such coupling can significantly reduce signal margin and system SNR. Therefore, during ADC layout, the signal characteristics of adjacent layers should be carefully evaluated. High-noise digital layers should be kept away from sensitive analog layers where practical, while appropriate stackup, routing, and return-path design should be used to reduce interlayer coupling. 5. Analog and Digital Grounding in ADC PCB Design In ADC PCB design, there is no universal requirement to divide the ground plane into analog ground (AGND) and digital ground (DGND). The appropriate approach depends on the device manufacturer's recommendations, system partitioning, and current return paths. In many conventional applications, a continuous ground plane is preferable to unnecessary segmentation. （Backflow Path） Why Avoid Unnecessary Ground Plane Splitting? Unnecessary ground-plane splitting can increase the inductance of current return paths. According to V = L(di/dt), higher return-path inductance increases transient voltage noise caused by rapidly changing currents and may also worsen the high-frequency impedance characteristics of the local power and ground network. As ADC sampling rates increase, switching currents can change more rapidly, making parasitic inductance in the return path increasingly important. Therefore, a continuous ground plane should generally be maintained unless system requirements indicate otherwise. Optimize ADC Return Paths Through Functional Partitioning The core of grounding design is functional partitioning and return-path optimization. By separating analog and digital circuits through appropriate component placement and controlling the return paths of high-speed digital signals, unwanted interaction between analog and digital sections can be reduced. In many applications, proper PCB layout, a continuous ground reference plane, and controlled return paths can provide good grounding performance without physically splitting the ground plane. Should AGND and DGND Be Connected at a Single Point? Ground-plane segmentation may be considered when layout constraints prevent effective functional partitioning or when high-noise digital circuits and power buses cannot be sufficiently separated from sensitive analog circuitry. However, a single-point AGND-DGND connection is not universally appropriate for every ADC system. The grounding method should be selected based on device characteristics, PCB return-path distribution, and overall system noise performance, with the device datasheet and system requirements serving as the primary references. 6. High-Speed ADC Layout Design Summary High-speed ADC layout should focus on the key factors that directly affect signal-chain performance rather than adding unnecessary design complexity. For system-level, module-level, and evaluation-board designs, a continuous ground plane can generally be preferred, with functional partitioning used to optimize return paths and reduce layer-to-layer coupling. PCB assembly processes can also directly affect system performance. Manufacturing documentation should specify EPAD segmentation, via treatment, and other relevant assembly requirements according to the device and manufacturing process to ensure reliable solder connections. Power decoupling should be based on accurate component selection and targeted placement. Combined with a PCB stackup that places power and ground planes closely together, this approach can improve high-frequency decoupling performance. Conventional low-frequency decoupling capacitors can then be used at appropriate locations to optimize PDS impedance over a broad frequency range. For high-speed analog-to-digital converter applications, ADC PCB design should be adapted to the specific system requirements. A well-planned ADC layout should focus on device connectivity, power integrity, high-frequency impedance, layer-to-layer coupling, and grounding and return paths. By addressing these factors together, designers can improve the stability and overall performance of high-speed ADC systems. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac.
