Depending on the application, this area can support grounding, thermal management, high-frequency decoupling, or mechanical positioning for a bottom-side thermal structure. （exposed pad pcb design） EPAD Pad Segmentation A large EPAD can be divided into multiple smaller areas using a cross-hatched stencil pattern or solder mask segmentation. During reflow soldering, solder paste distribution can vary across a large continuous pad, potentially resulting in uneven soldering, voids, or insufficient effective contact. Proper EPAD segmentation helps improve solder paste distribution and create a more uniform and stable connection between the device and PCB, improving both electrical and thermal reliability. EPAD Ground Vias and Via Filling Ground vias can be added to individual EPAD sections according to the device recommendations and PCB manufacturing requirements. Whether these vias require solder paste filling, epoxy filling, or other treatment depends on the via dimensions, pad structure, and manufacturing process. For via structures that may allow solder paste to flow into the holes during reflow, appropriate via filling or solder mask treatment should be considered. This helps reduce soldering defects and improves the reliability of the EPAD electrical and thermal connection. (EPAD design: large vs segmented) 2. Power Decoupling and PDS Design for High-Speed ADC The primary goal of PCB power decoupling is to reduce the impedance of the power delivery system (PDS) to ground. A common mistake is to place large numbers of capacitors with different capacitance values without considering their actual frequency response. In practice, a large number of redundant capacitors is not always necessary. Carefully selecting capacitors based on capacitance, component type, package, and process characteristics can optimize PDS impedance while saving PCB space and reducing component cost. Redundant capacitors can introduce layout congestion, additional cost, and potential resonance risks. They do not inherently violate PCB manufacturing requirements, but excessive or poorly planned decoupling can reduce overall design efficiency. Capacitor Selection and PCB Decoupling Layout The performance of a capacitor varies with its package and construction. Even capacitors from the same supplier can have different frequency responses depending on package size, process, and component type. Therefore, there is no universal frequency limit for capacitor decoupling performance. The effective frequency range depends on package size, equivalent series inductance (ESL), component characteristics, and the actual PCB layout. If capacitor selection or placement is inappropriate, multiple capacitors can introduce additional inductive loops. Capacitors with different parameters may also resonate at specific frequencies, potentially increasing rather than reducing PDS impedance. Capacitor frequency-response characteristics should therefore be considered before placement and selection. （ADC decoupling capacitor layout） 3. High-Frequency PDS and PCB Stackup Design The effective decoupling range of discrete capacitors depends on their electrical characteristics and PCB layout, and there is no universal high-frequency cutoff. As frequency increases, package parasitics and ESL increasingly limit the high-frequency performance of discrete capacitors. At higher frequencies, the intrinsic capacitance formed between PCB power and ground planes becomes an important part of PDS design. Proper stackup design can therefore complement conventional discrete decoupling. This optimization is achieved primarily through the PCB stackup and does not require additional components. The required stackup and dielectric thickness simply need to be specified in the PCB fabrication documentation. This can significantly increase the intrinsic plane capacitance, although the actual increase is not necessarily double. It depends on dielectric thickness, copper area, and the overall configuration of the power and ground layers. Compared with simply adding more high-frequency discrete capacitors, stackup optimization can reduce component count and provide a cleaner high-frequency PDS structure. PDS Impedance and Dynamic Current The primary function of the PDS is to suppress voltage fluctuations caused by the dynamic current demand of the circuit. Low-impedance power and ground planes, combined with an appropriate PCB stackup, can reduce voltage fluctuations caused by rapidly changing currents. According to V = IR, if the dynamic current is 1 A and the PDS impedance is 10 mΩ, the corresponding voltage variation is approximately 10 mV. Optimizing the PCB stackup can extend the effective high-frequency low-impedance range, but overall PDS performance is also affected by power-plane integrity, ground-via placement, package parasitics, and local current-loop design. Therefore, conventional low-frequency decoupling capacitors can be placed at key locations such as power-entry points, high-power devices, and surge-current devices. Combining different decoupling mechanisms can help optimize PDS impedance over a broad frequency range. Dense capacitor placement around every IC is not always necessary and may introduce unnecessary cost, space consumption, and resonance risks. （discrete vs plane capacitance） 4. PCB Layer-to-Layer Coupling and Noise Suppression In multilayer PCB layouts, sensitive analog layers, including analog power, ground, and signal layers, can experience crosstalk when placed close to high-frequency digital layers. Because some noise sources are located directly above or below sensitive analog layers, this type of coupling can easily be overlooked. Layer Coupling in ADC Layout Adjacent PCB conductor layers form parasitic capacitive structures, which can produce electric-field coupling under certain frequency and layout conditions. The actual coupling level has no fixed value and depends on factors such as layer spacing, dielectric thickness, copper area, routing length, signal edge rate, return path, and interlayer parasitic capacitance. For example, if simulation or measurement confirms that a high-speed digital signal produces approximately 1 mV of interference at a sensitive analog node through layer coupling, this interference corresponds to about 2 LSB for a 12-bit ADC with a 2 Vpp full-scale range and about 8 LSB for a 14-bit ADC. In high-resolution ADC systems, such coupling can significantly reduce signal margin and system SNR. Therefore, during ADC layout, the signal characteristics of adjacent layers should be carefully evaluated. High-noise digital layers should be kept away from sensitive analog layers where practical, while appropriate stackup, routing, and return-path design should be used to reduce interlayer coupling. 5. Analog and Digital Grounding in ADC PCB Design In ADC PCB design, there is no universal requirement to divide the ground plane into analog ground (AGND) and digital ground (DGND). The appropriate approach depends on the device manufacturer's recommendations, system partitioning, and current return paths. In many conventional applications, a continuous ground plane is preferable to unnecessary segmentation. （Backflow Path） Why Avoid Unnecessary Ground Plane Splitting? Unnecessary ground-plane splitting can increase the inductance of current return paths. According to V = L(di/dt), higher return-path inductance increases transient voltage noise caused by rapidly changing currents and may also worsen the high-frequency impedance characteristics of the local power and ground network. As ADC sampling rates increase, switching currents can change more rapidly, making parasitic inductance in the return path increasingly important. Therefore, a continuous ground plane should generally be maintained unless system requirements indicate otherwise. Optimize ADC Return Paths Through Functional Partitioning The core of grounding design is functional partitioning and return-path optimization. By separating analog and digital circuits through appropriate component placement and controlling the return paths of high-speed digital signals, unwanted interaction between analog and digital sections can be reduced. In many applications, proper PCB layout, a continuous ground reference plane, and controlled return paths can provide good grounding performance without physically splitting the ground plane. Should AGND and DGND Be Connected at a Single Point? Ground-plane segmentation may be considered when layout constraints prevent effective functional partitioning or when high-noise digital circuits and power buses cannot be sufficiently separated from sensitive analog circuitry. However, a single-point AGND-DGND connection is not universally appropriate for every ADC system. The grounding method should be selected based on device characteristics, PCB return-path distribution, and overall system noise performance, with the device datasheet and system requirements serving as the primary references. 6. High-Speed ADC Layout Design Summary High-speed ADC layout should focus on the key factors that directly affect signal-chain performance rather than adding unnecessary design complexity. For system-level, module-level, and evaluation-board designs, a continuous ground plane can generally be preferred, with functional partitioning used to optimize return paths and reduce layer-to-layer coupling. PCB assembly processes can also directly affect system performance. Manufacturing documentation should specify EPAD segmentation, via treatment, and other relevant assembly requirements according to the device and manufacturing process to ensure reliable solder connections. Power decoupling should be based on accurate component selection and targeted placement. Combined with a PCB stackup that places power and ground planes closely together, this approach can improve high-frequency decoupling performance. Conventional low-frequency decoupling capacitors can then be used at appropriate locations to optimize PDS impedance over a broad frequency range. For high-speed analog-to-digital converter applications, ADC PCB design should be adapted to the specific system requirements. A well-planned ADC layout should focus on device connectivity, power integrity, high-frequency impedance, layer-to-layer coupling, and grounding and return paths. By addressing these factors together, designers can improve the stability and overall performance of high-speed ADC systems. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > How to Properly Handle Unused IC Pins in Schematic Design How to Properly Handle Unused IC Pins in Schematic Design by: Mila Sep 09,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout schematic design cmos pins nc pins When working on schematic design , engineers often encounter situations like this: to meet the core functional requirements, a 100-pin MCU is selected, but only 60 pins are actually used. Or a 4-channel op-amp is selected, but only three channels are needed. Some ICs may also have pins marked as NC. Seeing all those pins labeled as "Not Connected" on the schematic can be confusing. Should these unused pins simply be left floating? Should they be connected to ground? Or should they be connected to a power supply? Improper handling of unused pins can lead to undefined input states, increased power consumption, or noise interference, and in severe cases may even affect device reliability. This article explains how to properly handle these seemingly minor but important details in schematic design. 1. Why Should Unused IC Pins Be Handled Carefully? Many ICs today use CMOS technology. One key rule to remember is: do not leave CMOS inputs floating, especially digital input pins. （CMOS device） This can be understood from the internal structure of CMOS circuits. A typical CMOS input stage consists of an inverter made up of a PMOS and an NMOS connected in series. When the input is low, the PMOS is on and the NMOS is off. When the input is high, the PMOS is off and the NMOS is on. Under ideal static conditions, only a very small leakage current flows, giving CMOS circuits very low static power consumption. 2. What Happens When CMOS Pins Are Left Floating? What happens when an input is left floating? Because the input has very high impedance, it can easily be affected by surrounding electromagnetic noise, parasitic coupling, and leakage current. As a result, the input voltage may become undefined and fluctuate between low and high levels. When the input voltage falls within the transition region of the CMOS input stage, the PMOS and NMOS may both be partially turned on, causing increased supply current. In other words, floating CMOS pins have no guaranteed logic state, so it is impossible to reliably determine whether the input will be interpreted as a high or low level. 3. How to Handle Unused MCU GPIOs? Modern MCUs usually provide multifunctional GPIOs. For unused GPIOs, follow the requirements in the device datasheet and configure the corresponding IO as an output with a defined state, such as driving it low or high. If supported by the device, it can also be configured as an input with an internal pull-up or pull-down. When permitted by the device, this eliminates the need for external pull-up or pull-down resistors, saving components and PCB space. For critical pins such as interrupt, reset, and mode-selection pins, however, their default logic states should be clearly defined. Whether an external pull-up or pull-down resistor is required should be determined according to the datasheet and reference design to prevent unintended triggering. 4. How to Handle Unused Op-Amp Channels? Op-amps and ADCs require special attention because analog circuits are more sensitive to noise, and their unused pins may need to be handled differently from digital circuits. For example, if you use a dual-channel op-amp but only need one channel, what should you do with the unused channel? （IC Pins） Leaving it floating is generally not recommended because the input pins can pick up noise, causing the output to saturate and potentially increasing power consumption. What if both the non-inverting and inverting inputs are connected to ground? This puts the op-amp in an open-loop configuration, so its output may not be well controlled. For a typical voltage-feedback op-amp, if permitted by the datasheet, a better approach is to configure the unused channel as a voltage follower: connect the output to the inverting input to create negative feedback, and connect the non-inverting input to GND. However, the op-amp's input common-mode range and output swing must also be checked to ensure that this configuration is within the device's specifications. 5. What About Unused ADC Inputs? Unused ADC channels should be handled according to the device datasheet. Some devices recommend connecting unused ADC inputs to GND or another stable reference level to prevent the channel from picking up noise. However, directly connecting the input to ground should not be treated as a universal rule for all ADCs. Therefore, unused ADC inputs should not simply be treated in the same way as digital GPIOs. Always check the manufacturer's recommended connection method before finalizing the schematic design. 6. What Do NC Pins Mean on an IC? IC datasheets often contain pins marked as NC, or "No Connect." These NC pins need to be examined carefully. NC does not necessarily mean that the pin can be connected in any way. Some NC pins may have no internal connection and should simply be left floating. However, other pins marked as NC may have internal connections related to testing, reserved functions, or other circuits. The handling method must strictly follow the datasheet. For example, some datasheets specify "Must be left floating," while others specify "Must be tied to GND." If you connect NC pins to ground without checking the datasheet, you could potentially cause unexpected behavior or interfere with internal test or reserved functions. 7. The Key Rule: Always Check the Datasheet When dealing with unused IC pins, the most important principle is not simply whether a pin should be left floating or connected to ground. Instead, first identify the pin type and then follow the connection requirements specified in the datasheet. （DBV package） Different types of GPIOs, analog inputs, op-amp channels, and NC pins may require completely different handling methods. In simple terms: Unused GPIOs: Configure them to a defined state according to the datasheet. Critical input pins: Make sure they have a clearly defined default logic level. Unused op-amp channels: Use a stable negative-feedback configuration when recommended. Unused ADC inputs: Follow the device manufacturer's recommended connection method. NC pins: Strictly follow the datasheet requirements. A simple "Not Connected" label on a schematic may involve power consumption, noise, stability, and even device reliability. Verify Now Blog > How to Properly Handle Unused IC Pins in Schematic Design How to Properly Handle Unused IC Pins in Schematic Design by: Mila Sep 09,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout schematic design cmos pins nc pins When working on schematic design , engineers often encounter situations like this: to meet the core functional requirements, a 100-pin MCU is selected, but only 60 pins are actually used. Or a 4-channel op-amp is selected, but only three channels are needed. Some ICs may also have pins marked as NC. Seeing all those pins labeled as "Not Connected" on the schematic can be confusing. Should these unused pins simply be left floating? Should they be connected to ground? Or should they be connected to a power supply? Improper handling of unused pins can lead to undefined input states, increased power consumption, or noise interference, and in severe cases may even affect device reliability. This article explains how to properly handle these seemingly minor but important details in schematic design. 1. Why Should Unused IC Pins Be Handled Carefully? Many ICs today use CMOS technology. One key rule to remember is: do not leave CMOS inputs floating, especially digital input pins. （CMOS device） This can be understood from the internal structure of CMOS circuits. A typical CMOS input stage consists of an inverter made up of a PMOS and an NMOS connected in series. When the input is low, the PMOS is on and the NMOS is off. When the input is high, the PMOS is off and the NMOS is on. Under ideal static conditions, only a very small leakage current flows, giving CMOS circuits very low static power consumption. 2. What Happens When CMOS Pins Are Left Floating? What happens when an input is left floating? Because the input has very high impedance, it can easily be affected by surrounding electromagnetic noise, parasitic coupling, and leakage current. As a result, the input voltage may become undefined and fluctuate between low and high levels. When the input voltage falls within the transition region of the CMOS input stage, the PMOS and NMOS may both be partially turned on, causing increased supply current. In other words, floating CMOS pins have no guaranteed logic state, so it is impossible to reliably determine whether the input will be interpreted as a high or low level. 3. How to Handle Unused MCU GPIOs? Modern MCUs usually provide multifunctional GPIOs. For unused GPIOs, follow the requirements in the device datasheet and configure the corresponding IO as an output with a defined state, such as driving it low or high. If supported by the device, it can also be configured as an input with an internal pull-up or pull-down. When permitted by the device, this eliminates the need for external pull-up or pull-down resistors, saving components and PCB space. For critical pins such as interrupt, reset, and mode-selection pins, however, their default logic states should be clearly defined. Whether an external pull-up or pull-down resistor is required should be determined according to the datasheet and reference design to prevent unintended triggering. 4. How to Handle Unused Op-Amp Channels? Op-amps and ADCs require special attention because analog circuits are more sensitive to noise, and their unused pins may need to be handled differently from digital circuits. For example, if you use a dual-channel op-amp but only need one channel, what should you do with the unused channel? （IC Pins） Leaving it floating is generally not recommended because the input pins can pick up noise, causing the output to saturate and potentially increasing power consumption. What if both the non-inverting and inverting inputs are connected to ground? This puts the op-amp in an open-loop configuration, so its output may not be well controlled. For a typical voltage-feedback op-amp, if permitted by the datasheet, a better approach is to configure the unused channel as a voltage follower: connect the output to the inverting input to create negative feedback, and connect the non-inverting input to GND. However, the op-amp's input common-mode range and output swing must also be checked to ensure that this configuration is within the device's specifications. 5. What About Unused ADC Inputs? Unused ADC channels should be handled according to the device datasheet. Some devices recommend connecting unused ADC inputs to GND or another stable reference level to prevent the channel from picking up noise. However, directly connecting the input to ground should not be treated as a universal rule for all ADCs. Therefore, unused ADC inputs should not simply be treated in the same way as digital GPIOs. Always check the manufacturer's recommended connection method before finalizing the schematic design. 6. What Do NC Pins Mean on an IC? IC datasheets often contain pins marked as NC, or "No Connect." These NC pins need to be examined carefully. NC does not necessarily mean that the pin can be connected in any way. Some NC pins may have no internal connection and should simply be left floating. However, other pins marked as NC may have internal connections related to testing, reserved functions, or other circuits. The handling method must strictly follow the datasheet. For example, some datasheets specify "Must be left floating," while others specify "Must be tied to GND." If you connect NC pins to ground without checking the datasheet, you could potentially cause unexpected behavior or interfere with internal test or reserved functions. 7. The Key Rule: Always Check the Datasheet When dealing with unused IC pins, the most important principle is not simply whether a pin should be left floating or connected to ground. Instead, first identify the pin type and then follow the connection requirements specified in the datasheet. （DBV package） Different types of GPIOs, analog inputs, op-amp channels, and NC pins may require completely different handling methods. In simple terms: Unused GPIOs: Configure them to a defined state according to the datasheet. Critical input pins: Make sure they have a clearly defined default logic level. Unused op-amp channels: Use a stable negative-feedback configuration when recommended. Unused ADC inputs: Follow the device manufacturer's recommended connection method. NC pins: Strictly follow the datasheet requirements. A simple "Not Connected" label on a schematic may involve power consumption, noise, stability, and even device reliability. Do not rely on assumptions. Check the datasheet first, then decide how the pin should be connected. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > How to Properly Handle Unused IC Pins in Schematic Design How to Properly Handle Unused IC Pins in Schematic Design by: Mila Sep 09,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout schematic design cmos pins nc pins When working on schematic design , engineers often encounter situations like this: to meet the core functional requirements, a 100-pin MCU is selected, but only 60 pins are actually used. Or a 4-channel op-amp is selected, but only three channels are needed. Some ICs may also have pins marked as NC. Seeing all those pins labeled as "Not Connected" on the schematic can be confusing. Should these unused pins simply be left floating? Should they be connected to ground? Or should they be connected to a power supply? Improper handling of unused pins can lead to undefined input states, increased power consumption, or noise interference, and in severe cases may even affect device reliability. This article explains how to properly handle these seemingly minor but important details in schematic design. 1. Why Should Unused IC Pins Be Handled Carefully? Many ICs today use CMOS technology. One key rule to remember is: do not leave CMOS inputs floating, especially digital input pins. （CMOS device） This can be understood from the internal structure of CMOS circuits. A typical CMOS input stage consists of an inverter made up of a PMOS and an NMOS connected in series. When the input is low, the PMOS is on and the NMOS is off. When the input is high, the PMOS is off and the NMOS is on. Under ideal static conditions, only a very small leakage current flows, giving CMOS circuits very low static power consumption. 2. What Happens When CMOS Pins Are Left Floating? What happens when an input is left floating? Because the input has very high impedance, it can easily be affected by surrounding electromagnetic noise, parasitic coupling, and leakage current. As a result, the input voltage may become undefined and fluctuate between low and high levels. When the input voltage falls within the transition region of the CMOS input stage, the PMOS and NMOS may both be partially turned on, causing increased supply current. In other words, floating CMOS pins have no guaranteed logic state, so it is impossible to reliably determine whether the input will be interpreted as a high or low level. 3. How to Handle Unused MCU GPIOs? Modern MCUs usually provide multifunctional GPIOs. For unused GPIOs, follow the requirements in the device datasheet and configure the corresponding IO as an output with a defined state, such as driving it low or high. If supported by the device, it can also be configured as an input with an internal pull-up or pull-down. When permitted by the device, this eliminates the need for external pull-up or pull-down resistors, saving components and PCB space. For critical pins such as interrupt, reset, and mode-selection pins, however, their default logic states should be clearly defined. Whether an external pull-up or pull-down resistor is required should be determined according to the datasheet and reference design to prevent unintended triggering. 4. How to Handle Unused Op-Amp Channels? Op-amps and ADCs require special attention because analog circuits are more sensitive to noise, and their unused pins may need to be handled differently from digital circuits. For example, if you use a dual-channel op-amp but only need one channel, what should you do with the unused channel? （IC Pins） Leaving it floating is generally not recommended because the input pins can pick up noise, causing the output to saturate and potentially increasing power consumption. What if both the non-inverting and inverting inputs are connected to ground? This puts the op-amp in an open-loop configuration, so its output may not be well controlled. For a typical voltage-feedback op-amp, if permitted by the datasheet, a better approach is to configure the unused channel as a voltage follower: connect the output to the inverting input to create negative feedback, and connect the non-inverting input to GND. However, the op-amp's input common-mode range and output swing must also be checked to ensure that this configuration is within the device's specifications. 5. What About Unused ADC Inputs? Unused ADC channels should be handled according to the device datasheet. Some devices recommend connecting unused ADC inputs to GND or another stable reference level to prevent the channel from picking up noise. However, directly connecting the input to ground should not be treated as a universal rule for all ADCs. Therefore, unused ADC inputs should not simply be treated in the same way as digital GPIOs. Always check the manufacturer's recommended connection method before finalizing the schematic design. 6. What Do NC Pins Mean on an IC? IC datasheets often contain pins marked as NC, or "No Connect." These NC pins need to be examined carefully. NC does not necessarily mean that the pin can be connected in any way. Some NC pins may have no internal connection and should simply be left floating. However, other pins marked as NC may have internal connections related to testing, reserved functions, or other circuits. The handling method must strictly follow the datasheet. For example, some datasheets specify "Must be left floating," while others specify "Must be tied to GND." If you connect NC pins to ground without checking the datasheet, you could potentially cause unexpected behavior or interfere with internal test or reserved functions. 7. The Key Rule: Always Check the Datasheet When dealing with unused IC pins, the most important principle is not simply whether a pin should be left floating or connected to ground. Instead, first identify the pin type and then follow the connection requirements specified in the datasheet. （DBV package） Different types of GPIOs, analog inputs, op-amp channels, and NC pins may require completely different handling methods. In simple terms: Unused GPIOs: Configure them to a defined state according to the datasheet. Critical input pins: Make sure they have a clearly defined default logic level. Unused op-amp channels: Use a stable negative-feedback configuration when recommended. Unused ADC inputs: Follow the device manufacturer's recommended connection method. NC pins: Strictly follow the datasheet requirements. A simple "Not Connected" label on a schematic may involve power consumption, noise, stability, and even device reliability. Do not rely on assumptions. Check the datasheet first, then decide how the pin should be connected. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > USB Type-C Design and CC Pin Configuration: A Practical Hardware Design Guide USB Type-C Design and CC Pin Configuration: A Practical Hardware Design Guide by: Mila Sep 08,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout hardware design type c design usb design usb type c design usb pcb design One of the most common pitfalls in Hardware Design for Type-C interfaces is confusing the legacy protocols used by USB-A ports with the native USB Type-C protocol. Some designers mistakenly treat D+ / D− as the core charging detection pins of Type-C, which can lead to design failures. The voltage is a normal 5V, the polarity is correct, but the device still does not charge, fails to be recognized, only works in one plug orientation, or has limited charging current. Compatibility issues may also occur with some phones. In many cases, there is basically one reason: CC1 and CC2 are not connected correctly. Let's look at the most common 5V Type-C charging configuration. Once you understand it, you can use it directly in your Type C Design. 1. The Most Important Conclusion For a Type-C interface, CC1 / CC2 are the core channels for power role detection, connection detection, current capability detection, and USB PD communication. D+ and D− do not handle basic Type-C power detection or USB PD negotiation in a standard C-to-C connection. This is one of the key differences between traditional USB and modern USB Type C Design: CC pins: The dedicated Type-C configuration channel used for power role detection, connection detection, plug orientation detection, Type-C current capability detection, and USB PD communication. D+ / D− pins: Mainly used for USB 2.0 data transmission and compatibility with certain legacy charging protocols, such as BC1.2. In simple terms: C-to-C charging: Basic power detection mainly relies on CC, not D+ / D−. A-to-C charging: Legacy USB-A charging protocols may use D+ / D− for charging detection. 2. Why Does C-to-C Charging Mainly Rely on CC? Taking a standard USB-C-to-USB-C charging connection as an example, the Source and Sink first establish a connection through the CC pins. The basic process is: 1. The charger provides Rp pull-ups on CC1 and CC2. 2. The phone or other powered device uses Rd pull-downs to indicate that it is a Sink. 3. The two sides detect the connection and determine the available Type-C current capability through CC. 4. If both sides support USB PD, they can further communicate through the CC channel to negotiate voltage, current, and power. It is important to note that 56KΩ, 22KΩ, and 10KΩ Rp values correspond to different advertised current capabilities. They should not be interpreted as “56KΩ directly unlocks 5V/3A.” Therefore, Type-C current capability detection and USB PD fast charging should be distinguished: Type-C current capability detection → Rp / Rd USB PD power negotiation → PD communication over CC D+ / D− mainly handle USB 2.0 data and certain legacy charging protocols. 3. CC vs. D+ / D−: What Does Each One Actually Do? CC1 / CC2: The Core Type-C Power and Connection Pins CC stands for Configuration Channel and is an important feature that distinguishes USB Type-C from traditional USB-A interfaces. CC1 and CC2 are mainly responsible for: Power role detection: Rp indicates a Source, while Rd indicates a Sink. Connection detection: Determines whether a valid connection has been established. Plug orientation detection: The active CC pin helps determine the plug orientation. Type-C current capability detection: The Source uses Rp to advertise its power capability. USB PD communication: USB PD devices use the CC channel to negotiate voltage, current, and power. Therefore, in a standard Type-C C-to-C power connection: Correct CC configuration is critical to proper device detection and power delivery. This is why CC routing and component placement are important in USB PCB Design. D+ / D−: Data Transmission and Legacy Charging Compatibility D+ / D− are essentially USB 2.0 differential data lines. They are mainly used for: 1. USB 2.0 data transmission, programming, and communication 2. Compatibility with certain legacy USB-A charging protocols For example, USB BC1.2 charging detection mechanisms may use D+ / D−. The key distinction is: C-to-C architecture: Basic Type-C power detection relies on CC. A-to-C architecture: Legacy USB-A charging protocols may involve D+ / D−. Therefore, the fact that D+ / D− were widely used for charging detection in the USB-A era does not mean that they are required for basic charging in a USB-C-to-USB-C connection. This distinction is important in practical USB Design . 4. Three Common CC Configurations + Applicable Scenarios The most common Type-C CC configurations can be divided into three categories: Sink, Source, and DRP. Typical resistor values include: Rp = 56KΩ / 22KΩ / 10KΩ Rd = 5.1KΩ The exact configuration depends on the device role and the Type-C / USB PD requirements. Configuration 1: Dual 5.1KΩ Pull-Down Resistors on CC1 / CC2 Typical connection: CC1 → 5.1KΩ → GND CC2 → 5.1KΩ → GND Applicable to: Phones, development boards, microcontroller boards, small appliances, and other Type-C devices that work as Sink devices. Function: The device indicates that it is a powered device, allowing the Source to detect the connection and determine the plug orientation. For basic Type-C power, this configuration can support standard 5V operation. Note: Two 5.1KΩ resistors do not automatically give the device USB PD fast-charging capability. If the device needs 9V, 12V, 15V, 20V, or other USB PD voltages, an appropriate USB PD Controller and supporting power-management circuitry are normally required. （Pull-Down Resistors） Configuration 2: Dual Rp Pull-Up Resistors on CC1 / CC2 Typical connection: CC1 → Rp → VBUS CC2 → Rp → VBUS Applicable to: Standard USB Type-C chargers, power banks with Type-C output ports, and other devices that work as a Source. Function: The Source uses CC to advertise its power capability so that the connected Type-C device can identify the power source. Different Rp configurations correspond to different Type-C default current capabilities. If USB PD fast charging is required, the design needs to support PD communication through the CC channel rather than relying on Rp alone. If compatibility with legacy USB-A charging protocols is also required, additional D+ / D− charging-detection circuitry or a charging protocol IC can be added according to the product requirements. （Pull-Up Resistors） Configuration 3: Dynamic Rp / Rd Switching for DRP Applicable to: Expansion docks, power banks, portable energy-storage devices, and other Type-C devices that need to dynamically switch between Source and Sink roles. Function: The device can determine its role according to the connected device and connection state, allowing it to operate as either a power source or a powered device. Note: DRP does not simply mean connecting Rp and Rd to CC1 / CC2 at the same time. In practical designs, a Type-C Controller or USB PD Controller is typically used to dynamically manage Rp / Rd, together with power-path control for safe bidirectional power delivery. （Rp / Rd Switching Resistors） Configuration 4: Type-C + USB PD Controller for Fast Charging If the product needs more than basic 5V power, such as: 9V / 12V / 15V / 20V or needs: Voltage, current, and power negotiation then Rp / Rd resistors alone are not sufficient. A typical architecture is: CC1 / CC2 → USB PD Controller → Power Path / DC-DC The PD Controller communicates through the CC channel and controls the downstream power circuitry according to the negotiated power profile. For USB Type C Design , this distinction is important when moving from basic 5V charging to USB PD fast charging. 5. A Common Mistake: Do Not Simply Short CC1 and CC2 Together Some Type-C designs try to make the interface work in both orientations by simply connecting: CC1 + CC2 → Shorted → One Rp or Rd. This should not be treated as a standard Type-C CC configuration. Simply shorting CC1 and CC2 can cause problems with proper connection detection and orientation handling, and may lead to compatibility issues in some applications. This is especially important for designs involving USB PD, higher current levels, or E-Marker cables. The correct approach is to configure the CC pins according to the required device role: Sink: CC1 → Rd CC2 → Rd Source: CC1 → Rp CC2 → Rp DRP: CC1 / CC2 → Type-C / PD Controller for dynamic role management Therefore, in USB PCB Design, CC1 and CC2 should be treated as separate configuration paths rather than simply tying them together. （CC1 and CC2 are shorted） 6. Final Takeaway: Check CC Before D+ / D− If you are designing a basic Type-C 5V Sink interface, the first thing to remember is simple: CC1 and CC2 each use a 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor to GND. For a Type-C Source, select the appropriate Rp configuration according to the required power capability. If the product requires: Bidirectional charging → DRP 9V / 12V / 15V / 20V → USB PD Higher-current applications → Consider USB PD, cable capability, E-Marker requirements, and the complete power path D+ / D− should be determined separately according to whether the product needs: USB 2.0 data transmissionOr Legacy USB-A charging protocol compatibility. The biggest pitfall in Type-C Hardware Design is not simply whether VBUS measures 5V. The key is whether the interface correctly follows the USB Type-C rules for CC1 / CC2, Rp, Rd, DRP, and USB PD. Once these concepts are clear, basic Type-C charging interfaces become much easier to design correctly. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > USB Type-C Design and CC Pin Configuration: A Practical Hardware Design Guide USB Type-C Design and CC Pin Configuration: A Practical Hardware Design Guide by: Mila Sep 08,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout hardware design type c design usb design usb type c design usb pcb design One of the most common pitfalls in Hardware Design for Type-C interfaces is confusing the legacy protocols used by USB-A ports with the native USB Type-C protocol. The voltage is a normal 5V, the polarity is correct, but the device still does not charge, fails to be recognized, only works in one plug orientation, or has limited charging current. Compatibility issues may also occur with some phones. In many cases, there is basically one reason: CC1 and CC2 are not connected correctly. Let's look at the most common 5V Type-C charging configuration. Once you understand it, you can use it directly in your Type C Design. 1. The Most Important Conclusion For a Type-C interface, CC1 / CC2 are the core channels for power role detection, connection detection, current capability detection, and USB PD communication. D+ and D− do not handle basic Type-C power detection or USB PD negotiation in a standard C-to-C connection. This is one of the key differences between traditional USB and modern USB Type C Design: CC pins: The dedicated Type-C configuration channel used for power role detection, connection detection, plug orientation detection, Type-C current capability detection, and USB PD communication. D+ / D− pins: Mainly used for USB 2.0 data transmission and compatibility with certain legacy charging protocols, such as BC1.2. In simple terms: C-to-C charging: Basic power detection mainly relies on CC, not D+ / D−. A-to-C charging: Legacy USB-A charging protocols may use D+ / D− for charging detection. 2. Why Does C-to-C Charging Mainly Rely on CC? Taking a standard USB-C-to-USB-C charging connection as an example, the Source and Sink first establish a connection through the CC pins. The basic process is: 1. The charger provides Rp pull-ups on CC1 and CC2. 2. The phone or other powered device uses Rd pull-downs to indicate that it is a Sink. 3. The two sides detect the connection and determine the available Type-C current capability through CC. 4. If both sides support USB PD, they can further communicate through the CC channel to negotiate voltage, current, and power. It is important to note that 56KΩ, 22KΩ, and 10KΩ Rp values correspond to different advertised current capabilities. They should not be interpreted as “56KΩ directly unlocks 5V/3A.” Therefore, Type-C current capability detection and USB PD fast charging should be distinguished: Type-C current capability detection → Rp / Rd USB PD power negotiation → PD communication over CC D+ / D− mainly handle USB 2.0 data and certain legacy charging protocols. 3. CC vs. D+ / D−: What Does Each One Actually Do? CC1 / CC2: The Core Type-C Power and Connection Pins CC stands for Configuration Channel and is an important feature that distinguishes USB Type-C from traditional USB-A interfaces. CC1 and CC2 are mainly responsible for: Power role detection: Rp indicates a Source, while Rd indicates a Sink. Connection detection: Determines whether a valid connection has been established. Plug orientation detection: The active CC pin helps determine the plug orientation. Type-C current capability detection: The Source uses Rp to advertise its power capability. USB PD communication: USB PD devices use the CC channel to negotiate voltage, current, and power. Therefore, in a standard Type-C C-to-C power connection: Correct CC configuration is critical to proper device detection and power delivery. This is why CC routing and component placement are important in USB PCB Design. D+ / D−: Data Transmission and Legacy Charging Compatibility D+ / D− are essentially USB 2.0 differential data lines. They are mainly used for: 1. USB 2.0 data transmission, programming, and communication 2. Compatibility with certain legacy USB-A charging protocols For example, USB BC1.2 charging detection mechanisms may use D+ / D−. The key distinction is: C-to-C architecture: Basic Type-C power detection relies on CC. A-to-C architecture: Legacy USB-A charging protocols may involve D+ / D−. Therefore, the fact that D+ / D− were widely used for charging detection in the USB-A era does not mean that they are required for basic charging in a USB-C-to-USB-C connection. This distinction is important in practical USB Design . 4. Three Common CC Configurations + Applicable Scenarios The most common Type-C CC configurations can be divided into three categories: Sink, Source, and DRP. Typical resistor values include: Rp = 56KΩ / 22KΩ / 10KΩ Rd = 5.1KΩ The exact configuration depends on the device role and the Type-C / USB PD requirements. Configuration 1: Dual 5.1KΩ Pull-Down Resistors on CC1 / CC2 Typical connection: CC1 → 5.1KΩ → GND CC2 → 5.1KΩ → GND Applicable to: Phones, development boards, microcontroller boards, small appliances, and other Type-C devices that work as Sink devices. Function: The device indicates that it is a powered device, allowing the Source to detect the connection and determine the plug orientation. For basic Type-C power, this configuration can support standard 5V operation. Note: Two 5.1KΩ resistors do not automatically give the device USB PD fast-charging capability. If the device needs 9V, 12V, 15V, 20V, or other USB PD voltages, an appropriate USB PD Controller and supporting power-management circuitry are normally required. （Pull-Down Resistors） Configuration 2: Dual Rp Pull-Up Resistors on CC1 / CC2 Typical connection: CC1 → Rp → VBUS CC2 → Rp → VBUS Applicable to: Standard USB Type-C chargers, power banks with Type-C output ports, and other devices that work as a Source. Function: The Source uses CC to advertise its power capability so that the connected Type-C device can identify the power source. Different Rp configurations correspond to different Type-C default current capabilities. If USB PD fast charging is required, the design needs to support PD communication through the CC channel rather than relying on Rp alone. If compatibility with legacy USB-A charging protocols is also required, additional D+ / D− charging-detection circuitry or a charging protocol IC can be added according to the product requirements. （Pull-Up Resistors） Configuration 3: Dynamic Rp / Rd Switching for DRP Applicable to: Expansion docks, power banks, portable energy-storage devices, and other Type-C devices that need to dynamically switch between Source and Sink roles. Function: The device can determine its role according to the connected device and connection state, allowing it to operate as either a power source or a powered device. Note: DRP does not simply mean connecting Rp and Rd to CC1 / CC2 at the same time. In practical designs, a Type-C Controller or USB PD Controller is typically used to dynamically manage Rp / Rd, together with power-path control for safe bidirectional power delivery. （Rp / Rd Switching Resistors） Configuration 4: Type-C + USB PD Controller for Fast Charging If the product needs more than basic 5V power, such as: 9V / 12V / 15V / 20V or needs: Voltage, current, and power negotiation then Rp / Rd resistors alone are not sufficient. A typical architecture is: CC1 / CC2 → USB PD Controller → Power Path / DC-DC The PD Controller communicates through the CC channel and controls the downstream power circuitry according to the negotiated power profile. For USB Type C Design , this distinction is important when moving from basic 5V charging to USB PD fast charging. 5. A Common Mistake: Do Not Simply Short CC1 and CC2 Together Some Type-C designs try to make the interface work in both orientations by simply connecting: CC1 + CC2 → Shorted → One Rp or Rd. This should not be treated as a standard Type-C CC configuration. Simply shorting CC1 and CC2 can cause problems with proper connection detection and orientation handling, and may lead to compatibility issues in some applications. This is especially important for designs involving USB PD, higher current levels, or E-Marker cables. For a Type-C Source, select the appropriate Rp configuration according to the required power capability. If the product requires: Bidirectional charging → DRP 9V / 12V / 15V / 20V → USB PD Higher-current applications → Consider USB PD, cable capability, E-Marker requirements, and the complete power path D+ / D− should be determined separately according to whether the product needs: USB 2.0 data transmissionOr Legacy USB-A charging protocol compatibility. The biggest pitfall in Type-C Hardware Design is not simply whether VBUS measures 5V. The key is whether the interface correctly follows the USB Type-C rules for CC1 / CC2, Rp, Rd, DRP, and USB PD. Verify Now Blog > USB Type-C Design and CC Pin Configuration: A Practical Hardware Design Guide USB Type-C Design and CC Pin Configuration: A Practical Hardware Design Guide by: Mila Sep 08,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout hardware design type c design usb design usb type c design usb pcb design One of the most common pitfalls in Hardware Design for Type-C interfaces is confusing the legacy protocols used by USB-A ports with the native USB Type-C protocol. Some designers mistakenly treat D+ / D− as the core charging detection pins of Type-C, which can lead to design failures. The voltage is a normal 5V, the polarity is correct, but the device still does not charge, fails to be recognized, only works in one plug orientation, or has limited charging current. Compatibility issues may also occur with some phones. In many cases, there is basically one reason: CC1 and CC2 are not connected correctly. Let's look at the most common 5V Type-C charging configuration. Once you understand it, you can use it directly in your Type C Design. 1. The Most Important Conclusion For a Type-C interface, CC1 / CC2 are the core channels for power role detection, connection detection, current capability detection, and USB PD communication. D+ and D− do not handle basic Type-C power detection or USB PD negotiation in a standard C-to-C connection. This is one of the key differences between traditional USB and modern USB Type C Design: CC pins: The dedicated Type-C configuration channel used for power role detection, connection detection, plug orientation detection, Type-C current capability detection, and USB PD communication. D+ / D− pins: Mainly used for USB 2.0 data transmission and compatibility with certain legacy charging protocols, such as BC1.2. In simple terms: C-to-C charging: Basic power detection mainly relies on CC, not D+ / D−. A-to-C charging: Legacy USB-A charging protocols may use D+ / D− for charging detection. 2. Why Does C-to-C Charging Mainly Rely on CC? Taking a standard USB-C-to-USB-C charging connection as an example, the Source and Sink first establish a connection through the CC pins. The basic process is: 1. The charger provides Rp pull-ups on CC1 and CC2. 2. The phone or other powered device uses Rd pull-downs to indicate that it is a Sink. 3. The two sides detect the connection and determine the available Type-C current capability through CC. 4. If both sides support USB PD, they can further communicate through the CC channel to negotiate voltage, current, and power. It is important to note that 56KΩ, 22KΩ, and 10KΩ Rp values correspond to different advertised current capabilities. They should not be interpreted as “56KΩ directly unlocks 5V/3A.” Therefore, Type-C current capability detection and USB PD fast charging should be distinguished: Type-C current capability detection → Rp / Rd USB PD power negotiation → PD communication over CC D+ / D− mainly handle USB 2.0 data and certain legacy charging protocols. 3. CC vs. D+ / D−: What Does Each One Actually Do? CC1 / CC2: The Core Type-C Power and Connection Pins CC stands for Configuration Channel and is an important feature that distinguishes USB Type-C from traditional USB-A interfaces. CC1 and CC2 are mainly responsible for: Power role detection: Rp indicates a Source, while Rd indicates a Sink. Connection detection: Determines whether a valid connection has been established. Plug orientation detection: The active CC pin helps determine the plug orientation. Type-C current capability detection: The Source uses Rp to advertise its power capability. USB PD communication: USB PD devices use the CC channel to negotiate voltage, current, and power. Therefore, in a standard Type-C C-to-C power connection: Correct CC configuration is critical to proper device detection and power delivery. This is why CC routing and component placement are important in USB PCB Design. D+ / D−: Data Transmission and Legacy Charging Compatibility D+ / D− are essentially USB 2.0 differential data lines. They are mainly used for: 1. USB 2.0 data transmission, programming, and communication 2. Compatibility with certain legacy USB-A charging protocols For example, USB BC1.2 charging detection mechanisms may use D+ / D−. The key distinction is: C-to-C architecture: Basic Type-C power detection relies on CC. A-to-C architecture: Legacy USB-A charging protocols may involve D+ / D−. Therefore, the fact that D+ / D− were widely used for charging detection in the USB-A era does not mean that they are required for basic charging in a USB-C-to-USB-C connection. This distinction is important in practical USB Design . 4. Three Common CC Configurations + Applicable Scenarios The most common Type-C CC configurations can be divided into three categories: Sink, Source, and DRP. Typical resistor values include: Rp = 56KΩ / 22KΩ / 10KΩ Rd = 5.1KΩ The exact configuration depends on the device role and the Type-C / USB PD requirements. Configuration 1: Dual 5.1KΩ Pull-Down Resistors on CC1 / CC2 Typical connection: CC1 → 5.1KΩ → GND CC2 → 5.1KΩ → GND Applicable to: Phones, development boards, microcontroller boards, small appliances, and other Type-C devices that work as Sink devices. Function: The device indicates that it is a powered device, allowing the Source to detect the connection and determine the plug orientation. For basic Type-C power, this configuration can support standard 5V operation. Note: Two 5.1KΩ resistors do not automatically give the device USB PD fast-charging capability. If the device needs 9V, 12V, 15V, 20V, or other USB PD voltages, an appropriate USB PD Controller and supporting power-management circuitry are normally required. （Pull-Down Resistors） Configuration 2: Dual Rp Pull-Up Resistors on CC1 / CC2 Typical connection: CC1 → Rp → VBUS CC2 → Rp → VBUS Applicable to: Standard USB Type-C chargers, power banks with Type-C output ports, and other devices that work as a Source. Function: The Source uses CC to advertise its power capability so that the connected Type-C device can identify the power source. Different Rp configurations correspond to different Type-C default current capabilities. If USB PD fast charging is required, the design needs to support PD communication through the CC channel rather than relying on Rp alone. If compatibility with legacy USB-A charging protocols is also required, additional D+ / D− charging-detection circuitry or a charging protocol IC can be added according to the product requirements. （Pull-Up Resistors） Configuration 3: Dynamic Rp / Rd Switching for DRP Applicable to: Expansion docks, power banks, portable energy-storage devices, and other Type-C devices that need to dynamically switch between Source and Sink roles. Function: The device can determine its role according to the connected device and connection state, allowing it to operate as either a power source or a powered device. Note: DRP does not simply mean connecting Rp and Rd to CC1 / CC2 at the same time. In practical designs, a Type-C Controller or USB PD Controller is typically used to dynamically manage Rp / Rd, together with power-path control for safe bidirectional power delivery. （Rp / Rd Switching Resistors） Configuration 4: Type-C + USB PD Controller for Fast Charging If the product needs more than basic 5V power, such as: 9V / 12V / 15V / 20V or needs: Voltage, current, and power negotiation then Rp / Rd resistors alone are not sufficient. A typical architecture is: CC1 / CC2 → USB PD Controller → Power Path / DC-DC The PD Controller communicates through the CC channel and controls the downstream power circuitry according to the negotiated power profile. For USB Type C Design , this distinction is important when moving from basic 5V charging to USB PD fast charging. 5. A Common Mistake: Do Not Simply Short CC1 and CC2 Together Some Type-C designs try to make the interface work in both orientations by simply connecting: CC1 + CC2 → Shorted → One Rp or Rd. This should not be treated as a standard Type-C CC configuration. Simply shorting CC1 and CC2 can cause problems with proper connection detection and orientation handling, and may lead to compatibility issues in some applications. This is especially important for designs involving USB PD, higher current levels, or E-Marker cables. The correct approach is to configure the CC pins according to the required device role: Sink: CC1 → Rd CC2 → Rd Source: CC1 → Rp CC2 → Rp DRP: CC1 / CC2 → Type-C / PD Controller for dynamic role management Therefore, in USB PCB Design, CC1 and CC2 should be treated as separate configuration paths rather than simply tying them together. （CC1 and CC2 are shorted） 6. Final Takeaway: Check CC Before D+ / D− If you are designing a basic Type-C 5V Sink interface, the first thing to remember is simple: CC1 and CC2 each use a 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor to GND. For a Type-C Source, select the appropriate Rp configuration according to the required power capability. If the product requires: Bidirectional charging → DRP 9V / 12V / 15V / 20V → USB PD Higher-current applications → Consider USB PD, cable capability, E-Marker requirements, and the complete power path D+ / D− should be determined separately according to whether the product needs: USB 2.0 data transmissionOr Legacy USB-A charging protocol compatibility. The biggest pitfall in Type-C Hardware Design is not simply whether VBUS measures 5V. The key is whether the interface correctly follows the USB Type-C rules for CC1 / CC2, Rp, Rd, DRP, and USB PD. Once these concepts are clear, basic Type-C charging interfaces become much easier to design correctly. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing by: Mila Sep 16,2025 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb layout design schematic design pcb layout services pcb layout design services PCB layout design is the process of transforming an electrical schematic into a complete, manufacturable printed circuit board (PCB). A well-designed PCB layout must do more than simply connect components. It needs to balance electrical performance, signal integrity, power integrity, thermal management, mechanical constraints, manufacturability, and reliability. For complex electronic products, decisions made during PCB layout can have a significant impact on product performance, production yield, cost, and time to market. A professional PCB layout workflow therefore requires systematic planning, engineering review, design verification, and manufacturing preparation. Below is an overview of the PCB layout design process we follow, from the initial schematic review to final manufacturing data.You can also find more information on our PCB Layout page . Step 1 – Design Preparation and Engineering Review The PCB layout process begins with a detailed review of the design requirements and source files. Before starting the layout, our engineers review the schematic and project specifications to make sure the design is ready for PCB implementation. This includes checking: Schematic completeness and connectivity Component information and footprints Board dimensions and mechanical constraints Layer count and stack-up requirements Component placement restrictions High-speed and differential signals Power distribution requirements Impedance-control requirements Thermal considerations Manufacturing capabilities and design rules If the customer only provides a PDF or image-based schematic, we can recreate the schematic in professional EDA software before proceeding with PCB layout. If the original schematic file is available, we can directly import the design data, generate the netlist, and establish the PCB design environment. At this stage, we also identify potential design issues that could affect layout, manufacturing, or product performance. Resolving these issues early helps reduce design iterations later in the process. Step 2 – PCB Stack-Up and Design Rule Setup Before component placement and routing, the PCB layer structure and key design rules need to be established. For multilayer and high-speed PCBs, the stack-up directly affects signal integrity, impedance control, power integrity, EMI performance, and manufacturability. Depending on the application, we may define: Number of PCB layers Core and prepreg materials Copper thickness Dielectric thickness Controlled impedance requirements Power and ground reference planes Minimum trace width and spacing Via structures and drill sizes Manufacturing constraints For high-speed designs, impedance-controlled traces and their reference planes are considered from the beginning rather than being treated as an afterthought. The design rules are then configured in the EDA software to ensure that the layout remains consistent with both the electrical requirements and the PCB manufacturer's manufacturing capabilities. Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing by: Mila Sep 16,2025 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb layout design schematic design pcb layout services pcb layout design services PCB layout design is the process of transforming an electrical schematic into a complete, manufacturable printed circuit board (PCB). A well-designed PCB layout must do more than simply connect components. It needs to balance electrical performance, signal integrity, power integrity, thermal management, mechanical constraints, manufacturability, and reliability. For complex electronic products, decisions made during PCB layout can have a significant impact on product performance, production yield, cost, and time to market. A professional PCB layout workflow therefore requires systematic planning, engineering review, design verification, and manufacturing preparation. Below is an overview of the PCB layout design process we follow, from the initial schematic review to final manufacturing data.You can also find more information on our PCB Layout page . Step 1 – Design Preparation and Engineering Review The PCB layout process begins with a detailed review of the design requirements and source files. Before starting the layout, our engineers review the schematic and project specifications to make sure the design is ready for PCB implementation. This includes checking: Schematic completeness and connectivity Component information and footprints Board dimensions and mechanical constraints Layer count and stack-up requirements Component placement restrictions High-speed and differential signals Power distribution requirements Impedance-control requirements Thermal considerations Manufacturing capabilities and design rules If the customer only provides a PDF or image-based schematic, we can recreate the schematic in professional EDA software before proceeding with PCB layout. If the original schematic file is available, we can directly import the design data, generate the netlist, and establish the PCB design environment. At this stage, we also identify potential design issues that could affect layout, manufacturing, or product performance. Resolving these issues early helps reduce design iterations later in the process. Step 2 – PCB Stack-Up and Design Rule Setup Before component placement and routing, the PCB layer structure and key design rules need to be established. For multilayer and high-speed PCBs, the stack-up directly affects signal integrity, impedance control, power integrity, EMI performance, and manufacturability. Depending on the application, we may define: Number of PCB layers Core and prepreg materials Copper thickness Dielectric thickness Controlled impedance requirements Power and ground reference planes Minimum trace width and spacing Via structures and drill sizes Manufacturing constraints For high-speed designs, impedance-controlled traces and their reference planes are considered from the beginning rather than being treated as an afterthought. The design rules are then configured in the EDA software to ensure that the layout remains consistent with both the electrical requirements and the PCB manufacturer's manufacturing capabilities. Step 3 – Component Placement Component placement is one of the most important stages of PCB layout because it establishes the physical structure of the entire board. The placement strategy typically starts with components whose locations are constrained by the mechanical design, such as: Connectors Switches and buttons Mounting holes Displays Mechanical interfaces Heat sinks and other thermal components Core components such as MCUs, CPUs, FPGAs, memory devices, power ICs, and communication ICs are then positioned according to signal flow, functional relationships, and electrical requirements. Supporting components are placed close to their corresponding devices to minimize unnecessary routing length and improve electrical performance. During placement, we consider several factors simultaneously: Signal Integrity High-speed interfaces and sensitive signals require appropriate component relationships and short, well-controlled routing paths. Power Integrity Decoupling capacitors should be positioned close to the relevant power pins, while power distribution paths should be kept short and low impedance. Thermal Management Heat-generating components need sufficient copper area, thermal vias, airflow consideration, and appropriate spacing from temperature-sensitive devices. EMI/EMC Performance Sensitive analog circuits, high-speed digital circuits, switching power supplies, and other potential noise sources need to be appropriately positioned to reduce interference. Manufacturability Component spacing, assembly orientation, soldering requirements, and accessibility for inspection and rework are also considered. A well-planned placement makes subsequent routing more efficient while improving the overall reliability and manufacturability of the PCB. Step 4 – PCB Routing Once the component placement is finalized, the next stage is PCB routing. Routing is not simply about finding a path between two pads. The routing strategy must consider electrical performance, signal integrity, power distribution, EMI/EMC, and manufacturing constraints. Depending on the design, routing priorities may include: High-Speed and Critical Signals High-speed interfaces such as USB, DDR, PCIe, Ethernet, HDMI, LVDS, and other differential interfaces may require: Controlled impedance Differential-pair routing Length matching Skew control Appropriate reference planes Minimized discontinuities Careful via transitions Critical signals are routed according to their electrical requirements rather than simply following the shortest available path. Power and Ground Power distribution networks are designed to provide stable and low-impedance power delivery. Ground planes are carefully maintained to provide appropriate return paths and reduce unwanted noise and electromagnetic interference. General Signals After critical nets have been addressed, general signal routing is completed according to the defined design rules for: Trace width Trace spacing Via size Clearance Routing layers Manufacturing limitations For dense boards, routing may require multiple iterations of placement and routing optimization to achieve a balance between electrical performance and manufacturability. Step 5– Layout Optimization and Verification After routing is completed, the PCB layout undergoes a detailed optimization and verification process. This stage may include: Copper Pour and Plane Optimization Copper pours and power/ground planes are optimized to improve current return paths, grounding, shielding, and thermal performance. Silkscreen Optimization Reference designators, polarity markings, pin-1 indicators, and other assembly information are adjusted to improve readability and prevent interference with pads or other components. Design Rule Check (DRC) Automated DRC is performed to identify potential violations such as: Clearance violations Trace width violations Unconnected nets Via and drill violations Component spacing issues Copper-to-board-edge violations Other manufacturer-specific rule violations Engineer Review Beyond automated DRC, the layout is also reviewed from an engineering perspective. Depending on the project, this may include checking: Signal integrity Power integrity Thermal performance EMI/EMC considerations High-speed routing Manufacturing constraints Assembly requirements Mechanical compatibility Automated checks can identify rule violations, but they cannot replace engineering judgment. A professional PCB review therefore combines software-based verification with engineering inspection. Step 6 – Design Review and Customer Approval Before generating final manufacturing data, the completed PCB layout is provided to the customer for review. The customer can verify key aspects of the design, including: Component locations Board dimensions Connector positions Mechanical interfaces Silkscreen information Routing and design intent Any required changes are incorporated before the design is released for manufacturing. This review stage provides an important checkpoint between PCB design and production and helps ensure that the final layout accurately reflects the customer's design requirements. Step 7 – Manufacturing Data Generation Once the PCB layout has been approved, the final manufacturing data is generated. Depending on the project, the manufacturing package may include: Gerber files NC drill files PCB fabrication drawings Bill of Materials (BOM) Pick-and-place files Assembly drawings Stack-up information Other manufacturing documentation Gerber files contain the graphical information required to manufacture the PCB, including copper layers, solder mask, silkscreen, and other fabrication layers. For PCB assembly projects, the BOM and pick-and-place files provide the component and placement information required for SMT assembly. Before release, the output files are checked to ensure that the generated manufacturing data is consistent with the approved PCB design. Step 8 – DFM and PCB Manufacturing The final stage is transferring the verified manufacturing data into production. Before fabrication, the manufacturing data can be evaluated against the PCB manufacturer's capabilities through Design for Manufacturability (DFM) checks. Typical DFM considerations include: Minimum trace width and spacing Minimum drill size Copper-to-edge clearance Annular ring requirements Solder mask clearance Via structures Board thickness Copper thickness Surface finish Manufacturing tolerances Manufacturing requirements are considered from the very beginning of PCBWay's PCB layout process, helping minimize production issues and unnecessary manufacturing delays. What’s more, upon completion of the PCB Layout order, free technical support and a permanent 5% discount on PCBA production will be provided. Why Professional PCB Layout Matters PCB layout has a direct impact on the performance and manufacturability of an electronic product. A professional PCB layout should consider the entire product development process—not just whether all components are electrically connected. Depending on the application, the layout may need to address: Signal Integrity (SI) Power Integrity (PI) EMI/EMC Thermal Management High-Speed Design Design for Manufacturability (DFM) Design for Assembly (DFA) Mechanical Integration Reliability and Serviceability The earlier these factors are considered, the fewer problems are likely to appear during prototype validation and mass production. At PCBWay, our PCB design engineers work with customers throughout the layout process, helping transform circuit concepts and schematics into manufacturable, reliable, and production-ready PCB designs.
