Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Guide to Interface Driver and Connector Placement PCB Layout Guide to Interface Driver and Connector Placement by: Mila Sep 11,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB layout interface driver PCB connector placement interface PCB design People who design PCBs for embedded, industrial control, and communication hardware have probably heard a common PCB layout rule: interface drivers should be placed as close as possible to board-edge connectors. This is a practical guideline rather than an absolute requirement. For CAN and RS485, a slightly longer path may not immediately cause problems, while for high-speed interfaces such as USB, HDMI, and PCIe, longer traces can increase impedance discontinuities, parasitic effects, and return-path issues. If the driver is placed deep inside the board with a long trace between it and the connector, problems such as excessive radiated emissions, ESD-related MCU resets, closed high-speed eye diagrams, or communication errors may occur. This is why PCB connector placement and interface driver placement should be considered together in an interface PCB design . （Driver far from connector vs Driver close to connector ） 1. Three Common Types of Interface Drivers Interface drivers handle signal conversion and driving between the main controller on the PCB and external cables. Different interfaces have different transmission speeds, electrical standards, and communication protocols. From a functional perspective, they can be divided into three main categories. Level Translators / Interface Transceivers These devices primarily perform level conversion and interface adaptation, allowing two electrically incompatible systems on the PCB and external side to communicate correctly. RS232 transceiver (MAX232): Uses an internal charge pump to generate the positive and negative voltages required by RS-232. It converts TTL/CMOS logic levels on the MCU side into RS-232 levels, while the receiver performs the reverse conversion. RS-232 is a single-ended interface referenced to signal ground, not a differential interface. RS485/RS422 transceiver (MAX485): Converts single-ended TTL signals into differential signals and provides the drive capability required for long-distance bus transmission. CAN transceiver (TJA1050): Handles level conversion between the MCU logic side and the CAN bus, and drives and receives bus signals according to the dominant and recessive states defined by CAN. A practical CAN interface normally also requires external protection devices such as TVS diodes. High-Speed Physical Layer / PHY PHY devices for USB, Ethernet, HDMI/DisplayPort, and other high-speed interfaces integrate physical-layer functions for signal transmission and reception, including functions such as equalization and swing control. From a PCB layout perspective, controlled impedance, continuous reference planes, and an appropriate routing topology are required to maintain signal integrity. Differential impedance, such as 90Ω or 100Ω, is primarily determined by trace width, trace spacing, dielectric thickness, dielectric constant, and the reference plane. These parameters are implemented through the PCB stackup and routing design rather than being determined by the PHY itself. Differential Interface Drivers / Receivers Differential drivers and receivers such as LVDS and CML devices are used for high-speed point-to-point transmission. They precisely control differential common-mode voltage and signal swing to reduce jitter and overshoot during high-speed transmission. 2. Why Should Interface Drivers Usually Be Placed Close to Board-Edge Connectors? The following four factors apply differently depending on the interface type and should be evaluated as part of the overall interface PCB design. Shorten the Boundary Trace and Reduce EMI and ESD Risks Long traces between a connector and its driver increase the distance over which high-speed signals travel across the PCB and may increase the effective loop area of high-frequency currents. When the reference plane is discontinuous or the return path is interrupted, these traces are more likely to generate common-mode currents and additional EMI radiation. External ESD, surges, and environmental interference may also couple into the board through these paths. Placing the driver close to the connector shortens this section of the trace and reduces the high-frequency loop area, helping to lower the risk of radiated emissions and internal interference coupling. This can also reduce the workload during EMC debugging. However, EMI risk is not determined by trace length alone. Return paths, reference planes, loop area, signal edge rate, common-mode current, connector structure, and cable coupling all play important roles in PCB layout. Reduce Parasitic Effects and Maintain High-Speed Signal Integrity PCB traces inherently have parasitic capacitance and inductance. For high-speed differential interfaces such as USB, PCIe, MIPI, and HDMI, longer traces can increase the accumulated parasitic effects and make it more difficult to maintain impedance continuity. This can lead to slower signal edges, overshoot, ringing, and reflections, resulting in eye closure and increased bit error rates. Placing the driver close to the connector shortens the signal path, reduces unnecessary parasitic effects, and simplifies the routing topology, making it easier to maintain a continuous controlled-impedance transmission path. This is particularly important in high-speed interface PCB design. Shorten the ESD Discharge Path and Improve Protection Effectiveness Serial ports, Ethernet ports, and HDMI connectors are common entry points for ESD and surge energy. The effectiveness of ESD protection depends on many factors, including the type and location of the TVS device, dynamic clamping voltage, discharge path, grounding structure, PCB stackup, MCU tolerance, and interface isolation. It is therefore not determined by trace length alone. Placing the driver and ESD protection devices close to the connector and connecting them to the ground plane with short, direct traces helps provide a low-impedance discharge path. This reduces the risk of high-voltage pulses coupling into the core circuitry. During ESD testing, a system may experience MCU resets, communication errors, or, in severe cases, component damage. These problems need to be addressed through the overall protection architecture rather than relying on connector placement alone. Maintain a Continuous Path Between the Transceiver and Connector For differential interfaces such as RS485 and CAN, the relatively small signal swing makes differential transmission an important part of their noise immunity. Rather than simply assuming that the signal will experience significant amplitude loss along a long PCB trace, it is more important to consider whether the path between the transceiver and connector is short, continuous, and supported by a clear return path. Excessive trace length, too many vias, branches, and impedance discontinuities can increase parasitic effects and reflections while also increasing the possibility of external noise coupling into the signal path. Therefore, as part of good PCB connector placement, the differential path between the transceiver and connector should generally be kept as short and continuous as practical. 3. Practical PCB Layout Guidelines for Interface Circuit Guideline 1: Typical Placement Order — Connector → Protection → Filtering / Common-Mode Processing → Interface Transceiver → Controller From the board edge toward the center, a common arrangement is: Outer edge: Board-edge connector; Protection layer: TVS diodes, ceramic discharge devices, gas discharge tubes, and other ESD protection components; Filtering / common-mode layer: Common-mode chokes, ferrite beads, and filtering capacitors; Driver layer: MAX485, PHY, CAN transceivers, and other interface ICs; Core circuitry: MCU/FPGA and other main processing devices. This is a general placement approach rather than a universal rule. The actual order should be determined based on the interface standard, device datasheet, ESD current path, and EMC requirements. Ethernet, USB, CAN, RS485, and HDMI do not necessarily use the same protection and filtering structures, so the component sequence should be adapted to the specific interface PCB design. Guideline 2: Plan the Ground Plane and Return Path in the Interface Area External interfaces such as RS485, CAN, and Ethernet may require a dedicated interface ground that is isolated from the digital or analog ground on the main board. The ground structure and return path should be planned according to the isolation architecture. Avoid routing high-speed signals across reference-plane splits, which can interrupt the return path and increase radiated noise; For isolated RS485/CAN interfaces, plan the interface-side and system-side grounds according to the isolation components and isolated power architecture; When the two ground domains must be connected, select an appropriate connection method based on the isolation and EMC design, while controlling the connection location and return path to avoid unnecessary ground loops; Avoid routing signals across split regions for long distances. A good PCB layout should always consider the signal path and its corresponding return path together. Guideline 3: Treat Differential Interfaces According to Their Speed High-speed differential interfaces (USB, HDMI, LVDS, PCIe, etc.): Perform length matching according to the interface specification and device requirements, while maintaining consistent coupling within each differential pair. Key considerations include differential impedance, intra-pair skew, and reference-plane continuity. Length matching should follow the requirements of the specific interface rather than a universal numerical limit. Routing near the connector should be as straight as practical, avoiding unnecessary 90° corners and repeated bends. RS485, CAN, and similar interfaces: These interfaces generally do not require extremely strict length matching. Greater attention should be paid to topology, such as bus or star configurations, termination, return paths, and the parasitic effects of protection devices. Avoid routing unrelated signals between differential pairs to reduce crosstalk and preserve differential performance. Guideline 4: Minimize Vias in High-Speed Paths and Provide Nearby Ground Vias Keep high-speed signals on a single routing layer from the driver to the connector whenever practical, avoiding unnecessary layer transitions; If a layer transition is unavoidable, place nearby ground vias around the signal vias to provide a continuous, low-impedance return path for high-frequency currents. The exact number and spacing of ground vias should be determined based on the stackup, via dimensions, and interface speed to reduce signal distortion and radiation caused by layer transitions. 4. Conclusion Placing interface drivers close to board-edge connectors is a practical design guideline based on signal integrity (SI) and electromagnetic compatibility (EMC), rather than an absolute rule that applies to every interface. In general, placing the driver close to the connector provides three main benefits: Shortens boundary traces and reduces high-frequency loop area, helping lower EMI radiation and interference coupling; Shortens high-speed signal paths, reduces parasitic effects, and makes controlled-impedance routing easier; Provides a low-impedance path for ESD discharge and reduces the risk of ESD-related interference to the main controller. Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Guide to Interface Driver and Connector Placement PCB Layout Guide to Interface Driver and Connector Placement by: Mila Sep 11,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB layout interface driver PCB connector placement interface PCB design People who design PCBs for embedded, industrial control, and communication hardware have probably heard a common PCB layout rule: interface drivers should be placed as close as possible to board-edge connectors. This is a practical guideline rather than an absolute requirement. For CAN and RS485, a slightly longer path may not immediately cause problems, while for high-speed interfaces such as USB, HDMI, and PCIe, longer traces can increase impedance discontinuities, parasitic effects, and return-path issues. If the driver is placed deep inside the board with a long trace between it and the connector, problems such as excessive radiated emissions, ESD-related MCU resets, closed high-speed eye diagrams, or communication errors may occur. This is why PCB connector placement and interface driver placement should be considered together in an interface PCB design . （Driver far from connector vs Driver close to connector ） 1. Three Common Types of Interface Drivers Interface drivers handle signal conversion and driving between the main controller on the PCB and external cables. Different interfaces have different transmission speeds, electrical standards, and communication protocols. From a functional perspective, they can be divided into three main categories. Level Translators / Interface Transceivers These devices primarily perform level conversion and interface adaptation, allowing two electrically incompatible systems on the PCB and external side to communicate correctly. RS232 transceiver (MAX232): Uses an internal charge pump to generate the positive and negative voltages required by RS-232. It converts TTL/CMOS logic levels on the MCU side into RS-232 levels, while the receiver performs the reverse conversion. RS-232 is a single-ended interface referenced to signal ground, not a differential interface. RS485/RS422 transceiver (MAX485): Converts single-ended TTL signals into differential signals and provides the drive capability required for long-distance bus transmission. CAN transceiver (TJA1050): Handles level conversion between the MCU logic side and the CAN bus, and drives and receives bus signals according to the dominant and recessive states defined by CAN. A practical CAN interface normally also requires external protection devices such as TVS diodes. High-Speed Physical Layer / PHY PHY devices for USB, Ethernet, HDMI/DisplayPort, and other high-speed interfaces integrate physical-layer functions for signal transmission and reception, including functions such as equalization and swing control. From a PCB layout perspective, controlled impedance, continuous reference planes, and an appropriate routing topology are required to maintain signal integrity. Differential impedance, such as 90Ω or 100Ω, is primarily determined by trace width, trace spacing, dielectric thickness, dielectric constant, and the reference plane. These parameters are implemented through the PCB stackup and routing design rather than being determined by the PHY itself. Differential Interface Drivers / Receivers Differential drivers and receivers such as LVDS and CML devices are used for high-speed point-to-point transmission. They precisely control differential common-mode voltage and signal swing to reduce jitter and overshoot during high-speed transmission. 2. Why Should Interface Drivers Usually Be Placed Close to Board-Edge Connectors? The following four factors apply differently depending on the interface type and should be evaluated as part of the overall interface PCB design. Shorten the Boundary Trace and Reduce EMI and ESD Risks Long traces between a connector and its driver increase the distance over which high-speed signals travel across the PCB and may increase the effective loop area of high-frequency currents. When the reference plane is discontinuous or the return path is interrupted, these traces are more likely to generate common-mode currents and additional EMI radiation. External ESD, surges, and environmental interference may also couple into the board through these paths. Placing the driver close to the connector shortens this section of the trace and reduces the high-frequency loop area, helping to lower the risk of radiated emissions and internal interference coupling. This can also reduce the workload during EMC debugging. However, EMI risk is not determined by trace length alone. Return paths, reference planes, loop area, signal edge rate, common-mode current, connector structure, and cable coupling all play important roles in PCB layout. Reduce Parasitic Effects and Maintain High-Speed Signal Integrity PCB traces inherently have parasitic capacitance and inductance. For high-speed differential interfaces such as USB, PCIe, MIPI, and HDMI, longer traces can increase the accumulated parasitic effects and make it more difficult to maintain impedance continuity. This can lead to slower signal edges, overshoot, ringing, and reflections, resulting in eye closure and increased bit error rates. Placing the driver close to the connector shortens the signal path, reduces unnecessary parasitic effects, and simplifies the routing topology, making it easier to maintain a continuous controlled-impedance transmission path. This is particularly important in high-speed interface PCB design. Shorten the ESD Discharge Path and Improve Protection Effectiveness Serial ports, Ethernet ports, and HDMI connectors are common entry points for ESD and surge energy. The effectiveness of ESD protection depends on many factors, including the type and location of the TVS device, dynamic clamping voltage, discharge path, grounding structure, PCB stackup, MCU tolerance, and interface isolation. It is therefore not determined by trace length alone. Placing the driver and ESD protection devices close to the connector and connecting them to the ground plane with short, direct traces helps provide a low-impedance discharge path. This reduces the risk of high-voltage pulses coupling into the core circuitry. During ESD testing, a system may experience MCU resets, communication errors, or, in severe cases, component damage. These problems need to be addressed through the overall protection architecture rather than relying on connector placement alone. Maintain a Continuous Path Between the Transceiver and Connector For differential interfaces such as RS485 and CAN, the relatively small signal swing makes differential transmission an important part of their noise immunity. Rather than simply assuming that the signal will experience significant amplitude loss along a long PCB trace, it is more important to consider whether the path between the transceiver and connector is short, continuous, and supported by a clear return path. Excessive trace length, too many vias, branches, and impedance discontinuities can increase parasitic effects and reflections while also increasing the possibility of external noise coupling into the signal path. Therefore, as part of good PCB connector placement, the differential path between the transceiver and connector should generally be kept as short and continuous as practical. 3. Practical PCB Layout Guidelines for Interface Circuit Guideline 1: Typical Placement Order — Connector → Protection → Filtering / Common-Mode Processing → Interface Transceiver → Controller From the board edge toward the center, a common arrangement is: Outer edge: Board-edge connector; Protection layer: TVS diodes, ceramic discharge devices, gas discharge tubes, and other ESD protection components; Filtering / common-mode layer: Common-mode chokes, ferrite beads, and filtering capacitors; Driver layer: MAX485, PHY, CAN transceivers, and other interface ICs; Core circuitry: MCU/FPGA and other main processing devices. This is a general placement approach rather than a universal rule. The actual order should be determined based on the interface standard, device datasheet, ESD current path, and EMC requirements. Ethernet, USB, CAN, RS485, and HDMI do not necessarily use the same protection and filtering structures, so the component sequence should be adapted to the specific interface PCB design. Guideline 2: Plan the Ground Plane and Return Path in the Interface Area External interfaces such as RS485, CAN, and Ethernet may require a dedicated interface ground that is isolated from the digital or analog ground on the main board. The ground structure and return path should be planned according to the isolation architecture. Avoid routing high-speed signals across reference-plane splits, which can interrupt the return path and increase radiated noise; For isolated RS485/CAN interfaces, plan the interface-side and system-side grounds according to the isolation components and isolated power architecture; When the two ground domains must be connected, select an appropriate connection method based on the isolation and EMC design, while controlling the connection location and return path to avoid unnecessary ground loops; Avoid routing signals across split regions for long distances. A good PCB layout should always consider the signal path and its corresponding return path together. Guideline 3: Treat Differential Interfaces According to Their Speed High-speed differential interfaces (USB, HDMI, LVDS, PCIe, etc.): Perform length matching according to the interface specification and device requirements, while maintaining consistent coupling within each differential pair. Key considerations include differential impedance, intra-pair skew, and reference-plane continuity. Length matching should follow the requirements of the specific interface rather than a universal numerical limit. Routing near the connector should be as straight as practical, avoiding unnecessary 90° corners and repeated bends. RS485, CAN, and similar interfaces: These interfaces generally do not require extremely strict length matching. Greater attention should be paid to topology, such as bus or star configurations, termination, return paths, and the parasitic effects of protection devices. Avoid routing unrelated signals between differential pairs to reduce crosstalk and preserve differential performance. Guideline 4: Minimize Vias in High-Speed Paths and Provide Nearby Ground Vias Keep high-speed signals on a single routing layer from the driver to the connector whenever practical, avoiding unnecessary layer transitions; If a layer transition is unavoidable, place nearby ground vias around the signal vias to provide a continuous, low-impedance return path for high-frequency currents. The exact number and spacing of ground vias should be determined based on the stackup, via dimensions, and interface speed to reduce signal distortion and radiation caused by layer transitions. 4. Conclusion Placing interface drivers close to board-edge connectors is a practical design guideline based on signal integrity (SI) and electromagnetic compatibility (EMC), rather than an absolute rule that applies to every interface. In general, placing the driver close to the connector provides three main benefits: Shortens boundary traces and reduces high-frequency loop area, helping lower EMI radiation and interference coupling; Shortens high-speed signal paths, reduces parasitic effects, and makes controlled-impedance routing easier; Provides a low-impedance path for ESD discharge and reduces the risk of ESD-related interference to the main controller. Differential Interface Drivers / Receivers Differential drivers and receivers such as LVDS and CML devices are used for high-speed point-to-point transmission. They precisely control differential common-mode voltage and signal swing to reduce jitter and overshoot during high-speed transmission. 2. Why Should Interface Drivers Usually Be Placed Close to Board-Edge Connectors? The following four factors apply differently depending on the interface type and should be evaluated as part of the overall interface PCB design. When the reference plane is discontinuous or the return path is interrupted, these traces are more likely to generate common-mode currents and additional EMI radiation. External ESD, surges, and environmental interference may also couple into the board through these paths. Placing the driver close to the connector shortens this section of the trace and reduces the high-frequency loop area, helping to lower the risk of radiated emissions and internal interference coupling. This can also reduce the workload during EMC debugging. However, EMI risk is not determined by trace length alone. Return paths, reference planes, loop area, signal edge rate, common-mode current, connector structure, and cable coupling all play important roles in PCB layout. For high-speed differential interfaces such as USB, PCIe, MIPI, and HDMI, longer traces can increase the accumulated parasitic effects and make it more difficult to maintain impedance continuity. This can lead to slower signal edges, overshoot, ringing, and reflections, resulting in eye closure and increased bit error rates. Placing the driver close to the connector shortens the signal path, reduces unnecessary parasitic effects, and simplifies the routing topology, making it easier to maintain a continuous controlled-impedance transmission path. This is particularly important in high-speed interface PCB design. Shorten the ESD Discharge Path and Improve Protection Effectiveness Serial ports, Ethernet ports, and HDMI connectors are common entry points for ESD and surge energy. The effectiveness of ESD protection depends on many factors, including the type and location of the TVS device, dynamic clamping voltage, discharge path, grounding structure, PCB stackup, MCU tolerance, and interface isolation. It is therefore not determined by trace length alone. Placing the driver and ESD protection devices close to the connector and connecting them to the ground plane with short, direct traces helps provide a low-impedance discharge path. This reduces the risk of high-voltage pulses coupling into the core circuitry. During ESD testing, a system may experience MCU resets, communication errors, or, in severe cases, component damage. These problems need to be addressed through the overall protection architecture rather than relying on connector placement alone. Maintain a Continuous Path Between the Transceiver and Connector For differential interfaces such as RS485 and CAN, the relatively small signal swing makes differential transmission an important part of their noise immunity. Rather than simply assuming that the signal will experience significant amplitude loss along a long PCB trace, it is more important to consider whether the path between the transceiver and connector is short, continuous, and supported by a clear return path. Excessive trace length, too many vias, branches, and impedance discontinuities can increase parasitic effects and reflections while also increasing the possibility of external noise coupling into the signal path. Therefore, as part of good PCB connector placement, the differential path between the transceiver and connector should generally be kept as short and continuous as practical. 3. This is a general placement approach rather than a universal rule. The actual order should be determined based on the interface standard, device datasheet, ESD current path, and EMC requirements. Ethernet, USB, CAN, RS485, and HDMI do not necessarily use the same protection and filtering structures, so the component sequence should be adapted to the specific interface PCB design. Guideline 2: Plan the Ground Plane and Return Path in the Interface Area External interfaces such as RS485, CAN, and Ethernet may require a dedicated interface ground that is isolated from the digital or analog ground on the main board. The ground structure and return path should be planned according to the isolation architecture. Avoid routing high-speed signals across reference-plane splits, which can interrupt the return path and increase radiated noise; For isolated RS485/CAN interfaces, plan the interface-side and system-side grounds according to the isolation components and isolated power architecture; When the two ground domains must be connected, select an appropriate connection method based on the isolation and EMC design, while controlling the connection location and return path to avoid unnecessary ground loops; Avoid routing signals across split regions for long distances. A good PCB layout should always consider the signal path and its corresponding return path together. Guideline 3: Treat Differential Interfaces According to Their Speed High-speed differential interfaces (USB, HDMI, LVDS, PCIe, etc.): Perform length matching according to the interface specification and device requirements, while maintaining consistent coupling within each differential pair. Key considerations include differential impedance, intra-pair skew, and reference-plane continuity. Length matching should follow the requirements of the specific interface rather than a universal numerical limit. Routing near the connector should be as straight as practical, avoiding unnecessary 90° corners and repeated bends. RS485, CAN, and similar interfaces: These interfaces generally do not require extremely strict length matching. Greater attention should be paid to topology, such as bus or star configurations, termination, return paths, and the parasitic effects of protection devices. Avoid routing unrelated signals between differential pairs to reduce crosstalk and preserve differential performance. Guideline 4: Minimize Vias in High-Speed Paths and Provide Nearby Ground Vias Keep high-speed signals on a single routing layer from the driver to the connector whenever practical, avoiding unnecessary layer transitions; If a layer transition is unavoidable, place nearby ground vias around the signal vias to provide a continuous, low-impedance return path for high-frequency currents. The exact number and spacing of ground vias should be determined based on the stackup, via dimensions, and interface speed to reduce signal distortion and radiation caused by layer transitions. 4. Conclusion Placing interface drivers close to board-edge connectors is a practical design guideline based on signal integrity (SI) and electromagnetic compatibility (EMC), rather than an absolute rule that applies to every interface. In general, placing the driver close to the connector provides three main benefits: Shortens boundary traces and reduces high-frequency loop area, helping lower EMI radiation and interference coupling; Shortens high-speed signal paths, reduces parasitic effects, and makes controlled-impedance routing easier; Provides a low-impedance path for ESD discharge and reduces the risk of ESD-related interference to the main controller. Verify Now Blog > Remote-Sense Guidelines in Power Supply Design for DC-DC Converters Remote-Sense Guidelines in Power Supply Design for DC-DC Converters by: Mila Sep 07,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout power supply design power module ir drop remote sens Many DC-DC power chips provide a Remote-Sense function. However, many designers mistake it for an optional secondary connection and wire it directly near the power module's local output. This setup effectively renders remote sampling useless. During the debugging phase, various anomalies may occur: while the local output voltage of the power module appears normal, the supply voltage at the BGA core experiences continuous droop; the power supply may exhibit audible noise, Loop Stability degradation, and severe output voltage ripple fluctuations. Remote-Sense is not a redundant line, but a Kelvin Sensing line used to measure the actual voltage at the load. The main power path carries high load currents, whereas the Force & Sense architecture ensures the Force & Sense signal paths remain isolated. Because the Force & Sense sensing line features high input impedance with minimal input bias current, it avoids the significant voltage drops present along the power delivery path, thereby measuring the load voltage more accurately. 1. Root Cause of Remote-Sense Application: DC IR Drop Modern processor core supply voltages continue to drop, with typical values around 0.8V or 0.85V, while operating currents can reach tens to hundreds of amperes. Even with wide copper traces and dense via arrays on the PCB, inherent DC resistance remains in the copper foil, connectors, vias, and BGA fanout regions along the power path. As large load currents pass through these impedances, a noticeable IR Drop occurs. For example, assume a DC-DC module has a local output voltage of 1.0V, and the total equivalent resistance of the power path from the module to an FPGA's BGA power pins is 1.5mΩ. Under a 100A load current, the voltage drop VIR Drop = I × R = 100A × 1.5mΩ = 150mV. Thus, while the local output stays at 1.0V, the actual voltage at the FPGA BGA pins drops to approximately 0.85V due to IR Drop along the copper, connectors, vias, and BGA fanout. If the sampling point is placed locally at the DC-DC output, the Feedback Loop can only detect the local 1.0V rail. The Feedback Loop remains unaware of the 0.15V lost before reaching the load. For low-voltage core supplies, the allowable voltage tolerance is tight, depending on processor, FPGA, or ASIC specifications. Such voltage degradation caused by IR Drop leads to full-load crashes, frequency throttling, and inadequate timing margins on high-speed interfaces. Remote-Sense resolves this problem: by routing the Remote-Sense sampling line directly near the load chip's power pins, the system detects the true voltage at the load. When the detected load voltage falls below the target, the Feedback Loop increases the power stage output to compensate for the IR Drop along the power delivery path. (Remote-Sense Working Principle) 2. Kelvin Remote Voltage Sensing: Force & Sense At its core, Remote-Sense relies on Kelvin Sensing principles to segregate the high-current power path from the voltage detection line. Force Power Path The power path delivers actual energy to the load and requires sufficient copper width, copper weight, and parallel vias to lower impedance. Because this pathway carries the full load current, it inevitably suffers from IR Drop. Sense Sampling Path The Force & Sense sensing line has high impedance and carries only a tiny input bias current. According to V = I × R, because the current flowing through the Force & Sense sensing line is negligible, its trace resistance creates virtually no voltage drop compared to the high-current power line. Consequently, Kelvin Sensing measures the electrical potential at the load with high accuracy. The power converter's internal Feedback Loop continuously measures the error between the sense voltage and an internal reference voltage, adjusting power delivery to compensate for PCB power losses. For ICs featuring Differential Sensing, both VSENSE+ and VSENSE- must be fully connected as specified in the datasheet. Incorrectly connecting only a single sense line may cause reference errors or disable remote sampling altogether. （Kelvin Force/Sense Schematic ） 3. Remote-Sense PCB Layout Guidelines Remote-Sense is far more than a simple jumper trace. Sampling point placement, routing methods, Noise Isolation, filtering, and Multi-Load Topology configurations all impose strict constraints. Improper implementation fails to compensate for IR Drop and risks introducing high-frequency noise into the Feedback Loop, inducing output fluctuations, degraded Loop Stability, or audible squealing. VSENSE+ / VSENSE- Differential Pair Routing VSENSE+ and VSENSE- must be routed using Differential Pair Routing, kept closely coupled in identical environments. Avoid placing either trace near SW Nodes, clock lines, or other noisy sources, and never run them parallel to power switching nodes over long distances. Adequate Noise Isolation is essential to prevent interference. If the two traces experience different distances to noise sources, varying Ground Plane Reference structures, or unequal surrounding copper, external interference couples unevenly into the lines. This asymmetry converts into differential-mode noise, directly corrupting the Feedback Loop. Therefore, the main objective of Differential Pair Routing is not simply maximizing line width, but ensuring both lines share a symmetrical, low-noise environment with effective Noise Isolation, minimal loop area, and a solid Ground Plane Reference. Sensing Point Placement Incorrect: Placing the Sensing Point Placement directly across the DC-DC module's local output capacitors. This neutralizes the benefits of Remote-Sense, as the controller senses only the local output while uncompensated losses persist down the line. Correct: Proper Sensing Point Placement requires connecting the lines as close as possible to the load chip's actual power pins (e.g., near the BGA power pins), adhering to the manufacturer's recommended Sensing Point Placement guidelines. Input filtering and Decoupling Capacitors must be placed as close to the chip power pins as possible to lower the high-frequency current loop impedance at the load. The core principle of Remote-Sense layout is: The sense point must represent the true voltage received by the load, not an intermediate node along the power path. Never place sense points arbitrarily along intermediate nodes or directly on power copper pour for layout convenience. Even if schematics correctly define Differential Sensing, improper Sensing Point Placement on the PCB invalidates the feature. （Remote-Sense PCB Layout） Controller-Side RC Low-Pass Filter Sense traces often traverse long PCB paths, making them vulnerable to high-frequency interference from switching SW Nodes, DDR buses, clocks, and high-speed traces. Proper Noise Isolation helps, but if high-frequency noise reaches the sensing node, it induces output jitter and degrades Loop Stability. For long sense traces or noisy environments, place an RC Low-Pass Filter near the sense pins according to datasheet recommendations to suppress coupled switching noise. Some IC manufacturers recommend an RC Low-Pass Filter consisting of tens of ohms in series and nanofarad-range capacitors. However, specific R and C parameters must strictly follow vendor datasheets and be validated through Loop Stability testing rather than using generic values. Note that an RC Low-Pass Filter introduces an additional time constant, requiring evaluation regarding its impact on loop bandwidth, Transient Response, and overall stability. Multi-Load Topology: Reference Point at Key Load When a single power rail supplies multiple BGA devices, a Multi-Load Topology must not place the sense point at a random common node or simply at the load closest to the converter. In a Multi-Load Topology, evaluate system voltage tolerances, load currents, and power path drops to position the reference point at the most voltage-sensitive load experiencing the highest drop. For example, in a chain of DC-DC -> Load A -> Load B -> Load C, if Load C has the tightest tolerance and highest line drop in this Multi-Load Topology, connect the sense reference point directly to Load C's supply pins. This ensures the loop prioritizes the voltage margin of the critical load, while closer loads are powered via the main power path without serving as feedback references. Handling Unused Remote-Sense Pins If a design does not enable Remote-Sense, do not leave the VSENSE+ and VSENSE- pins floating, as a Floating Pin Hazard will disrupt feedback control. For controllers relying on external sense inputs, a Floating Pin Hazard leaves input potentials uncontrolled, causing abnormal output voltages and potential device damage. To avoid a Floating Pin Hazard, consult the datasheet. Devices supporting local sense mode typically require connecting VSENSE+ to local VOUT+ and VSENSE- to local GND. Always follow the manufacturer's specified wiring for local sensing, as internal architectures vary. 4. Remote-Sense Cannot Replace Power Integrity / PDN Design Remote-Sense is not a substitute for proper load-side decoupling and low-impedance Power Integrity / PDN design. Remote-Sense primarily compensates for DC or low-frequency voltage losses along the power path. When a CPU, FPGA, GPU, or ASIC undergoes a fast step change, the Transient Response of the feedback loop cannot react instantaneously. Verify Now Blog > Remote-Sense Guidelines in Power Supply Design for DC-DC Converters Remote-Sense Guidelines in Power Supply Design for DC-DC Converters by: Mila Sep 07,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout power supply design power module ir drop remote sens Many DC-DC power chips provide a Remote-Sense function. However, many designers mistake it for an optional secondary connection and wire it directly near the power module's local output. This setup effectively renders remote sampling useless. During the debugging phase, various anomalies may occur: while the local output voltage of the power module appears normal, the supply voltage at the BGA core experiences continuous droop; the power supply may exhibit audible noise, Loop Stability degradation, and severe output voltage ripple fluctuations. Remote-Sense is not a redundant line, but a Kelvin Sensing line used to measure the actual voltage at the load. The main power path carries high load currents, whereas the Force & Sense architecture ensures the Force & Sense signal paths remain isolated. Because the Force & Sense sensing line features high input impedance with minimal input bias current, it avoids the significant voltage drops present along the power delivery path, thereby measuring the load voltage more accurately. 1. Root Cause of Remote-Sense Application: DC IR Drop Modern processor core supply voltages continue to drop, with typical values around 0.8V or 0.85V, while operating currents can reach tens to hundreds of amperes. Even with wide copper traces and dense via arrays on the PCB, inherent DC resistance remains in the copper foil, connectors, vias, and BGA fanout regions along the power path. As large load currents pass through these impedances, a noticeable IR Drop occurs. For example, assume a DC-DC module has a local output voltage of 1.0V, and the total equivalent resistance of the power path from the module to an FPGA's BGA power pins is 1.5mΩ. Under a 100A load current, the voltage drop VIR Drop = I × R = 100A × 1.5mΩ = 150mV. Thus, while the local output stays at 1.0V, the actual voltage at the FPGA BGA pins drops to approximately 0.85V due to IR Drop along the copper, connectors, vias, and BGA fanout. If the sampling point is placed locally at the DC-DC output, the Feedback Loop can only detect the local 1.0V rail. The Feedback Loop remains unaware of the 0.15V lost before reaching the load. For low-voltage core supplies, the allowable voltage tolerance is tight, depending on processor, FPGA, or ASIC specifications. Such voltage degradation caused by IR Drop leads to full-load crashes, frequency throttling, and inadequate timing margins on high-speed interfaces. Remote-Sense resolves this problem: by routing the Remote-Sense sampling line directly near the load chip's power pins, the system detects the true voltage at the load. When the detected load voltage falls below the target, the Feedback Loop increases the power stage output to compensate for the IR Drop along the power delivery path. (Remote-Sense Working Principle) 2. Kelvin Remote Voltage Sensing: Force & Sense At its core, Remote-Sense relies on Kelvin Sensing principles to segregate the high-current power path from the voltage detection line. Force Power Path The power path delivers actual energy to the load and requires sufficient copper width, copper weight, and parallel vias to lower impedance. Because this pathway carries the full load current, it inevitably suffers from IR Drop. Sense Sampling Path The Force & Sense sensing line has high impedance and carries only a tiny input bias current. According to V = I × R, because the current flowing through the Force & Sense sensing line is negligible, its trace resistance creates virtually no voltage drop compared to the high-current power line. Consequently, Kelvin Sensing measures the electrical potential at the load with high accuracy. The power converter's internal Feedback Loop continuously measures the error between the sense voltage and an internal reference voltage, adjusting power delivery to compensate for PCB power losses. For ICs featuring Differential Sensing, both VSENSE+ and VSENSE- must be fully connected as specified in the datasheet. Incorrectly connecting only a single sense line may cause reference errors or disable remote sampling altogether. （Kelvin Force/Sense Schematic ） 3. Remote-Sense PCB Layout Guidelines Remote-Sense is far more than a simple jumper trace. Sampling point placement, routing methods, Noise Isolation, filtering, and Multi-Load Topology configurations all impose strict constraints. Improper implementation fails to compensate for IR Drop and risks introducing high-frequency noise into the Feedback Loop, inducing output fluctuations, degraded Loop Stability, or audible squealing. VSENSE+ / VSENSE- Differential Pair Routing VSENSE+ and VSENSE- must be routed using Differential Pair Routing, kept closely coupled in identical environments. Avoid placing either trace near SW Nodes, clock lines, or other noisy sources, and never run them parallel to power switching nodes over long distances. Adequate Noise Isolation is essential to prevent interference. If the two traces experience different distances to noise sources, varying Ground Plane Reference structures, or unequal surrounding copper, external interference couples unevenly into the lines. This asymmetry converts into differential-mode noise, directly corrupting the Feedback Loop. Therefore, the main objective of Differential Pair Routing is not simply maximizing line width, but ensuring both lines share a symmetrical, low-noise environment with effective Noise Isolation, minimal loop area, and a solid Ground Plane Reference. Sensing Point Placement Incorrect: Placing the Sensing Point Placement directly across the DC-DC module's local output capacitors. This neutralizes the benefits of Remote-Sense, as the controller senses only the local output while uncompensated losses persist down the line. Correct: Proper Sensing Point Placement requires connecting the lines as close as possible to the load chip's actual power pins (e.g., near the BGA power pins), adhering to the manufacturer's recommended Sensing Point Placement guidelines. Input filtering and Decoupling Capacitors must be placed as close to the chip power pins as possible to lower the high-frequency current loop impedance at the load. The core principle of Remote-Sense layout is: The sense point must represent the true voltage received by the load, not an intermediate node along the power path. Never place sense points arbitrarily along intermediate nodes or directly on power copper pour for layout convenience. Even if schematics correctly define Differential Sensing, improper Sensing Point Placement on the PCB invalidates the feature. （Remote-Sense PCB Layout） Controller-Side RC Low-Pass Filter Sense traces often traverse long PCB paths, making them vulnerable to high-frequency interference from switching SW Nodes, DDR buses, clocks, and high-speed traces. Proper Noise Isolation helps, but if high-frequency noise reaches the sensing node, it induces output jitter and degrades Loop Stability. For long sense traces or noisy environments, place an RC Low-Pass Filter near the sense pins according to datasheet recommendations to suppress coupled switching noise. Some IC manufacturers recommend an RC Low-Pass Filter consisting of tens of ohms in series and nanofarad-range capacitors. However, specific R and C parameters must strictly follow vendor datasheets and be validated through Loop Stability testing rather than using generic values. Note that an RC Low-Pass Filter introduces an additional time constant, requiring evaluation regarding its impact on loop bandwidth, Transient Response, and overall stability. Multi-Load Topology: Reference Point at Key Load When a single power rail supplies multiple BGA devices, a Multi-Load Topology must not place the sense point at a random common node or simply at the load closest to the converter. In a Multi-Load Topology, evaluate system voltage tolerances, load currents, and power path drops to position the reference point at the most voltage-sensitive load experiencing the highest drop. For example, in a chain of DC-DC -> Load A -> Load B -> Load C, if Load C has the tightest tolerance and highest line drop in this Multi-Load Topology, connect the sense reference point directly to Load C's supply pins. This ensures the loop prioritizes the voltage margin of the critical load, while closer loads are powered via the main power path without serving as feedback references. For controllers relying on external sense inputs, a Floating Pin Hazard leaves input potentials uncontrolled, causing abnormal output voltages and potential device damage. To avoid a Floating Pin Hazard, consult the datasheet. Devices supporting local sense mode typically require connecting VSENSE+ to local VOUT+ and VSENSE- to local GND. Always follow the manufacturer's specified wiring for local sensing, as internal architectures vary. 4. Remote-Sense Cannot Replace Power Integrity / PDN Design Remote-Sense is not a substitute for proper load-side decoupling and low-impedance Power Integrity / PDN design. Remote-Sense primarily compensates for DC or low-frequency voltage losses along the power path. Verify Now Blog > Remote-Sense Guidelines in Power Supply Design for DC-DC Converters Remote-Sense Guidelines in Power Supply Design for DC-DC Converters by: Mila Sep 07,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout power supply design power module ir drop remote sens Many DC-DC power chips provide a Remote-Sense function. However, many designers mistake it for an optional secondary connection and wire it directly near the power module's local output. This setup effectively renders remote sampling useless. During the debugging phase, various anomalies may occur: while the local output voltage of the power module appears normal, the supply voltage at the BGA core experiences continuous droop; the power supply may exhibit audible noise, Loop Stability degradation, and severe output voltage ripple fluctuations. Remote-Sense is not a redundant line, but a Kelvin Sensing line used to measure the actual voltage at the load. The main power path carries high load currents, whereas the Force & Sense architecture ensures the Force & Sense signal paths remain isolated. Because the Force & Sense sensing line features high input impedance with minimal input bias current, it avoids the significant voltage drops present along the power delivery path, thereby measuring the load voltage more accurately. 1. Root Cause of Remote-Sense Application: DC IR Drop Modern processor core supply voltages continue to drop, with typical values around 0.8V or 0.85V, while operating currents can reach tens to hundreds of amperes. Even with wide copper traces and dense via arrays on the PCB, inherent DC resistance remains in the copper foil, connectors, vias, and BGA fanout regions along the power path. As large load currents pass through these impedances, a noticeable IR Drop occurs. For example, assume a DC-DC module has a local output voltage of 1.0V, and the total equivalent resistance of the power path from the module to an FPGA's BGA power pins is 1.5mΩ. Under a 100A load current, the voltage drop VIR Drop = I × R = 100A × 1.5mΩ = 150mV. Thus, while the local output stays at 1.0V, the actual voltage at the FPGA BGA pins drops to approximately 0.85V due to IR Drop along the copper, connectors, vias, and BGA fanout. If the sampling point is placed locally at the DC-DC output, the Feedback Loop can only detect the local 1.0V rail. The Feedback Loop remains unaware of the 0.15V lost before reaching the load. For low-voltage core supplies, the allowable voltage tolerance is tight, depending on processor, FPGA, or ASIC specifications. Such voltage degradation caused by IR Drop leads to full-load crashes, frequency throttling, and inadequate timing margins on high-speed interfaces. Remote-Sense resolves this problem: by routing the Remote-Sense sampling line directly near the load chip's power pins, the system detects the true voltage at the load. When the detected load voltage falls below the target, the Feedback Loop increases the power stage output to compensate for the IR Drop along the power delivery path. (Remote-Sense Working Principle) 2. Kelvin Remote Voltage Sensing: Force & Sense At its core, Remote-Sense relies on Kelvin Sensing principles to segregate the high-current power path from the voltage detection line. Force Power Path The power path delivers actual energy to the load and requires sufficient copper width, copper weight, and parallel vias to lower impedance. Because this pathway carries the full load current, it inevitably suffers from IR Drop. Sense Sampling Path The Force & Sense sensing line has high impedance and carries only a tiny input bias current. According to V = I × R, because the current flowing through the Force & Sense sensing line is negligible, its trace resistance creates virtually no voltage drop compared to the high-current power line. Consequently, Kelvin Sensing measures the electrical potential at the load with high accuracy. The power converter's internal Feedback Loop continuously measures the error between the sense voltage and an internal reference voltage, adjusting power delivery to compensate for PCB power losses. For ICs featuring Differential Sensing, both VSENSE+ and VSENSE- must be fully connected as specified in the datasheet. Incorrectly connecting only a single sense line may cause reference errors or disable remote sampling altogether. （Kelvin Force/Sense Schematic ） 3. Remote-Sense PCB Layout Guidelines Remote-Sense is far more than a simple jumper trace. Sampling point placement, routing methods, Noise Isolation, filtering, and Multi-Load Topology configurations all impose strict constraints. Improper implementation fails to compensate for IR Drop and risks introducing high-frequency noise into the Feedback Loop, inducing output fluctuations, degraded Loop Stability, or audible squealing. VSENSE+ / VSENSE- Differential Pair Routing VSENSE+ and VSENSE- must be routed using Differential Pair Routing, kept closely coupled in identical environments. Avoid placing either trace near SW Nodes, clock lines, or other noisy sources, and never run them parallel to power switching nodes over long distances. Adequate Noise Isolation is essential to prevent interference. If the two traces experience different distances to noise sources, varying Ground Plane Reference structures, or unequal surrounding copper, external interference couples unevenly into the lines. This asymmetry converts into differential-mode noise, directly corrupting the Feedback Loop. Therefore, the main objective of Differential Pair Routing is not simply maximizing line width, but ensuring both lines share a symmetrical, low-noise environment with effective Noise Isolation, minimal loop area, and a solid Ground Plane Reference. Sensing Point Placement Incorrect: Placing the Sensing Point Placement directly across the DC-DC module's local output capacitors. This neutralizes the benefits of Remote-Sense, as the controller senses only the local output while uncompensated losses persist down the line. Correct: Proper Sensing Point Placement requires connecting the lines as close as possible to the load chip's actual power pins (e.g., near the BGA power pins), adhering to the manufacturer's recommended Sensing Point Placement guidelines. Input filtering and Decoupling Capacitors must be placed as close to the chip power pins as possible to lower the high-frequency current loop impedance at the load. The core principle of Remote-Sense layout is: The sense point must represent the true voltage received by the load, not an intermediate node along the power path. Never place sense points arbitrarily along intermediate nodes or directly on power copper pour for layout convenience. Even if schematics correctly define Differential Sensing, improper Sensing Point Placement on the PCB invalidates the feature. （Remote-Sense PCB Layout） Controller-Side RC Low-Pass Filter Sense traces often traverse long PCB paths, making them vulnerable to high-frequency interference from switching SW Nodes, DDR buses, clocks, and high-speed traces. Proper Noise Isolation helps, but if high-frequency noise reaches the sensing node, it induces output jitter and degrades Loop Stability. For long sense traces or noisy environments, place an RC Low-Pass Filter near the sense pins according to datasheet recommendations to suppress coupled switching noise. Some IC manufacturers recommend an RC Low-Pass Filter consisting of tens of ohms in series and nanofarad-range capacitors. However, specific R and C parameters must strictly follow vendor datasheets and be validated through Loop Stability testing rather than using generic values. Note that an RC Low-Pass Filter introduces an additional time constant, requiring evaluation regarding its impact on loop bandwidth, Transient Response, and overall stability. Multi-Load Topology: Reference Point at Key Load When a single power rail supplies multiple BGA devices, a Multi-Load Topology must not place the sense point at a random common node or simply at the load closest to the converter. In a Multi-Load Topology, evaluate system voltage tolerances, load currents, and power path drops to position the reference point at the most voltage-sensitive load experiencing the highest drop. For example, in a chain of DC-DC -> Load A -> Load B -> Load C, if Load C has the tightest tolerance and highest line drop in this Multi-Load Topology, connect the sense reference point directly to Load C's supply pins. This ensures the loop prioritizes the voltage margin of the critical load, while closer loads are powered via the main power path without serving as feedback references. Handling Unused Remote-Sense Pins If a design does not enable Remote-Sense, do not leave the VSENSE+ and VSENSE- pins floating, as a Floating Pin Hazard will disrupt feedback control. For controllers relying on external sense inputs, a Floating Pin Hazard leaves input potentials uncontrolled, causing abnormal output voltages and potential device damage. To avoid a Floating Pin Hazard, consult the datasheet. Devices supporting local sense mode typically require connecting VSENSE+ to local VOUT+ and VSENSE- to local GND. Always follow the manufacturer's specified wiring for local sensing, as internal architectures vary. 4. Remote-Sense Cannot Replace Power Integrity / PDN Design Remote-Sense is not a substitute for proper load-side decoupling and low-impedance Power Integrity / PDN design. Remote-Sense primarily compensates for DC or low-frequency voltage losses along the power path. When a CPU, FPGA, GPU, or ASIC undergoes a fast step change, the Transient Response of the feedback loop cannot react instantaneously. During these events, Decoupling Capacitors and a low-impedance Power Integrity / PDN supply transient current and mitigate sharp voltage dips. Therefore, comprehensive Power Integrity / PDN design requires integrating multiple strategies: Low-impedance Power/GND planes with a continuous Ground Plane Reference Adequate copper width and parallel via arrays Load-side MLCC Decoupling Capacitors Bulk capacitors Optimized power routing Remote-Sense implementation High Transient Response and stable loop margins Remote-Sense, power path optimization, and Decoupling Capacitors complement each other rather than act as replacements. 5. Additional Remote-Sense Constraints and Safety Considerations If Remote-Sense is connected to a distant load without being properly configured or enabled, incorrect feedback compensation may drive the local voltage too high, triggering OVP / UVP Protection, instability, or exceeding maximum operating limits. Always consult the datasheet to confirm: Support for Remote-Sense and Differential Sensing Allowable voltage ranges for sense inputs Correct connections for local sensing mode Requirements for an RC Low-Pass Filter Optimal Sensing Point Placement Interaction between Remote-Sense and OVP / UVP Protection thresholds Maximum allowable sense trace lengths and routing layouts If the sense voltage drops excessively due to open circuits or extreme line losses, improperly configured controllers may trigger OVP / UVP Protection to prevent overvoltage damage at the local output or undervoltage failures at the load. Ultimately, Remote-Sense is not just about routing two lines to the load. It ensures the feedback loop accurately measures the actual voltage delivered to the load while maintaining reliable OVP / UVP Protection and preventing noise or parasitics from degrading system stability.l Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. For low-voltage core supplies, the allowable voltage tolerance is tight, depending on processor, FPGA, or ASIC specifications. Such voltage degradation caused by IR Drop leads to full-load crashes, frequency throttling, and inadequate timing margins on high-speed interfaces. Remote-Sense resolves this problem: by routing the Remote-Sense sampling line directly near the load chip's power pins, the system detects the true voltage at the load. When the detected load voltage falls below the target, the Feedback Loop increases the power stage output to compensate for the IR Drop along the power delivery path. (Remote-Sense Working Principle) 2. Kelvin Remote Voltage Sensing: Force & Sense At its core, Remote-Sense relies on Kelvin Sensing principles to segregate the high-current power path from the voltage detection line. Force Power Path The power path delivers actual energy to the load and requires sufficient copper width, copper weight, and parallel vias to lower impedance. Because this pathway carries the full load current, it inevitably suffers from IR Drop. Sense Sampling Path The Force & Sense sensing line has high impedance and carries only a tiny input bias current. According to V = I × R, because the current flowing through the Force & Sense sensing line is negligible, its trace resistance creates virtually no voltage drop compared to the high-current power line. Consequently, Kelvin Sensing measures the electrical potential at the load with high accuracy. The power converter's internal Feedback Loop continuously measures the error between the sense voltage and an internal reference voltage, adjusting power delivery to compensate for PCB power losses. For ICs featuring Differential Sensing, both VSENSE+ and VSENSE- must be fully connected as specified in the datasheet. Incorrectly connecting only a single sense line may cause reference errors or disable remote sampling altogether. （Kelvin Force/Sense Schematic ） 3. Remote-Sense PCB Layout Guidelines Remote-Sense is far more than a simple jumper trace. Sampling point placement, routing methods, Noise Isolation, filtering, and Multi-Load Topology configurations all impose strict constraints. Improper implementation fails to compensate for IR Drop and risks introducing high-frequency noise into the Feedback Loop, inducing output fluctuations, degraded Loop Stability, or audible squealing. VSENSE+ / VSENSE- Differential Pair Routing VSENSE+ and VSENSE- must be routed using Differential Pair Routing, kept closely coupled in identical environments. Avoid placing either trace near SW Nodes, clock lines, or other noisy sources, and never run them parallel to power switching nodes over long distances. Adequate Noise Isolation is essential to prevent interference. If the two traces experience different distances to noise sources, varying Ground Plane Reference structures, or unequal surrounding copper, external interference couples unevenly into the lines. This asymmetry converts into differential-mode noise, directly corrupting the Feedback Loop. Therefore, the main objective of Differential Pair Routing is not simply maximizing line width, but ensuring both lines share a symmetrical, low-noise environment with effective Noise Isolation, minimal loop area, and a solid Ground Plane Reference. Sensing Point Placement Incorrect: Placing the Sensing Point Placement directly across the DC-DC module's local output capacitors. This neutralizes the benefits of Remote-Sense, as the controller senses only the local output while uncompensated losses persist down the line. Correct: Proper Sensing Point Placement requires connecting the lines as close as possible to the load chip's actual power pins (e.g., near the BGA power pins), adhering to the manufacturer's recommended Sensing Point Placement guidelines. Input filtering and Decoupling Capacitors must be placed as close to the chip power pins as possible to lower the high-frequency current loop impedance at the load. The core principle of Remote-Sense layout is: The sense point must represent the true voltage received by the load, not an intermediate node along the power path. Never place sense points arbitrarily along intermediate nodes or directly on power copper pour for layout convenience. Even if schematics correctly define Differential Sensing, improper Sensing Point Placement on the PCB invalidates the feature. （Remote-Sense PCB Layout） Controller-Side RC Low-Pass Filter Sense traces often traverse long PCB paths, making them vulnerable to high-frequency interference from switching SW Nodes, DDR buses, clocks, and high-speed traces. Proper Noise Isolation helps, but if high-frequency noise reaches the sensing node, it induces output jitter and degrades Loop Stability. For long sense traces or noisy environments, place an RC Low-Pass Filter near the sense pins according to datasheet recommendations to suppress coupled switching noise. Some IC manufacturers recommend an RC Low-Pass Filter consisting of tens of ohms in series and nanofarad-range capacitors. However, specific R and C parameters must strictly follow vendor datasheets and be validated through Loop Stability testing rather than using generic values. Note that an RC Low-Pass Filter introduces an additional time constant, requiring evaluation regarding its impact on loop bandwidth, Transient Response, and overall stability. Multi-Load Topology: Reference Point at Key Load When a single power rail supplies multiple BGA devices, a Multi-Load Topology must not place the sense point at a random common node or simply at the load closest to the converter. In a Multi-Load Topology, evaluate system voltage tolerances, load currents, and power path drops to position the reference point at the most voltage-sensitive load experiencing the highest drop. For example, in a chain of DC-DC -> Load A -> Load B -> Load C, if Load C has the tightest tolerance and highest line drop in this Multi-Load Topology, connect the sense reference point directly to Load C's supply pins. This ensures the loop prioritizes the voltage margin of the critical load, while closer loads are powered via the main power path without serving as feedback references. Handling Unused Remote-Sense Pins If a design does not enable Remote-Sense, do not leave the VSENSE+ and VSENSE- pins floating, as a Floating Pin Hazard will disrupt feedback control. For controllers relying on external sense inputs, a Floating Pin Hazard leaves input potentials uncontrolled, causing abnormal output voltages and potential device damage. To avoid a Floating Pin Hazard, consult the datasheet. Devices supporting local sense mode typically require connecting VSENSE+ to local VOUT+ and VSENSE- to local GND. Always follow the manufacturer's specified wiring for local sensing, as internal architectures vary. 4. Remote-Sense Cannot Replace Power Integrity / PDN Design Remote-Sense is not a substitute for proper load-side decoupling and low-impedance Power Integrity / PDN design. Remote-Sense primarily compensates for DC or low-frequency voltage losses along the power path. When a CPU, FPGA, GPU, or ASIC undergoes a fast step change, the Transient Response of the feedback loop cannot react instantaneously. During these events, Decoupling Capacitors and a low-impedance Power Integrity / PDN supply transient current and mitigate sharp voltage dips. Therefore, comprehensive Power Integrity / PDN design requires integrating multiple strategies: Low-impedance Power/GND planes with a continuous Ground Plane Reference Adequate copper width and parallel via arrays Load-side MLCC Decoupling Capacitors Bulk capacitors Optimized power routing Remote-Sense implementation High Transient Response and stable loop margins Remote-Sense, power path optimization, and Decoupling Capacitors complement each other rather than act as replacements. 5. Additional Remote-Sense Constraints and Safety Considerations If Remote-Sense is connected to a distant load without being properly configured or enabled, incorrect feedback compensation may drive the local voltage too high, triggering OVP / UVP Protection, instability, or exceeding maximum operating limits. Always consult the datasheet to confirm: Support for Remote-Sense and Differential Sensing Allowable voltage ranges for sense inputs Correct connections for local sensing mode Requirements for an RC Low-Pass Filter Optimal Sensing Point Placement Interaction between Remote-Sense and OVP / UVP Protection thresholds Maximum allowable sense trace lengths and routing layouts If the sense voltage drops excessively due to open circuits or extreme line losses, improperly configured controllers may trigger OVP / UVP Protection to prevent overvoltage damage at the local output or undervoltage failures at the load. Ultimately, Remote-Sense is not just about routing two lines to the load. It ensures the feedback loop accurately measures the actual voltage delivered to the load while maintaining reliable OVP / UVP Protection and preventing noise or parasitics from degrading system stability.l Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac.
