Its zinc-magnesium-copper alloying system enables mechanical properties that approach those of some steels while remaining significantly lighter. These characteristics make it a primary material choice for aerospace, defense, and high-performance automotive applications where structural efficiency is critical. At the same time, its poor weldability and susceptibility to stress corrosion cracking in certain environments require careful engineering consideration. Understanding both its capabilities and limitations is essential when selecting 7075 aluminum for demanding, load-bearing designs." Dr. Mahder Tewolde PhD What are the Material Properties of 7075 Aluminum? The material properties of 7075 Aluminum are listed below. Tensile Strength ( 570 MPa) :570 MPa is the upper-range ultimate tensile strength for 7075-T6/T651 temper, not for all 7075 aluminum. Yield Strength (505 MPa) : 505 MPa is typical for 7075-T6, not annealed or overaged tempers (e.g., T73). Density (2.81 g/cm³) : The value shows that 7075 aluminum is lighter compared to steel, making it an optimal choice for applications where weight reduction is crucial, particularly in aerospace. Hardness (150 HB) : 150 HB applies specifically to 7075-T6; other tempers exhibit lower hardness. Thermal Conductivity (130 W/m·K) : The value indicates how well 7075 aluminum can conduct heat. It is useful in applications where thermal management is critical. Solidus temperature ~477 °C and Liquidus temperature: ~635°C : The melting point defines the temperature at which the alloy transitions from solid to liquid. 7075 rapidly loses strength above ~120–150 °C and is not recommended for sustained high-temperature applications. How Do 7075 Aluminum Properties Impact Performance? 7075 aluminum properties impact performance by enabling it to resist high loads, making it ideal for applications that require strength under stress. The material’s high tensile strength allows it to perform well under pressure, while its High hardness contributes to wear resistance, while fatigue resistance is governed by microstructure, surface condition, stress concentration, and loading cycles, not hardness alone. Its low ductility limits its ability to deform, making it unsuitable for applications requiring significant bending or stretching. The strength of 7075 aluminum outweighs its formability, making it the best choice for rigid parts that need to maintain structural integrity under demanding conditions in aerospace and military applications, where high performance and durability are essential. Does 7075 Aluminum Offer Higher Strength Than Most Aluminum Alloys? Yes, 7075 aluminum offers higher strength than most aluminum alloys. 7075 aluminum's strength is largely attributed to the zinc-based alloying elements, which improve its tensile strength and make it capable of withstanding high stress. The combination of zinc, magnesium, and copper gives 7075 aluminum near-steel strength while maintaining a relatively low weight, making it a preferred material for high-performance applications where strength and lightweight properties are essential. The unique combination of features places 7075 aluminum in a category of alloys with strength comparable to steel, but 7075 aluminum is lighter than steel, but it has moderate to poor corrosion resistance compared to many other aluminum alloys (e.g., 5xxx and 6xxx series) and often requires protective coatings. Does 7075 Aluminum Have a Higher Yield Strength Than 6061 Aluminum? Yes, 7075 aluminum has a higher yield strength than 6061 aluminum. 7075-T6 yield strength: ~480–505 MPa 6061-T6 yield strength: ~240–275 MPa 7075-T6 has ~75–100% higher yield strength, not “nearly double” in all cases. The higher yield strength allows 7075 aluminum to support much heavier loads and withstand greater stress before permanent deformation occurs. The alloy’s improved yield strength makes it suitable for applications requiring high strength and resistance to heavy loads in aerospace, military, and structural components. 7075 excels in high-strength applications where load-bearing capacity and durability are essential, while 6061 aluminum is a versatile alloy known for its good balance of properties. Where is 7075 Aluminum Alloy Used? 7075 aluminum alloy is used in industries where high strength and low weight are essential. 7075 aluminum alloy is used for aircraft frames, wing spars, and fuselage components due to its ability to withstand high-stress loads while maintaining a lightweight structure in aerospace. The military industry favors 7075 aluminum for manufacturing parts like gun receivers, aircraft components, and vehicle structures, as it offers an excellent strength-to-weight ratio and resistance to fatigue. Sports equipment (bicycle frames, skis, and golf clubs) benefits from 7075 aluminum due to its high strength and durability, which are essential for performance under impact. 7075 aluminum is used in racing car components, suspension parts, and lightweight frames, where strength and low weight directly impact speed and handling in the automotive industry. Industries prefer 7075 aluminum for its exceptional strength and strength-to-weight ratio, while corrosion resistance is moderate to poor and often managed through surface treatments (anodizing, cladding, coatings). Which Industries Rely on 7075 Aluminum for High Stress Applications? Industries that rely on 7075 aluminum for high-stress applications include aerospace, defense, and motorsports. 7075 aluminum is used for critical parts (aircraft frames, wings, and fuselage components) due to its ability to handle immense stress while remaining lightweight in aerospace. The defense sector also utilizes 7075 aluminum for manufacturing high-performance equipment (military vehicle parts and gun components), where strength and reliability are essential under extreme conditions. 7075 aluminum is employed in racing car frames, suspension parts, and engine components because its strength-to-weight ratio directly impacts performance, speed, and handling in motorsports. Each industry favors 7075 aluminum for its high strength, resistance to fatigue, and 7075 aluminum is durable in high-stress mechanical environments, but it has moderate to poor corrosion resistance and may require protective treatments in harsh or corrosive environments, making it an ideal material for performance-driven applications. Is 7075 Aluminum Commonly Used in Aerospace Structures? Yes, 7075 aluminum is commonly used in aerospace structures. 7075 aluminum's high strength-to-weight ratio makes it ideal for critical components (aircraft frames, wing spars, and fittings), where strength is essential without adding excessive weight. The alloy's ability to withstand high-stress loads while maintaining a lightweight structure is a key reason for its widespread use in the aerospace industry. 7075 aluminum is preferred for applications where performance and durability are critical, ensuring reliable performance in the demanding environments encountered in aviation. Can 7075 Aluminum Be Used in Injection Molding Tooling? Yes, 7075 aluminum can be used in injection molding tooling for high-strength applications. 7075 aluminum's good machinability allows for precise fabrication of molds, making it suitable for short-run production. 7075 aluminum can withstand injection molding pressures for low- to moderate-volume molds and lower clamping-force applications, but it is not suitable for high-volume, long-life tooling compared to hardened tool steels, while its lightweight properties make it easier to handle and maintain. 7075 aluminum is chosen for tooling in industries that require high-performance molds capable of enduring repeated use without compromising structural integrity, as highlighted in the Injection Molding Material Selection Guide . How Strong is 7075 Aluminum? 7075 aluminum is very strong, Tensile strength of ~540–570 MPa and yield strength of ~480–505 MPa, which apply specifically to 7075-T6 / T651 temper, not all 7075 aluminum. The feature makes it stronger than 6061 aluminum, which has a tensile strength of around 310 MPa and a yield strength of 276 MPa. Compared to steel, 7075 aluminum is much lighter but provides high strength. 7075 aluminum offers a strong strength-to-weight ratio, which is crucial for applications where weight and strength are essential (aerospace and military components), while steel has a tensile strength of 400-550 MPa (depending on the type). Heat treatment plays a critical role in enhancing the strength of 7075 aluminum. 7075 aluminum achieves its maximum strength in the T6 temper, offering improved hardness and resistance to stress. T73 improves stress corrosion cracking resistance for aerospace service, but 7075 is generally not recommended for marine environments, even in T73, without heavy protection. The heat treatment processes make 7075 aluminum highly effective in high-stress applications, ensuring strength and durability. How Does the Strength-to-Weight Ratio of 7075 Aluminum Compare to Other Grades? The strength-to-weight ratio of 7075 aluminum compares favorably with other grades by offering one of the highest ratios available among aluminum alloys. Tensile strength of ~540–570 MPa and yield strength of ~480–505 MPa apply specifically to 7075-T6 / T651 temper, not all 7075 aluminum. In comparison, 6061 and 5052 alloys have tensile strengths of around 310 MPa and 260 MPa, respectively. Material selection is application-dependent; titanium, steels, or other aluminum alloys may outperform 7075 in specific conditions. Its exceptional strength-to-weight ratio ensures optimal performance in situations where minimizing weight without compromising strength is critical. Can 7075 Aluminum Replace Steel in Certain Load-Bearing Applications? Yes, 7075 aluminum can replace steel in certain load-bearing applications. 7075 aluminum provides an excellent strength-to-weight ratio, while steel generally offers higher strength in absolute terms, making it a viable alternative in applications where weight reduction is essential without sacrificing performance. For example, 7075 aluminum is used in parts (aircraft frames and structural components in aerospace and military sectors), where its strength and low weight help improve efficiency and fuel performance. 7075 aluminum excels in situations requiring strength and reduced weight, though it does not fully replace steel in applications requiring maximum tensile strength. 7075 aluminum offers advantages in weight reduction and ease of machining, but it has moderate to poor corrosion resistance and often requires surface treatments. Some steels—especially stainless and coated steels—have equal or superior corrosion resistance. Things to consider when choosing an Aluminum grade are listed below. Strength : The tensile strength and yield strength of the aluminum grade determine its ability to withstand applied loads without deformation or failure. Consider the required strength for the specific application. Corrosion Resistance : Aluminum alloys vary in their ability to resist corrosion, which is crucial for applications exposed to harsh environments, such as marine or outdoor conditions. Machinability : The ease with which an aluminum alloy can be machined into desired shapes or parts. Alloys with higher machinability are easier to process but may offer lower strength. Weldability : Some aluminum alloys are easier to weld than others. Choose a grade based on the need for welding and the type of welding process being used. Cost : Different aluminum grades come at varying price points. Consider budget constraints while selecting a grade that meets the performance requirements. Intended Application : The final choice of aluminum grade depends on the specific demands of the application (weight, strength, corrosion resistance), and whether the material needs to be welded or machined. Which Factors Determine Whether 7075 Aluminum Is the Right Choice for a Project? Factors that determine whether 7075 aluminum is the right choice for a project include the required strength. 7075 aluminum is one of the strongest alloys, making it ideal for high-stress applications (aerospace and military components). Corrosion resistance is another important consideration. 7075 aluminum has moderate to poor corrosion resistance and performs significantly worse than 6061 in corrosive or marine environments unless protected by cladding or coatings. Machinability plays a role. 7075 aluminum is harder than many aluminum alloys but still offers good machinability, especially compared to steels. However, it is less formable than softer aluminum grades. Weldability is a key factor since 7075 has poor weldability, making it unsuitable for projects that require welding. Cost is another consideration. 7075 aluminum is pricier than other grades, which limits its use for certain projects. The specific application requirements must be considered. 7075 excels in applications that require high strength and durability, but is not the best choice for projects that prioritize formability or corrosion resistance. Does the environment impact aluminum grade selection? Yes, the environment impacts aluminum grade selection in weight-critical designs. Aluminum alloys like 7075 offer comparable strength to steel but at a much lower weight, making them ideal for aerospace and military applications in environments where strength and low weight are important. Aluminum alloys are not suitable for environments with high heat exposure, as they lose strength at elevated temperatures. Most aluminum alloys lose strength rapidly above ~120–150 °C. For high-temperature environments, titanium alloys, nickel alloys, or steels are typically required. Environmental conditions, including exposure to chemicals, moisture, and temperature fluctuations, influence the choice of aluminum grade to ensure the material performs optimally in the given conditions. How is 7075 Aluminum Different from 6061 Aluminum? 7075 aluminum differs from 6061 aluminum by offering higher strength due to its composition, which includes zinc, magnesium, and copper, while 6061 aluminum is composed of aluminum, magnesium, and silicon. The tensile strength of 7075 aluminum is 570 MPa, compared to 6061 aluminum’s 310 MPa, making 7075 better suited for high-strength applications like aerospace and military components. 6061 aluminum excels in terms of corrosion resistance in marine environments, as it has better resistance to oxidation. 7075 aluminum is more susceptible to stress corrosion cracking (SCC), particularly in the T6 temper. 6061 aluminum has better general corrosion resistance and much lower SCC susceptibility. Machinability is another difference, with 7075 aluminum actually has excellent machinability, often better than 6061 in terms of chip formation and surface finish, though it causes higher tool wear due to hardness, making it a more cost-effective choice for complex machining projects. 7075 aluminum, with its higher strength, is more challenging to machine but offers superior durability in demanding applications. 6061 aluminum is more affordable compared to 7075 aluminum, which comes at a higher price due to its advanced properties. 7075 aluminum is the ideal choice for high-performance and high-strength applications, while 6061 Aluminum is better for applications requiring ease of machining and corrosion resistance. Is 7075 Aluminum as Strong as Stainless Steel? Yes, 7075 aluminum is as strong as stainless steel in terms of strength-to-weight ratio. 7075 aluminum offers a much lower weight, making it an ideal choice for applications where reducing weight is essential without compromising strength, while stainless steel generally has a higher tensile and yield strength than 7075 aluminum. Most stainless steels have a density of ~8.0 g/cm³ in terms of density, while 7075 aluminum has a density of 2.81 g/cm³, making aluminum about one-third the weight of stainless steel. The significant difference in weight allows 7075 aluminum to perform well in situations where the strength-to-weight ratio is more important than absolute strength, such as in aerospace and military applications. 7075 aluminum’s yield strength is around 505 MPa, while stainless steel has a yield strength between 250 and 550 MPa, depending on the grade. 7075 aluminum’s excellent strength-to-weight ratio makes it a highly effective alternative in applications where high strength and reduced weight are essential, while the absolute strength of stainless steel is higher in certain grades. Welding reduces the strength of the material around the weld area, making it unsuitable for applications that require extensive welding. Corrosion Susceptibility : 7075 aluminum has moderate to poor corrosion resistance, is more susceptible to stress corrosion cracking (SCC), and performs worse than 6061 aluminum in marine and highly corrosive environments unless protected by cladding or coatings. Higher Cost : 7075 aluminum is pricier than other aluminum alloys due to its complex composition and high strength. What Limitations Should Be Evaluated Before Using 7075 Aluminum? Corrosion, heat sensitivity, and welding limitations should be evaluated before using 7075 aluminum. 7075 aluminum is more susceptible to stress corrosion cracking in environments with high moisture or chemicals, which compromise its durability. Heat sensitivity is another factor, as the alloy loses significant strength at elevated temperatures, making it unsuitable for applications exposed to heat. Welding is challenging with 7075 aluminum, as its poor weldability leads to weakened areas around the welds, reducing its strength. Does 7075 Aluminum Require Protective Coatings in Corrosive Environments? Yes, 7075 aluminum requires protective coatings in corrosive environments. 7075 aluminum is more susceptible to stress corrosion cracking and oxidation compared to other aluminum alloys like 6061, while it has some resistance to corrosion. Coatings are recommended to improve their durability in harsh environments, with anodizing being one of the most common methods. Anodizing improves corrosion resistance, surface hardness, and wear resistance, but it does not increase the tensile strength or yield strength of 7075 aluminum. What are the Common Trade Names of 7075 Aluminum? The items listed are standard alloy designations used in different specification systems Alloy 7075 : The general designation used in most regions to refer to this high-strength aluminum alloy. UNS A97075 : The Unified Numbering System (UNS) designation for 7075 aluminum, used in North America for standardization. AlZn5.5MgCu : AlZn5.5MgCu is a chemical composition–based designation commonly used in European (EN/DIN) systems and corresponds to EN AW-7075. How Are Commercial and Industry Trade Names for 7075 Aluminum Used? The trade names (Alloy 7075, UNS A97075, and AlZn5.5MgCu) help distinguish different grades of 7075 aluminum, ensuring that the material meets the necessary specifications for particular applications. The alloy has poor weldability due to its high strength and specific alloying elements, which make it prone to hot cracking during the welding process. 7075 aluminum experiences a significant loss of strength near the weld zones when welded, reducing the material’s structural integrity. The presence of zinc in the alloy further complicates welding, as it leads to the formation of brittle phases in the heat-affected zones. The issues make 7075 aluminum less suitable for applications that require extensive welding. 6061 aluminum is preferred in some cases, which has better weldability. What is the Operating Temperature Range for 7075 Aluminum? The operating temperature range for 7075 aluminum spans from -50°C to 150°C. 7075 aluminum retains much of its strength at lower temperatures, making it suitable for use in cold environments. 7075 aluminum performance declines at elevated temperatures. The material begins to lose strength beyond 150 °C, with significant degradation occurring as the temperature increases. 7075 aluminum is inappropriate for high-heat applications. Most high-strength aluminum alloys, including 7075, 7050, and 2024, experience similar strength degradation above ~120–150 °C. For true high-temperature service, titanium alloys, steels, or nickel-based alloys are required. The alloy maintains good performance within its working temperature range but requires careful consideration when exposed to extreme heat, as its strength and hardness are notably affected by high temperatures. What is an Aluminum Alloy? An aluminum alloy is a mixture of aluminum with other elements (copper, magnesium, zinc, and manganese) to improve its properties. Pure aluminum is not as strong or long-lasting. The additional elements work together to improve the material's performance for applications (aerospace structures, automotive components, marine hardware, structural frames). For example, copper improves tensile strength and hardness, while magnesium primarily contributes to strength and hardenability rather than corrosion resistance. Zinc contributes to high strength, particularly in high-stress environments. The process of alloying allows manufacturers to tailor aluminum's properties to specific needs, making it ideal for industries like aerospace, automotive, and construction. Alloying allows for greater workability and better heat treatment responses, making aluminum alloys more versatile in demanding conditions. What is the Alloy Composition of 7075 Aluminum? The alloy is more prone to stress corrosion cracking compared to 6061, which has better inherent resistance to oxidation, while it does offer some corrosion resistance. 7075 aluminum requires surface treatments to improve its durability (anodizing or coating) to enhance its corrosion resistance. Each treatment helps protect the material from environmental factors and ensures long-term performance in marine or highly corrosive applications, where 6061 performs better without additional treatment. Does 7075 Aluminum Require Protective Coatings in Corrosive Environments? Yes, 7075 aluminum requires protective coatings in corrosive environments. 7075 aluminum is more susceptible to stress corrosion cracking and oxidation compared to other aluminum alloys like 6061, while it has some resistance to corrosion. Coatings are recommended to improve their durability in harsh environments, with anodizing being one of the most common methods. Anodizing improves corrosion resistance, surface hardness, and wear resistance, but it does not increase the tensile strength or yield strength of 7075 aluminum. The protective coating helps extend the service life of 7075 aluminum, making it more suitable for applications in marine, aerospace, and other environments where exposure to moisture, chemicals, or saltwater accelerates deterioration. What are the Common Trade Names of 7075 Aluminum? The items listed are standard alloy designations used in different specification systems Alloy 7075 : The general designation used in most regions to refer to this high-strength aluminum alloy. UNS A97075 : The Unified Numbering System (UNS) designation for 7075 aluminum, used in North America for standardization. AlZn5.5MgCu : AlZn5.5MgCu is a chemical composition–based designation commonly used in European (EN/DIN) systems and corresponds to EN AW-7075. How Are Commercial and Industry Trade Names for 7075 Aluminum Used? The identifiers Alloy 7075, UNS A97075, and AlZn5.5MgCu are standardized alloy designations, not trade names, and are used to identify certified grades of the alloy that meet specific standards and performance criteria. The trade names (Alloy 7075, UNS A97075, and AlZn5.5MgCu) help distinguish different grades of 7075 aluminum, ensuring that the material meets the necessary specifications for particular applications. The trade names are essential for sourcing the correct material and Mechanical properties are confirmed by temper designation and material certification, not by the alloy name alone. The use of trade names ensures that manufacturers and suppliers comply with industry standards and that the material performs as expected in high-stress applications (aerospace and military), where performance and reliability are essential. Are Trade Names Important When Sourcing Certified 7075 Aluminum Materials? Yes, Certification and authenticity of 7075 aluminum are established through standardized alloy designations, temper, governing specifications, and material test reports (MTRs)—not trade names. Authenticity and compliance are confirmed by Alloy designation (e.g., AA 7075 / UNS A97075 / EN AW-7075), Temper (e.g., T6, T73, T76), Applicable standard (ASTM, AMS, EN, ISO), Mill Test Certificate (EN 10204 3.1 / 3.2 or ASTM equivalent). Using the correct trade name helps prevent material mismatch, which leads to failure in high-performance applications. Aerospace qualification depends on AMS specifications, temper control, lot traceability, and certification, not trade names. Suppliers and manufacturers can verify that the material is genuine and certified by referencing the trade names, minimizing the risk of using substandard or incorrect alloys in critical components. Is 7075 Aluminum Good for Welding? No, 7075 aluminum is not good for welding. The alloy has poor weldability due to its high strength and specific alloying elements, which make it prone to hot cracking during the welding process. 7075 aluminum experiences a significant loss of strength near the weld zones when welded, reducing the material’s structural integrity. The presence of zinc in the alloy further complicates welding, as it leads to the formation of brittle phases in the heat-affected zones. The issues make 7075 aluminum less suitable for applications that require extensive welding. 6061 aluminum is preferred in some cases, which has better weldability. What is the Operating Temperature Range for 7075 Aluminum? The operating temperature range for 7075 aluminum spans from -50°C to 150°C. 7075 aluminum retains much of its strength at lower temperatures, making it suitable for use in cold environments. 7075 aluminum performance declines at elevated temperatures. The material begins to lose strength beyond 150 °C, with significant degradation occurring as the temperature increases. 7075 aluminum is inappropriate for high-heat applications. Most high-strength aluminum alloys, including 7075, 7050, and 2024, experience similar strength degradation above ~120–150 °C. For true high-temperature service, titanium alloys, steels, or nickel-based alloys are required. The alloy maintains good performance within its working temperature range but requires careful consideration when exposed to extreme heat, as its strength and hardness are notably affected by high temperatures. How does temperature affect 7075 aluminum performance? Temperature affects 7075 aluminum performance by reducing its strength at elevated temperatures. 7075 aluminum begins to progressively lose strength above ~120 °C, with accelerated degradation as temperature and exposure time increase beyond ~150 °C. The heat weakens the temper of the material, leading to a loss of the strength achieved through heat treatment processes, such as T6 tempering. 7075 aluminum becomes more prone to deformation and stress, limiting its use in high-temperature environments. The reduction in strength makes 7075 aluminum unsuitable for applications requiring continuous exposure to elevated temperatures, such as in engine components or other high-heat environments. Its use is restricted in high-temperature settings, while 7075 aluminum performs well in applications that require high strength at room temperature. Does Elevated Temperature Reduce the Strength of 7075 Aluminum? Yes, elevated temperature reduces the strength of 7075 aluminum. 7075 aluminum experiences a notable decline in tensile strength and hardness. 7075 aluminum begins to progressively lose strength above ~120°C, with more rapid degradation occurring as temperature and exposure time increase beyond ~150°C. The reduction in strength occurs due to the weakening of the temper achieved through heat treatment processes like T6. 7075 aluminum is not heat-resistant, and prolonged exposure to high temperatures causes it to become more prone to deformation and stress. 7075 aluminum is unsuitable for applications that require sustained exposure to high heat, such as engine components or high-temperature environments, where alloys with better heat resistance are more appropriate. How Xometry can Help with Aluminum Alloy Projects Xometry can help with aluminum alloy projects by providing comprehensive manufacturing services (CNC machining, sheet metal fabrication, and 3D printing). Xometry’s CNC machining services enable the precise production of parts in 7075 aluminum, making it ideal for high-strength applications in industries such as aerospace, defense, and automotive. Sheet metal fabrication supports the creation of structural components and enclosures from aluminum alloys, ensuring consistent quality. 3D printing is typically used for prototypes in other aluminum alloys or plastics, which may later be transitioned to machined 7075 aluminum for production. events.before: Resources / Materials / All About Engineering Plastics: Definition, Importance, Uses, Properties, and Types All About Engineering Plastics: Definition, Importance, Uses, Properties, and Types Written by Dean McClements 17 min read Published October 5, 2023 Updated September 3, 2026 Engineering plastics are specially designed and formulated to have improved properties compared to commodity plastics. These properties may include better mechanical, electrical, and thermal properties; improved chemical and ultraviolet light resistance; and biocompatibility for food packaging applications. While not every engineering plastic exhibits all of these traits, they are distinct from commodity plastics due to their ability to be used in a broader range of technically demanding applications — from gears in power transmission applications to medical implants and prosthetics. Examples of various engineering plastics include: nylon, polyethylene terephthalate (PET), acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS), polycarbonate (PC), and many more. The low density of engineering plastics compared to metals, coupled with their impressive material properties and economical price, make them a lighter-weight alternative to metals for a variety of applications. This article will review the subject of engineering plastics: their definition, their uses, their properties, and the many different types. What Are Engineering Plastics? Engineering plastics are a class of polymers that have been specially formulated to exhibit enhanced mechanical, electrical, thermal, and chemical properties compared to commodity plastics. These enhanced properties allow engineering plastics to be used in demanding industrial and engineering applications such as gears, bearings, bushings, and medical implants. The main difference between engineering plastics and commodity plastics is that engineering plastics are used in more technically demanding environments. While commodity plastics are also popular, they are not suitable for the same applications as engineering plastics as they do not exhibit the same degree of material properties. Engineering plastic parts are typically manufactured by plastic injection molding or plastic extrusion, although 3D printing is also possible. What Is the Importance of Engineering Plastics? Engineering plastics play a pivotal role in many industries, such as: automotive, aerospace, electronics, medical, and consumer goods manufacturing. Engineering plastics are known for their ability to be used in applications where metals may be too heavy, expensive, or susceptible to corrosion, and where commodity plastics lack the strength and durability required. They are durable and versatile owing to their mechanical strength and impact resistance, coupled with their desirable thermal, electrical, and chemical properties. Engineering plastics offer manufacturers an ideal balance between strength, cost, weight, and durability. What Are the Properties of Engineering Plastics? The desirable properties of engineering plastics are listed and described below: 1. Abrasion Resistance Abrasion resistance is a material’s ability to resist damage due to scratches, wearing, rubbing, marring, or any other friction-related phenomenon. Engineering plastics exhibit a high degree of abrasion resistance compared to commodity plastics due to their improved mechanical properties, specifically their hardness. Good abrasion resistance makes engineering plastics great for parts that are prone to wear, such as guide rollers, gears, and bushings. 2. Chemical Resistance Chemical resistance is a material’s ability to resist reacting with various compounds, oils, solvents, gasses, and other elements in its operating environment. Engineering plastics generally exhibit good chemical resistance. This property makes them good for use in environments where exposure to chemicals is common, e.g., machinery of all kinds, medical applications, and consumer goods like kitchenware, cookware, and bathroom products. 3. Dimensional Stability Dimensional stability refers to a material’s ability to retain its manufactured dimensions in the presence of high or low temperatures. Engineering plastics have varying levels of dimensional stability depending on the particular type of engineering plastic. The good dimensional stability of engineering plastics makes them useful for high-heat environments where thermal expansion is likely such as in the automotive, aerospace, and industrial industries. 4. Electrical Properties Electrical properties are related to a material’s ability to conduct or insulate electrical currents. Electrical conductivity and resistivity are the two critical electrical properties of engineering plastics. Most engineering plastics are poor electrical conductors which makes them ideal for applications where electrical insulation is desired, such as in various electronic and wiring applications. 5. Flammability Flammability is a material’s tendency to catch fire. Engineering plastics have varying levels of flammability depending on the particular type of engineering plastic. Some engineering plastics, such as PEEK or PPS, are specifically formulated for flame resistance and ignition prevention while other engineering plastics<dynamic-value> ABS, are flammable. Engineering plastics that are non-flammable are exceptional for use in applications where ignition is a concern such as in chemical processing. 6. Food Compatibility Food compatibility refers to a material’s safety for use with food, specifically in packaging. Some engineering plastics, such as PET, POM, PMMA, and ABS, are safe for use with food due to their chemical structure and lack of additives, dyes, and other harmful products. Others, for example, polycarbonate, are not safe. 7. Impact Strength Impact strength is a material’s ability to resist deformation due to a sudden or intense application of load, also known as a shock load. Impact strength is a critical property that characterizes how well a material can withstand sudden forces. Compared to commodity plastics, many engineering plastics exhibit high impact strength, which makes them good for load-bearing applications that are subjected to varying impact forces, such as machine guards and electronic housings. 8. Min/Max Operating Temperature (Thermal Resistance) Thermal resistance is the property that characterizes a material’s ability to resist changes in its properties due to varying temperatures. Specifically, the low temperature at which materials become brittle and the high temperature at which materials become soft and even melt. Engineering plastics have varying degrees of thermal resistance depending on the type of plastic. For instance, PEEK is specially formulated for use in high-temperature environments (up to 250 °C). High-temperature environments where plastics are used include various machinery and industrial applications. 9. Sliding Properties The sliding, or anti-friction, properties of engineering plastics make the materials more wear-resistant and abrasion-resistant compared to commodity plastics. Engineering plastics notably have a low coefficient of friction which enables these properties to be possible. The sliding properties of engineering plastics make them ideal for applications where repeated sliding, rubbing, or scraping are common such as in machinery components like wear pads, bearings, gears, pulleys, and rollers or medical applications like hip implants. 10. Ultraviolet (UV) Light Resistance UV resistance refers to a material’s ability to resist degradation and discoloration due to exposure to ultraviolet rays from sunlight and other sources. UV rays can break down polymer chains and cause chemical changes within the material. UV resistance is important for engineering plastics because it enhances their ability to be used outside or in other UV exposure-intense environments. Many engineering plastics, particularly polyamides, PMMA, and Ultem®, exhibit outstanding UV resistance, which makes them able to be used in environments with constant UV exposure. 11. Water Absorption Water absorption refers to a material’s affinity to absorb water. Engineering plastics are water-resistant and do not easily allow water to penetrate into the material. This makes engineering plastics ideal for applications where water contact is common. To learn more, see our full article on Common Types of Engineering Plastics. What Are the Different Types of Engineering Plastics? There are numerous types of engineering plastics which are listed and described below: 1. Nylon 6 Nylon 6 is a specific grade of nylon, or polyamide, material. Nylon 6 has good stiffness, toughness, electric and thermal insulation properties, and mechanical strength. Its properties can further be enhanced with glass fiber and other compounds. Nylon 6 is used for forming dies, insulators, washers, rollers, pulleys, valve seats, and more. 2. Polyethylene Terephthalate (PET) PET is a popular type of engineering plastic known for its high strength, chemical resistance, and recyclability. A type of polyester, PET is used in applications like textiles, food and beverage containers, pill bottles, and more. An illustration a PET bottle 3. Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene (ABS) ABS is another preferred type of engineering plastic that is valued for its chemical and thermal stability, strength, toughness, and glossy finish. Its host of desirable properties make it a versatile material. It is used in everything from consumer products like toys and bicycle helmets to automotive applications such as interior trim pieces, housings for electronics, and more. To learn more, see our guide on Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene . Try Xometry's Instant Quoting Engine® Test-drive a sample part to get instant pricing and DFM analysis Launch Demo A sample of Xometry's ABS material. 4. Nylon 6-6 Nylon 6-6 is another type of nylon (or polyamide) material. It has the same properties as nylon 6 but has a greater range of operating temperatures (up to 103 °C before deformation begins) and chemical resistance compared to Nylon 6 . Nylon 6-6 is used in applications such as conveyor belts, clothing and other textiles, bearings, bushings, sprockets, electronic housings, and more. 5. Polyimides Polyimides (PI) are formed by the combination of aromatic dianhydrides and aromatic diamines. This particular combination of chemicals yields a polyimide material with excellent thermal stability, high tensile strength, and good chemical resistance. These properties enable polyimides to be used in environments with temperature extremes up to 370 °C, in applications such as fuel cells, insulating coatings, structural adhesives, and more. 6. Polyether Ether Ketone (PEEK) PEEK stands out from other engineering plastics due to its wide range of operating temperatures (up to 250 °C), outstanding chemical resistance, high strength, and stiffness. PEEK is used for pump and valve components; bearings, bushings, and seals in machinery; electrical connectors; and medical device components. 7. Polyphenylene Sulfide (PPS) PPS is a high-performance, tough engineering plastic with great dimensional and thermal stability, as well as a wide operating temperature range of up to 260 °C and good chemical resistance. Moreover, PPS<dynamic-value> most other thermoplastics, is an electrical insulator. Its ability to be used at high temperatures coupled with its thermal stability makes PPS great for applications such as semiconductor components in machinery, bearings, and valve seats. 8. Poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) PMMA, also known as acrylic, is a common type of engineering plastic that is valued for its optical clarity, high strength, impact resistance, and light weight. For these reasons, PMMA is commonly used as a glass substitute. Applications of PMMA include windows, signage, display cases and fixtures, machine guards, and more. 9. Polybutylene Terephthalate (PBT) PBT has properties similar to those of PET (polyethylene terephthalate). It is known for its dimensional stability, low moisture absorption, high strength, stiffness, and chemical, UV, and thermal resistance. It is commonly used in automotive fenders and interior trim pieces, power tool housings, and electrical enclosures. 10. Polyphenylene Oxide (PPO) PPO, exhibits low moisture absorption, has excellent electrical and thermal insulating properties, great dimensional stability, and can be used in temperatures up to 155 °C. PPO is used for automotive fenders, electronics housings, and medical instruments. 11. Polyamides (PA) Polyamides are a class of engineering plastic formed by chains of amide molecules. Nylons and aramids are both types of polyamides. Polyamides are known for their high strength, impact resistance, and dimensional stability, which makes them useful for a wide range of applications in various industries. From clothes and textiles to automotive trim pieces, to bushings and bearings in industrial machines, polyamides are a common type of engineering plastic. 12. Polycarbonates (PC) Polycarbonates are known for their optical clarity, chemical resistance, tensile and impact strength, fire resistance, and recyclability. Polycarbonates are used in applications such as: machine guards, CDs, motorcycle face shields and windscreens, electronics housings, signage, streetlamps, safety glasses, and more. Polycarbonate 3D printed part made by Xometry 13. Polyetherimide (PEI) ULTEM® PEI, also known by the popular brand name ULTEM®, is an engineering plastic valued for its mechanical strength, rigidity, creep resistance over a wide temperature range, and electrical insulation properties. PEI boasts the highest dielectric strength of any commercially available thermoplastic and is therefore commonly used in the electronics industry for fuses and coils. Additionally, it is used in the aerospace industry, where it is used for interior trim pieces. 14. Polyetherketoneketone (PEKK) PEKK is an engineering plastic with characteristics similar to those of PEEK. This is because PEEK and PEKK are both part of a group of thermoplastics known as polyaryletherketones (PAEK). For additive manufacturing applications, a PEKK 3D printer can produce parts that take advantage of the material’s mechanical strength, thermal stability, and chemical resistance. PEKK is characterized by good mechanical strength, thermal stability, and chemical resistance. Because of its mechanical strength and chemical resistance, PEKK is used in high-pressure pumps, gear wheels, propellers, orthopedic and dental implants, and more. 15. Polyetherketone (PEK) PEK is a type of PAEK engineering plastic that is known for its low thermal expansion coefficient, creep resistance, chemical resistance, low flammability, and mechanical properties over a broad temperature range up to 260 °C. These properties make PEK useful for applications where loads are applied at high temperatures for an extended time such as in gears, bushings, bearings, shafts, and more. PEK is used in the aerospace, machinery, and automotive industries. 16. Polyketone (PK) Polyketone is an engineering plastic that is a type of PAEK. PK has high impact strength — about two to three times higher than nylon or PBT — and has excellent wear and chemical resistance. Its wear and chemical resistance make PK often used in the automotive, oil and gas, and chemical industries. 17. Polyoxymethylene Plastic (POM / Acetal) POM, also known as acetal or Delrin®, is one of the most popular engineering plastics due to its high strength, toughness, elasticity, dimensional stability, excellent machinability, impact strength, low friction coefficient, and chemical resistance. Acetal is used in everything from gears, pulleys, and rollers to snap fasteners like zippers and buckles due to its abrasion resistance and high strength. 18. Polysulfone (PSU) PSU is a translucent engineering plastic that is known for its food compatibility, biocompatibility, wide service temperature range of up to 160 °C, and good mechanical properties. PSU is used in the medical and food preparation industries due to its bio-friendliness for applications like manifolds in food processing or medical trays. 19. Polytetrafluroethylene (PTFE / Teflon®) PTFE is a popular engineering plastic known for its versatile properties. These properties include: broad temperature range from -240 °C to 260 °C and low moisture absorption, low coefficient of friction, flexibility, and chemical resistance. PTFE is used in many different applications, such as wiper blades, cookware, pipes for high-purity chemical processing, nail polish, and more. What Are the Most Common Types of Engineering Plastics? Different sources will list different engineering plastics as being the most common types. The list below was chosen based on which engineering plastics are most widely used across the largest variety of industries. PET: PET is a type of polyester with a broad range of uses such as: clothing, textiles, food and beverage containers, and pill bottles. PET is widely available, cheap to manufacture, easy to recycle, and has excellent mechanical properties. However, its low heat resistance, tendency to oxidize, and low biodegradability limit the applications where PET can be used. ABS: ABS is used in many different applications — from consumer components and automotive components to electronic devices of all kinds. ABS is inexpensive and plentiful, strong, lightweight, ductile, and thermally stable. However, ABS has poor resistance to fatigue, is flammable, and has a lower melting point compared to other engineering plastics. PC: Polycarbonate is used in applications such as machine guards, automotive headlamps, windows, safety glasses, and more. It is a fire-resistant material that is also lightweight, thermally insulating, strong, and fully recyclable. However, PC is sensitive to scratches and has a high coefficient of thermal expansion. How Does Plastic Engineering Work? Plastic engineering is a branch of engineering that focuses on the design and development of plastic materials and products. The boundaries of plastic engineering range from research and development in chemical laboratory settings to the plant floor where the process parameters for plastic machinery such as injection molding machines and plastic extruders are studied and optimized for a particular product. The purpose of plastic engineering is to create and optimize new plastic materials from organic polymers that are either petrochemical-based or naturally occurring. These plastic materials are synthesized via chemical reactions and are created to satisfy specific needs and applications. What Are the Advantages of Engineering Plastics? Engineering plastics have several advantages over commodity plastics, such as: Possess enhanced mechanical properties, such as improved tensile strength, impact strength, and toughness compared to commodity plastics’ properties Are lightweight and strong materials Exhibit a high degree of chemical resistance, making them great for applications where exposure to various oils, solvents, and chemicals is common Resist UV light damage (especially PMMA, ULTEM, and PTFE), making them reliable performers in outdoor environments What Are the Applications of Engineering Plastics? Listed below are some of the many applications of engineering plastics: Engineering plastics such as polycarbonate, ABS, nylon 6, and nylon 6-6 are widely used in the automotive industry for components like dashboards, interior trim pieces, electronic component housings, fuel caps, door handles, and more. PEEK, polyimides, PAI, and PTFE are engineering plastics commonly used in the aerospace industry. Examples are: pump gears, valve seats, electrical insulators and housings, and more. Food and beverage containers and disposable trays and plates are commonly made from engineering plastics. PET is the engineering plastic most frequently used in food and beverage applications due to its strength, chemical resistance, UV resistance, food compatibility, and recyclability. Electronic components such as housings, switches, end terminals, insulators, displays, and more can be made from engineering plastics. Such engineering plastics as nylon 6, nylon 6-6, PC, PBT, ABS, and PEI are often used in the electronics industry due to their mechanical properties such as: tensile strength and impact resistance, electrical insulation properties, wide operating temperature ranges, and chemical resistance. Consumer products range from toys and kitchenware to sporting goods and clothing. Engineering plastics such as PET, nylon, PMMA, and PTFE are used in a broad spectrum of consumer products due to their light weight, abrasion resistance, dimensional stability, chemical resistance, and UV resistance. What Is the Hardest Engineering Plastic? Which engineering plastic is judged to be the hardest depends on the measurement method used and the exact condition of the material. PMMA (acrylic) is the hardest engineering plastic as measured on the Shore D scale (Shore D 99) and on the Rockwell D hardness scale (105). Are Engineering Plastics Strong? Yes, engineering plastics are strong. They are specifically formulated to have high tensile strength and impact strength compared to standard commodity plastics such as polypropylene or polyethylene. What Is the Difference Between Engineering Plastics and Commodity Plastics? Engineering plastics are polymeric materials designed and formulated to have specific properties and to satisfy the requirements of various high-performance applications. They typically have enhanced mechanical, thermal, and chemical properties compared to commodity plastics. Commodity plastics are general-purpose plastics that do not need to satisfy stringent technical requirements. Commodity plastics are used for everyday items from toys and packaging to disposable plates and cutlery. While both engineering plastics and commodity plastics are useful in their own right, they are intended to satisfy vastly different purposes. To learn more, see our full article on Engineering Plastics vs Commodity Plastics . Most engineering plastics are poor electrical conductors which makes them ideal for applications where electrical insulation is desired, such as in various electronic and wiring applications. 5. Flammability Flammability is a material’s tendency to catch fire. Engineering plastics have varying levels of flammability depending on the particular type of engineering plastic. Some engineering plastics, such as PEEK or PPS, are specifically formulated for flame resistance and ignition prevention while other engineering plastics<dynamic-value> ABS, are flammable. Engineering plastics that are non-flammable are exceptional for use in applications where ignition is a concern such as in chemical processing. 6. Food Compatibility Food compatibility refers to a material’s safety for use with food, specifically in packaging. Some engineering plastics, such as PET, POM, PMMA, and ABS, are safe for use with food due to their chemical structure and lack of additives, dyes, and other harmful products. Others, for example, polycarbonate, are not safe. 7. Impact Strength Impact strength is a material’s ability to resist deformation due to a sudden or intense application of load, also known as a shock load. Impact strength is a critical property that characterizes how well a material can withstand sudden forces. Compared to commodity plastics, many engineering plastics exhibit high impact strength, which makes them good for load-bearing applications that are subjected to varying impact forces, such as machine guards and electronic housings. 8. Min/Max Operating Temperature (Thermal Resistance) Thermal resistance is the property that characterizes a material’s ability to resist changes in its properties due to varying temperatures. Specifically, the low temperature at which materials become brittle and the high temperature at which materials become soft and even melt. Engineering plastics have varying degrees of thermal resistance depending on the type of plastic. For instance, PEEK is specially formulated for use in high-temperature environments (up to 250 °C). High-temperature environments where plastics are used include various machinery and industrial applications. 9. Sliding Properties The sliding, or anti-friction, properties of engineering plastics make the materials more wear-resistant and abrasion-resistant compared to commodity plastics. Engineering plastics notably have a low coefficient of friction which enables these properties to be possible. The sliding properties of engineering plastics make them ideal for applications where repeated sliding, rubbing, or scraping are common such as in machinery components like wear pads, bearings, gears, pulleys, and rollers or medical applications like hip implants. 10. Ultraviolet (UV) Light Resistance UV resistance refers to a material’s ability to resist degradation and discoloration due to exposure to ultraviolet rays from sunlight and other sources. UV rays can break down polymer chains and cause chemical changes within the material. UV resistance is important for engineering plastics because it enhances their ability to be used outside or in other UV exposure-intense environments. Many engineering plastics, particularly polyamides, PMMA, and Ultem®, exhibit outstanding UV resistance, which makes them able to be used in environments with constant UV exposure. 11. Water Absorption Water absorption refers to a material’s affinity to absorb water. Engineering plastics are water-resistant and do not easily allow water to penetrate into the material. This makes engineering plastics ideal for applications where water contact is common. To learn more, see our full article on Common Types of Engineering Plastics. What Are the Different Types of Engineering Plastics? There are numerous types of engineering plastics which are listed and described below: 1. Nylon 6 Nylon 6 is a specific grade of nylon, or polyamide, material. Nylon 6 has good stiffness, toughness, electric and thermal insulation properties, and mechanical strength. Its properties can further be enhanced with glass fiber and other compounds. Nylon 6 is used for forming dies, insulators, washers, rollers, pulleys, valve seats, and more. 2. Polyethylene Terephthalate (PET) PET is a popular type of engineering plastic known for its high strength, chemical resistance, and recyclability. A type of polyester, PET is used in applications like textiles, food and beverage containers, pill bottles, and more. An illustration a PET bottle 3. Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene (ABS) ABS is another preferred type of engineering plastic that is valued for its chemical and thermal stability, strength, toughness, and glossy finish. Its host of desirable properties make it a versatile material. It is used in everything from consumer products like toys and bicycle helmets to automotive applications such as interior trim pieces, housings for electronics, and more. To learn more, see our guide on Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene . Try Xometry's Instant Quoting Engine® Test-drive a sample part to get instant pricing and DFM analysis Launch Demo A sample of Xometry's ABS material. 4. Nylon 6-6 Nylon 6-6 is another type of nylon (or polyamide) material. It has the same properties as nylon 6 but has a greater range of operating temperatures (up to 103 °C before deformation begins) and chemical resistance compared to Nylon 6 . Nylon 6-6 is used in applications such as conveyor belts, clothing and other textiles, bearings, bushings, sprockets, electronic housings, and more. 5. Polyimides Polyimides (PI) are formed by the combination of aromatic dianhydrides and aromatic diamines. This particular combination of chemicals yields a polyimide material with excellent thermal stability, high tensile strength, and good chemical resistance. These properties enable polyimides to be used in environments with temperature extremes up to 370 °C, in applications such as fuel cells, insulating coatings, structural adhesives, and more. 6. Polyether Ether Ketone (PEEK) PEEK stands out from other engineering plastics due to its wide range of operating temperatures (up to 250 °C), outstanding chemical resistance, high strength, and stiffness. PEEK is used for pump and valve components; bearings, bushings, and seals in machinery; electrical connectors; and medical device components. 7. Polyphenylene Sulfide (PPS) PPS is a high-performance, tough engineering plastic with great dimensional and thermal stability, as well as a wide operating temperature range of up to 260 °C and good chemical resistance. Moreover, PPS<dynamic-value> most other thermoplastics, is an electrical insulator. Its ability to be used at high temperatures coupled with its thermal stability makes PPS great for applications such as semiconductor components in machinery, bearings, and valve seats. 8. Poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) PMMA, also known as acrylic, is a common type of engineering plastic that is valued for its optical clarity, high strength, impact resistance, and light weight. For these reasons, PMMA is commonly used as a glass substitute. Applications of PMMA include windows, signage, display cases and fixtures, machine guards, and more. 9. Polybutylene Terephthalate (PBT) PBT has properties similar to those of PET (polyethylene terephthalate). It is known for its dimensional stability, low moisture absorption, high strength, stiffness, and chemical, UV, and thermal resistance. It is commonly used in automotive fenders and interior trim pieces, power tool housings, and electrical enclosures. 10. Polyphenylene Oxide (PPO) PPO, exhibits low moisture absorption, has excellent electrical and thermal insulating properties, great dimensional stability, and can be used in temperatures up to 155 °C. PPO is used for automotive fenders, electronics housings, and medical instruments. 11. Polyamides (PA) Polyamides are a class of engineering plastic formed by chains of amide molecules. Nylons and aramids are both types of polyamides. Polyamides are known for their high strength, impact resistance, and dimensional stability, which makes them useful for a wide range of applications in various industries. From clothes and textiles to automotive trim pieces, to bushings and bearings in industrial machines, polyamides are a common type of engineering plastic. 12. Polycarbonates (PC) Polycarbonates are known for their optical clarity, chemical resistance, tensile and impact strength, fire resistance, and recyclability. Polycarbonates are used in applications such as: machine guards, CDs, motorcycle face shields and windscreens, electronics housings, signage, streetlamps, safety glasses, and more. Polycarbonate 3D printed part made by Xometry 13. Polyetherimide (PEI) ULTEM® PEI, also known by the popular brand name ULTEM®, is an engineering plastic valued for its mechanical strength, rigidity, creep resistance over a wide temperature range, and electrical insulation properties. PEI boasts the highest dielectric strength of any commercially available thermoplastic and is therefore commonly used in the electronics industry for fuses and coils. Additionally, it is used in the aerospace industry, where it is used for interior trim pieces. 14. Polyetherketoneketone (PEKK) PEKK is an engineering plastic with characteristics similar to those of PEEK. This is because PEEK and PEKK are both part of a group of thermoplastics known as polyaryletherketones (PAEK). For additive manufacturing applications, a PEKK 3D printer can produce parts that take advantage of the material’s mechanical strength, thermal stability, and chemical resistance. PEKK is characterized by good mechanical strength, thermal stability, and chemical resistance. Because of its mechanical strength and chemical resistance, PEKK is used in high-pressure pumps, gear wheels, propellers, orthopedic and dental implants, and more. 15. Polyetherketone (PEK) PEK is a type of PAEK engineering plastic that is known for its low thermal expansion coefficient, creep resistance, chemical resistance, low flammability, and mechanical properties over a broad temperature range up to 260 °C. These properties make PEK useful for applications where loads are applied at high temperatures for an extended time such as in gears, bushings, bearings, shafts, and more. PEK is used in the aerospace, machinery, and automotive industries. 16. Polyketone (PK) Polyketone is an engineering plastic that is a type of PAEK. PK has high impact strength — about two to three times higher than nylon or PBT — and has excellent wear and chemical resistance. Its wear and chemical resistance make PK often used in the automotive, oil and gas, and chemical industries. 17. Polyoxymethylene Plastic (POM / Acetal) POM, also known as acetal or Delrin®, is one of the most popular engineering plastics due to its high strength, toughness, elasticity, dimensional stability, excellent machinability, impact strength, low friction coefficient, and chemical resistance. Acetal is used in everything from gears, pulleys, and rollers to snap fasteners like zippers and buckles due to its abrasion resistance and high strength. 18. Polysulfone (PSU) PSU is a translucent engineering plastic that is known for its food compatibility, biocompatibility, wide service temperature range of up to 160 °C, and good mechanical properties. PSU is used in the medical and food preparation industries due to its bio-friendliness for applications like manifolds in food processing or medical trays. 19. Polytetrafluroethylene (PTFE / Teflon®) PTFE is a popular engineering plastic known for its versatile properties. These properties include: broad temperature range from -240 °C to 260 °C and low moisture absorption, low coefficient of friction, flexibility, and chemical resistance. PTFE is used in many different applications, such as wiper blades, cookware, pipes for high-purity chemical processing, nail polish, and more. What Are the Most Common Types of Engineering Plastics? Different sources will list different engineering plastics as being the most common types. The list below was chosen based on which engineering plastics are most widely used across the largest variety of industries. PET: PET is a type of polyester with a broad range of uses such as: clothing, textiles, food and beverage containers, and pill bottles. PET is widely available, cheap to manufacture, easy to recycle, and has excellent mechanical properties. However, its low heat resistance, tendency to oxidize, and low biodegradability limit the applications where PET can be used. ABS: ABS is used in many different applications — from consumer components and automotive components to electronic devices of all kinds. ABS is inexpensive and plentiful, strong, lightweight, ductile, and thermally stable. However, ABS has poor resistance to fatigue, is flammable, and has a lower melting point compared to other engineering plastics. PC: Polycarbonate is used in applications such as machine guards, automotive headlamps, windows, safety glasses, and more. It is a fire-resistant material that is also lightweight, thermally insulating, strong, and fully recyclable. However, PC is sensitive to scratches and has a high coefficient of thermal expansion. How Does Plastic Engineering Work? Plastic engineering is a branch of engineering that focuses on the design and development of plastic materials and products. The boundaries of plastic engineering range from research and development in chemical laboratory settings to the plant floor where the process parameters for plastic machinery such as injection molding machines and plastic extruders are studied and optimized for a particular product. The purpose of plastic engineering is to create and optimize new plastic materials from organic polymers that are either petrochemical-based or naturally occurring. These plastic materials are synthesized via chemical reactions and are created to satisfy specific needs and applications. What Are the Advantages of Engineering Plastics? Engineering plastics have several advantages over commodity plastics, such as: Possess enhanced mechanical properties, such as improved tensile strength, impact strength, and toughness compared to commodity plastics’ properties Are lightweight and strong materials Exhibit a high degree of chemical resistance, making them great for applications where exposure to various oils, solvents, and chemicals is common Resist UV light damage (especially PMMA, ULTEM, and PTFE), making them reliable performers in outdoor environments What Are the Applications of Engineering Plastics? Listed below are some of the many applications of engineering plastics: Engineering plastics such as polycarbonate, ABS, nylon 6, and nylon 6-6 are widely used in the automotive industry for components like dashboards, interior trim pieces, electronic component housings, fuel caps, door handles, and more. PEEK, polyimides, PAI, and PTFE are engineering plastics commonly used in the aerospace industry. Examples are: pump gears, valve seats, electrical insulators and housings, and more. Food and beverage containers and disposable trays and plates are commonly made from engineering plastics. PET is the engineering plastic most frequently used in food and beverage applications due to its strength, chemical resistance, UV resistance, food compatibility, and recyclability. Electronic components such as housings, switches, end terminals, insulators, displays, and more can be made from engineering plastics. Such engineering plastics as nylon 6, nylon 6-6, PC, PBT, ABS, and PEI are often used in the electronics industry due to their mechanical properties such as: tensile strength and impact resistance, electrical insulation properties, wide operating temperature ranges, and chemical resistance. Consumer products range from toys and kitchenware to sporting goods and clothing. Engineering plastics such as PET, nylon, PMMA, and PTFE are used in a broad spectrum of consumer products due to their light weight, abrasion resistance, dimensional stability, chemical resistance, and UV resistance. What Is the Hardest Engineering Plastic? Which engineering plastic is judged to be the hardest depends on the measurement method used and the exact condition of the material. PMMA (acrylic) is the hardest engineering plastic as measured on the Shore D scale (Shore D 99) and on the Rockwell D hardness scale (105). Are Engineering Plastics Strong? Yes, engineering plastics are strong. They are specifically formulated to have high tensile strength and impact strength compared to standard commodity plastics such as polypropylene or polyethylene. What Is the Difference Between Engineering Plastics and Commodity Plastics? Engineering plastics are polymeric materials designed and formulated to have specific properties and to satisfy the requirements of various high-performance applications. They typically have enhanced mechanical, thermal, and chemical properties compared to commodity plastics. Commodity plastics are general-purpose plastics that do not need to satisfy stringent technical requirements. Commodity plastics are used for everyday items from toys and packaging to disposable plates and cutlery. While both engineering plastics and commodity plastics are useful in their own right, they are intended to satisfy vastly different purposes. To learn more, see our full article on Engineering Plastics vs Commodity Plastics .
